  return { decision: 'APPROVE', reason_code: 'VALID_CONDITION' };
}

The order is deliberate. The verification-key check comes first: if the proof was made under the wrong key, nothing else in the envelope matters. Proof reuse comes second because it is the cheapest correct answer in the whole loop — a lookup in seenProofs, a Set of proof references from earlier tasks, before any proving work happens. About 11% of tasks are replays, per the tournament's trap documentation, and reuse is the only trap you cannot catch by looking at a single envelope in isolation: it needs memory. The remaining four checks are plain field comparisons — balance against minimum, current block against expiry, recipient against recipient, amount against cap — and if all of them pass, the condition is valid.

Two details worth copying exactly: compare addresses and hashes case-insensitively (hex casing varies between sources), and compare amounts and blocks as BigInt, not as JS numbers, so large values never lose precision.

For a worked example, use a clean envelope: public balance 1,460 against a minimum of 1,000, amount 500 against a cap of 1,000, expiry block 19,842,201 against a current block of 19,832,000, recipient matching. decide() returns APPROVE / VALID_CONDITION.

Step 4: Build the circuit input

The prover needs the same thirteen fields as circuit inputs. Eleven are copies of the envelope; two need a small transformation:

function buildInput(task, decision) {
  const salt = '0x' + crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex');
  return {
    registeredVkHash: task.registered_vk,
    proofVkHash: task.proof_vk,
    minimum: String(task.minimum),
    publicBalance: String(task.public_balance),
    expiryBlock: String(task.expiry_block),
    currentBlock: String(task.current_block),
    recipient: task.recipient,
    conditionRecipient: task.condition_recipient,
    amount: String(task.amount),
    maxTransfer: String(task.max_transfer),
    decision: decision === 'APPROVE' ? '1' : '0',
    taskId: taskIdToField(task.task_id).toString(),
    salt,
  };
}

The taskId is the keccak-256 hash of the task-id string, reduced modulo the BN128 field prime — a one-liner with js-sha3:

const FIELD_PRIME = BigInt('21888242871839275222246405745257275088548364400416034343698204186575808495617');
function taskIdToField(taskId) {
  const h = '0x' + keccak_256(Buffer.from(String(taskId), 'utf8'));
  return BigInt(h) % FIELD_PRIME;
}

The salt is fresh random 32 bytes per proof. Pass numbers as strings: snarkjs handles big values through strings, and it keeps you out of JS-number trouble. The decision bit is '1' for APPROVE and '0' for REJECT — the circuit enforces that the bit matches the checks, which is exactly what Step 6 tests.

Step 5: Prove and verify locally

Three snarkjs calls are the whole loop:

const { proof, publicSignals } =
  await snarkjs.groth16.fullProve(input, 'gatekeeper.wasm', 'gatekeeper_final.zkey');
const vk = await snarkjs.zKey.exportVerificationKey('gatekeeper_final.zkey');
const ok = await snarkjs.groth16.verify(vk, publicSignals, proof);

Run it on the clean envelope from Step 3, then on a trap: the same envelope with the proof key swapped for a different hash (0xaaaa…aaaa), which decide() rejects as VK_SUBSTITUTION — and which still gets a proof, because a REJECT decision is a claim the circuit can verify too. Here is what I measured on 15 November 2026, every number from the run:

Case Decision Prove time Proof size Local verify
Valid condition APPROVE 1,581 ms 724 bytes OK in 37 ms
VK-substitution trap REJECT 488 ms 722 bytes OK in 96 ms
Reused proof reference REJECT — (decision only) — —

The first proof took 1,581 ms because it is cold: it includes loading the wasm and the zkey. The second, with everything warm, took 488 ms. Both proofs verified locally against the verification key exported from the official zkey, Groth16/BN128, 13 public signals. The reused-proof case never reached the prover at all — the seen-set caught it at the decision stage. The practical takeaway: proving costs well under two seconds even cold, a small fraction of the 60-second budget per task. The cryptography is not the bottleneck; the checks are the work.

Step 6: The lie test

Now the test that justifies the whole exercise. Take the VK-substitution trap — a task your logic correctly rejected — and force the decision bit to APPROVE anyway:

await proveAndVerify(buildInput(trappedTask, 'APPROVE'));

If the circuit is doing its job, there is no valid witness for that claim, and witness calculation must fail. It does:

Error: Assert Failed. Error in template GatekeeperEvaluation_79 line: 102

A lie has no valid witness. The constraint system refuses to produce a proof for a decision the inputs do not support — not because the agent is honest, but because the arithmetic will not cooperate. Run this test yourself: it is the fastest way to confirm your loop is wired to the real circuit and not to a stub that would happily prove anything.

Three gotchas

The registered vkHash is not a plain keccak-256 of the verification-key JSON. I tried both the compact and pretty-printed forms. The platform's hashing scheme is undocumented, so do not try to recompute the hash — take the value from /api/circuit-info as given and compare against it. The key itself is genuine: it comes from the official zkey, and proofs generated against it verify.

The seen-set must live across tasks. If you create a fresh Set per task, reuse detection silently stops working and replays sail through. Keep one set for the whole run (or the whole round) and add each proof reference after deciding.

Fail closed by construction. The check order in Step 3 already does this: anything unrecognized or unparseable should fall through to a REJECT, never to an APPROVE. A gatekeeper that approves on uncertainty is a gatekeeper waiting for its first wrong APPROVE.

Where this stops

You now have a loop that decides, proves, and verifies — locally, against the tournament's real circuit. What it is not: a live endpoint, a scored round, or a finished entry. The arena requires a public HTTPS endpoint the platform can reach, and that is a separate build (for me, still an open problem: the machine I work on has no public IP). But the loop is the part you can perfect offline, and every trap in the tournament is decided here, in decide(), long before any proof is generated.

I registered for the tournament as handle saimlu via wallet sign-in (SIWE) using an EOA wallet. If you reproduce this loop and find a trap case I missed, or a cleaner way to build the input, that is exactly the kind of thing the Creator Track is for — write it up.

Links

  • Agent Games: https://agentgames.zkverify.io
  • Builder Field Guide: https://agentgames.zkverify.io/build
  • Proof Gatekeeper track: https://agentgames.zkverify.io/events/proof-gatekeeper
  • Circuit info (official artifacts): https://agentgames.zkverify.io/api/circuit-info
  • snarkjs: https://github.com/iden3/snarkjs
  • Circuit-interface probing credited to @rday98's public repo.

title: What Is an Agent-Native Operating System?
description:
"AI operating system" has quietly become one of the most overloaded phrases in software. It
gets stuck on chat apps, on developer frameworks, on browser extensions, on anything with a
language model somewhere inside it. So it's worth being precise about what an agent-native
operating system actually is — because the distinction isn't marketing, it's architectural,
and it changes what the software can promise you.

The one-line version: AI as the OS, not AI on the OS. In an agent-native OS, the agent
is the interface you log into, and the traditional desktop — the compositor, the window
manager, the app model, the tray of background daemons — is gone, not decorated. This post
lays out what that means, how it differs from the AI features being bolted onto everything
else, and why the operating-system layer is the right place for it.

Start with what today's OS is actually for

Look at where a modern desktop spends its budget — RAM, CPU, attention, attack surface. Almost
all of it goes to helping a human drive a fleet of applications with a mouse and keyboard:
a compositor to draw overlapping windows, a window manager to arrange them, an application
model so programs can be launched and switched, and a constellation of background services to
keep it all humming. For forty years that was exactly right. The human was the intelligence in
the loop; the machine's job was to render windows and get out of the way.

An agent inverts that arrangement. The agent is now the thing doing the driving — perceiving,
deciding, acting. But it's being asked to drive through an interface built on the assumption
that a careful human is at the wheel. That mismatch is the whole reason "put an AI in the
sidebar" never quite feels like the future: you've added an intelligent driver to a car
designed to be driven by hand, and left all the manual controls in place.

The three things that make an OS "agent-native"

An agent-native OS isn't a desktop with an assistant added. It's a different set of primitives.
Three properties separate the real thing from the retrofit.

1. The agent is the surface, not a feature. You log in from your display manager into the
OS itself and talk to the agent. There's no launcher, no grid of app icons, no "open the
assistant" step — because there's nothing else to open. The agent is what you're using. That's
the literal meaning of agent-native: the agent is native to the system, not hosted by it.

2. Delivery windows replace application windows. When the agent does work, it renders that
work into typed panes, cards, and streams it opens, fills, and closes as it goes — delivery
windows, not application windows you operate.
You're watching work be delivered, not driving a toolbar. The unit of the interface shifts from
"an app you run" to "a result the agent produces."

3. Authority is brokered, not ambient. This is the deepest difference and the easiest to
miss. On a normal OS, a program acts with the ambient authority of whoever launched it — if
you can do it, the program can do it, up to and including a raw shell and sudo. That's
tolerable when a careful human is deciding what runs. It's the whole problem when the thing
deciding is a probabilistic model that can be wrong or manipulated. An agent-native OS instead
routes every consequential action through a typed capability
broker with a default-deny policy:
the agent presents a token for exactly the authority a task needs, and holds nothing more. The
shell never bypasses it. (Why that belongs in the OS, not the
app.)

What you get when those three hold

Those primitives aren't ends in themselves — they're what make a set of otherwise-unreasonable
promises actually keepable:

  • Inspectable. Every plan, tool call, approval, and result is logged, timestamped, and replayable. Agent work stops being write-only.
  • Trustworthy. No raw shell, no raw sudo; consequential actions pass the broker. Least privilege and containment are properties of the system, not promises of an app.
  • Local-first. The default is a model on your own machine, with hosted models on tap rather than on the critical path — so your files and context don't have to leave to get work done.
  • Durable. Sessions survive a reboot. The record of what happened is still there tomorrow.

Notice that every one of those is a statement about the environment the agent runs in. You
cannot bolt them onto an app, because the app doesn't control the environment — the OS does.
That's the argument for doing this at the operating-system layer instead of as one more
assistant in one more sidebar.

How it differs from the things it gets confused with

  • An AI assistant / copilot is an application that runs on your OS and helps you drive other applications. Useful, but it inherits the desktop's assumptions and its ambient authority. Agent-native means there's no "other applications" tier to drive.
  • An agent framework or SDK is a toolkit for developers to build agents. It's a library, not the system you log into. An agent-native OS is the runtime and the surface, not the scaffolding.
  • A chat app with tools is a conversation with function-calling attached. It has no OS-level authority model, no durable session at the system level, and no replaceable desktop — the three things that define the category.

If a product keeps the app model and adds intelligence, it's AI on the OS. If it deletes the
app model and makes the agent the system, it's AI as the OS. Only the second is agent-native.

Being honest about the phase

Categories get oversold, so here's the phase-honest version. Building this is staged. The
alpha replaces your desktop session — you log into the agent-native OS instead of GNOME or
KDE — while your machine keeps its kernel. It ships the runtime, the typed broker, a reference
agentic shell, and a display-manager session entry, as a package on Debian/Ubuntu. The later,
larger step is a full distribution with the compositor and desktop stack gone at the image
level. We're building it in the open, in Rust, under Apache 2.0, and we'd rather describe the
destination precisely than pretend we're already standing on it.

So: an agent-native operating system is one where the agent is the surface, delivery windows
replace application windows, and authority is brokered instead of ambient — which together make
an inspectable, trustworthy, local-first, durable system possible. It's for people who'd rather
drive their machine through an agent than through a grid of app icons. Everything else in this
blog is a closer look at one of those pillars.

MagenticOS is built by Mutagenic Labs, LLC. Open source, Apache 2.0.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/what-is-an-agent-native-operating-system. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Testing AI Agents: Why Unit Tests Aren't Enough
description:
You ship a change to your agent's system prompt. You run the tests. They pass. You deploy.

Three days later, your support agent starts filing refund requests as generic support tickets. The prompts look fine. The code looks fine. Nothing broke — except the part that matters.

This is the testing gap in AI systems. Traditional unit tests are still essential, but they don't tell you whether your agent behaves correctly across the range of inputs your users will send.

You need something else: evaluation tests, or evals.

Why Unit Tests Aren't Enough

A unit test checks deterministic behavior:

expect(parse_date("march 20", today: Date.new(2026, 1, 15))).to eq("2026-03-20")

Call it a thousand times, get the same result a thousand times. Any deviation is a bug. (Note the pinned today: — without it, even this test changes answer on January 1st.)

An LLM call is different. It's a probabilistic system. Given the same input, it generates a likely output — not necessarily an identical one. Sampling parameters influence this behavior, and even with temperature: 0, hosted models can produce slightly different results between runs.

The naive approach — run the agent and assert its output — fails in two ways:

  • False failures: The output is semantically correct but formatted slightly differently. Your test breaks on a Tuesday.
  • False passes: The output passes your specific assertion, but the model has regressed on cases you never tested.

Unit tests can verify the code around an LLM. They cannot, by themselves, establish that the model behaves correctly. You have to evaluate it.

What You're Actually Testing

When an agent processes a message, there are three distinct things that can go wrong:

1. The noop decision. Did the agent correctly decide to act — or not act?

"cn u snd towles to rom 305 thx" → should trigger an action.

"👍" → should not.

Getting this wrong is expensive: false positives flood your backend with phantom events, while false negatives silently drop real requests.

2. The action type. Did the agent pick the right action from the allowed list?

"My order ORD-8832 arrived damaged" should produce support.refund.process, not support.ticket.create. Both are valid action types. Only one is correct.

3. Field extraction. Did the agent extract the right information from the message?

booking_ref: "AB1234"
new_date: "2026-03-20"

These are the values your backend acts on. A wrong date changes a booking to the wrong day. A missing order ID stalls a refund.

A single pass/fail assertion can't tell you which of these three failed.

The Eval Dataset

An eval suite starts with a labeled dataset. Each case represents a realistic input with an explicit expected output:

- id: h05
  tags: [typo]
  message: "i nee to chaneg my bokking to april 3rd plz ref XY789"
  expected:
    action_type: hospitality.booking.modify
    noop: false
    fields:
      booking_ref: "XY789"
      new_date: "2026-04-03"

One detail that bites later: "april 3rd" only means 2026-04-03 relative to a reference date. Pin that date and pass it to the agent on every run, or your expected values silently rot when the calendar moves.

The tags are important. You don't just want a pass rate — you want to know where the model struggles.

For example:

Tag What it tests
clean Well-formed messages — the baseline
typo Spelling errors, autocorrect, missing vowels
emoji Heavy emoji usage
multilang French, Spanish, German mixed with English
ambiguous Multiple valid interpretations
implicit Intent not stated directly
multi_intent Two requests in one message
noop Should produce no action
context Follow-up requiring previous conversation state

The ambiguous and implicit tags are often where gaps appear first.

"The room is too cold" — is this a room service request, or just a complaint? (ambiguous)

"I don't think I'll make it" — is this a cancellation? (implicit)

Clean examples almost always pass. The interesting failures are the ones that look like real user messages.

The Scoring Model

The runner iterates over every case, calls the agent, and evaluates its output across three axes.

For repeatability, we use temperature: 0. This reduces sampling variability, but does not guarantee identical outputs across runs, especially when using hosted APIs.

Here's a simplified evaluator:

def evaluate(expected, output)
  errors = []

  # Axis 1: noop detection
  expected_noop = expected["noop"] == true
  actual_noop = noop_output?(output)

  unless expected_noop == actual_noop
    errors << "noop: expected=#{expected_noop}, got=#{actual_noop}"
  end

  # Axis 2: action type
  unless expected_noop
    expected_type = expected["action_type"]
    actual_type = extract_action_type(output)

    unless expected_type == actual_type
      errors << "action_type: expected=#{expected_type}, got=#{actual_type}"
    end
  end

  # Axis 3: field presence
  if expected["fields"]
    check_fields(expected["fields"], output, errors)
  end

  { pass: errors.empty?, errors: errors }
end

def check_fields(expected_fields, output, errors)
  actual = output.fetch("fields", {})

  expected_fields.each_key do |name|
    value = actual[name]
    errors << "fields.#{name}: missing" if value.nil? || value.to_s.strip.empty?
  end
end

Notice what we don't do here: exact value matching on every field. We start by checking field presence.

Why? Because different representations can express the same information. For example, "march 20" and "2026-03-20" may represent the same date. Exact equality would require normalization rules for each field type.

But there's an important trade-off. A presence check won't catch a wrong date. It only catches missing information. For fields that directly influence business operations — dates, amounts, IDs — value validation is essential.

A practical approach is to start with presence checks, then add field-specific validation and normalization as the system evolves. The goal isn't to make every assertion complicated. It's to catch the failures that matter.

Why not use an LLM as a judge? Because the output here is structured: a noop flag, an action type, a set of fields. Deterministic checks are free, fast, and don't add a second source of variance. A judge earns its place when the output is free text.

Baselines and Regression Detection

After each run, save the results to a timestamped file:

spec/eval/results/
  20260307_baseline.yml
  20260308_224748_support_recheck.yml
  20260309_122811_gemini-2.0-flash.yml

The label matters. You're not looking at a single score — you're tracking a trajectory. (All runs in this article date from March 2026; model names and prices reflect that period.)

For example:

# 20260307_baseline.yml
scores:
  action_type: 95.8
  fields: 85.7

These scores become your behavioral baseline. Break them down by tag too: a global score hides most of the signal, and a drop on multilang alone tells you far more than a one-point dip overall.

Improve the system prompt? Run the eval. Scores hold or improve → good sign. Scores drop significantly, or a category that previously scored 100% starts failing → investigate.

Don't treat every small variation as a regression. Hosted models exhibit run-to-run variance, so measure it: run the same configuration a few times and note how much the scores move on their own. Anything inside that spread is noise.

The key discipline:

Always run the eval before merging a change that affects model behavior.

A diff on a YAML prompt file won't tell you if you just broke field extraction on multilingual inputs.

CI integration is useful, but optional. Running the suite consistently matters more than automating it immediately.

What the Failures Teach You

The first baseline surfaced 10 failures. The patterns were instructive.

Ambiguous cases fail predictably.

"The room is too cold" produced no action at all. The model wasn't confident enough to commit to hospitality.room_service.request without more signals.

This isn't necessarily a bug. It's a calibration question: do you want confident-only extractions or best-effort behavior?

Fields fail on implicit mentions.

"✅ driver karim delivered everything in nice 🏁"

The model got the action type right (operations.driver.update) but missed destination: Nice. "Nice" is a city, but also an adjective. Field extraction on ambiguous proper nouns is genuinely hard.

Cross-domain routing underperforms.

"Cancel my booking ref HT9921 and also where is my order ORD-5500?"

The expected behavior is to route to both the hospitality and the support domains. The model picked one. Multi-intent cross-domain routing is a difficult case: a single model call has to recognize and preserve multiple intents.

These failures tell you exactly what to work on next — and give you a metric to validate whether your fix actually worked.

As the system evolves, the dataset should evolve too. Add new cases from production failures, edge cases and unexpected user behavior. Otherwise, your eval suite gradually becomes a collection of examples the model already knows how to handle.

The Cost Argument

Here's what makes this approach sustainable:

98 cases × gpt-4o-mini = $0.0106

Just over one cent for a full behavioral evaluation suite, based on the model and pricing used for this run. You can run it after every prompt change, every model swap, or every meaningful pipeline update.

Want to evaluate a different model — say, switching from gpt-4o-mini to gemini-2.0-flash? Run the same dataset against both and compare:

# gpt-4o-mini
scores:
  action_type: 95.8
  fields: 85.7

# gemini-2.0-flash
scores:
  action_type: 94.1
  fields: 83.2

The honest reading: on this dataset, a 1.7-point gap on action type is one or two cases — well within run-to-run variance. These two models are equivalent here, so the decision comes down to cost and latency. That's still a useful answer, and one you couldn't get from a gut feeling.

The exact cost will depend on model pricing, input size and output tokens, but the point remains: a small, focused eval suite can be surprisingly cheap.

Unit Tests, Evals and Integration Tests

These three testing approaches solve different problems.

  • Unit tests verify that your deterministic code works: parsing, validation, permissions and business logic.
  • Evals measure whether the model produces the expected behavior across a representative dataset.
  • Integration tests verify that the generated output works correctly within the rest of your system.

None replaces the others. A correctly classified request doesn't guarantee that the resulting action will execute successfully. Likewise, a passing integration test doesn't prove that the model will classify the next 100 user messages correctly.

The Pattern

Distilled, the approach looks like this:

  1. Build a dataset of realistic inputs with tagged categories
  2. Define scoring dimensions, not just pass/fail
  3. Save results after every significant change
  4. Protect the baseline and measure run-to-run variance
  5. Add new cases from real failures and edge cases
  6. Use the results to prioritize what to fix next

No framework required. It's a dataset, a runner, and a disciplined habit of checking model behavior before shipping changes.

Traditional tests tell you whether your code works. Evals tell you whether your AI system does what you expect.

The teams that skip this often discover regressions only after a user reports them. By then, you don't know which change caused the problem, and you're debugging blind.

If your AI system is important enough to ship, its behavior is important enough to test.

title: The Sandbox Is the Wrong Unit for AI Agents
description:
Every serious agent product now ships with a sandbox. Container, VM, namespace, seccomp profile, a browser in a browser. The pitch is the same everywhere: the agent runs in there, so whatever it does, it can't hurt you.

That claim is true in exactly the way it was true for the programs sandboxes were built for, and false in the way that matters for agents. An AI agent sandbox protects the host from the process. It does not protect you from the agent's decisions, because the decisions are the product, and the sandbox was never designed to see them.

What a sandbox was built to answer

Process isolation answers one question well: what can this program touch? Namespaces decide which filesystem, network, and process tree the program sees. Seccomp decides which system calls it may make. A container image decides which binaries exist at all. Draw the box, drop the program in, and the box holds regardless of what the program does inside it.

That model has an assumption baked so deep that nobody says it out loud: the program's behaviour is fixed before it runs. You know what ffmpeg does. You know what the payment worker does. The sandbox exists because you don't fully trust the implementation, so you bound the blast radius of bugs and of hostile input. The intent is not in question; the code's fidelity to the intent is.

An agent inverts that. The implementation is fine. The intent is decided at runtime, one step at a time, by a model reading whatever landed in its context. The agent that was supposed to summarize a folder decides, three steps in, that the summary would be better if it also emailed the folder to the person it thinks asked for it. Nothing in that sequence is a bug. Nothing escaped. The sandbox held perfectly, and it held around the wrong thing.

The failure mode is not escape

Look at the agent incidents people actually report. The duplicate purchase after a timeout. The repository force-pushed over. The calendar cleared because "reschedule" was read as "remove." The support reply that promised a refund the policy doesn't allow. The file shared with the whole org instead of one person.

Not one of these is a sandbox escape. Every one of them was a permitted action, taken by a process inside its box, using credentials that were legitimately available to it, doing something the box was never asked to prevent. Isolation was never the control that would have caught them, because isolation controls reach, and these were failures of judgment within reach.

That is the quiet compromise: we have accepted "it can't get out" as a proxy for "it won't do the wrong thing," when the two are not even about the same layer. The first is a property of the process. The second is a property of each action.

Why the box is the wrong size

Try to fix this with the sandbox and you find out why it is the wrong unit.

It is all-or-nothing per process. A sandbox grants the process a set of reach at start-up. Either the network is there or it isn't; either the directory is mounted or it isn't. An agent that needs to read one file to plan and write one different file to finish does not have a per-process shape. Its needs are per-step, and they are not known before the process starts. So the box gets drawn around the union of everything the agent might need, which is the same thing as not drawing a box.

It has no notion of intent. The sandbox sees a connect() and a write(). It cannot distinguish the email the user asked for from the email the agent decided to send. Both are the same syscall on the same socket. The information that would separate them, what the user requested and what the agent is trying to accomplish, exists only in the agent's context, which the sandbox cannot read and should not trust anyway.

It does not know who is acting. Inside the box there is one process identity. It does not carry "on behalf of whom" or "under which task." So there is nothing to revoke when a task ends, nothing to scope when a task begins, and nothing in the record afterwards that says which decision produced which side effect. The box's own logs, if any, say a process did a thing.

It leaks around the edges by design. Agents are useful precisely because they touch the systems we care about: mail, calendars, repositories, payment APIs, the actual filesystem. The sandbox that genuinely prevented all of that would be a sandbox around a toy. So every real deployment punches the holes the agent needs, and the holes are where the incidents happen.

None of this means sandboxes are bad. They are still the right answer to their own question. Run agent tool code in one; keep the blast radius of a bad dependency small. But defence-in-depth around the process is not the same as a control on the action, and calling the first the second is how teams end up with an incident report that says "the sandbox worked" on the same page as "the customer was charged twice."

The unit that fits is the action

If the agent's behaviour is decided one step at a time, then the boundary has to be checkable one step at a time. The unit of isolation for an agent is not the process. It is the action: this operation, on this resource, on behalf of this principal, under this task, right now.

That reframing changes what the questions are:

  • Not "can this process reach the network?" but "may this action send this message to this recipient?"
  • Not "is the directory mounted?" but "may this task write this file, and is that write the one the plan said it would make?"
  • Not "which user is the process running as?" but "which task is asking, on whose authority, and will the record show it?"

Answering those requires three properties that a per-process sandbox structurally cannot supply. Authority has to be typed and granted per action rather than per process, default-deny, so that "read one file" and "send one email" are different grants rather than the same open door. Every action has to pass through a single point that can see the request, not the syscall, so that intent-level checks are even possible. And the point that mediates the action has to write the record, so that what happened is attributable to a task and a decision, not to a process ID.

Those are operating-system responsibilities. Not because the OS is the only place they could live, but because it is the only place that sees every action regardless of which app, framework, or model produced it. A framework can add a permission prompt to its own tool calls. A model provider can add a refusal. Neither sees the action the other one took, and neither is still in the loop when the agent shells out to a script that does the real work. The layer beneath all of them is.

What this looks like from the outside

Picture the same "summarize a folder" task in an arrangement where the action is the unit. The task starts with authority to read that folder and write one summary file, and nothing else. Three steps in, the agent decides to email the folder. That decision is not blocked by a rule in a prompt; there is simply no grant that covers it, so the action cannot be issued. If the user wants it, the grant is a deliberate, visible act, scoped to that task, and it expires when the task does. Afterwards the record shows the reads, the one write, and the attempted send that had no authority, each tied to the task that produced it.

Nothing about that requires the model to be better behaved. It requires the surrounding system to stop treating the process as the thing it trusts or distrusts, and start treating each action as the thing it decides about.

Where we are with it

We are building toward exactly this arrangement, and we are in alpha. The honest description of the alpha is a runtime with a typed capability layer and a reference shell, running local-first, with the sandbox still present underneath as defence-in-depth rather than as the control. Much of what a mature system would do at the action boundary is still ahead of us, and some of what we have is rough. What is settled is the unit. Draw the box around the process and you have protected the host from the code. Draw it around the action and you have protected the person from the decision. Agents are made of decisions.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/sandbox-is-the-wrong-unit-for-ai-agents. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Capability-Based Security for AI Agents
description:
Ask yourself what an AI agent on your machine is actually allowed to do. Not what you'd like it to do — what the system will permit if the agent tries. On almost every setup in use today, the honest answer is: whatever you're allowed to do. The agent runs inside a process that runs as you, and "you" is a very large grant. Capability-based security for AI agents is the argument that this is the wrong trust model at its root — that an agent should start with the authority to do nothing, and receive narrow, typed, revocable grants for exactly the actions its task requires. It's an old idea in operating systems research. The actor it was waiting for has finally arrived.

The app-permission model assumes a human is driving

The permission model everyone actually lives under was designed around two comfortable assumptions: the unit of trust is the application, and the entity driving it is a person.

So the questions the system asks are app-shaped and person-shaped. "Allow this app to access your files?" "Allow this app to use the network?" You answer once, usually at install time, usually yes, and the grant persists forever at the granularity of an entire program. From then on, the app operates with what security people call ambient authority — it doesn't present credentials for each action; it simply acts, and the system checks whether you could have done it. Since you can do nearly everything, so can it.

This was always a coarse arrangement, but it held together because of the second assumption: a human was in the loop, clicking each button, more or less aware of what was happening. The app's authority was broad, but its actions were throttled by human attention. The grant was the size of a barn door, and a person walked through it one step at a time.

The actor changed. The model didn't.

Now put an agent in the driver's seat and watch both assumptions fail at once.

An agent is not throttled by human attention — issuing actions at machine speed is its entire value. And an agent is not a fixed program whose behavior you can audit once and trust forever; it's a probabilistic system whose next action depends on its context, which includes text it read five minutes ago from a source you've never vetted. The security community has a growing catalog of what follows — OWASP's Top 10 for LLM applications puts prompt injection and "excessive agency" near the top, and excessive agency is really just ambient authority wearing its new name.

The classic term for the resulting failure is the confused deputy: a program with legitimate authority tricked into using it for someone else's ends. Agents are the most confusable deputies ever built. They can be instructed by anything that can get words in front of them. Hand a confusable actor your full ambient authority and you haven't built an assistant-shaped tool; you've built a very fast intern with your keys, your badge, and a habit of taking directions from strangers.

The industry's current answer is supervision — watch every step, approve every action. That works, at the cost of the thing you wanted, which was delegation. All-or-nothing trust gives you exactly two settings: babysit, or hope. Neither is a security model. Both are coping strategies for a permission system that has no vocabulary for the thing we're now asking it to govern.

What capability-based security gets right

Capability systems invert the model's core assumption. Instead of an actor carrying broad ambient authority checked against an identity, authority lives in capabilities: unforgeable tokens that each designate a specific resource together with specific rights over it. If you hold the capability, you can perform the action. If you don't, there is no action to attempt — the request isn't denied so much as impossible to express.

Three properties follow, and each one lands directly on the agent problem.

Default-deny. An actor begins with nothing. Every authority it holds was explicitly granted, which means the complete answer to "what can this agent do?" is "here is the list of what it was handed" — a list you can read, rather than a subtraction problem over everything your account can reach. Least privilege stops being an aspiration written in a policy document and becomes a structural fact.

Typed grants. A capability isn't "disk access." It's append to this log, read this directory, send to this address. The grant carries its own meaning, narrow enough that granting it doesn't require faith. This matters enormously for a probabilistic actor: you don't have to predict everything the model might be talked into wanting. You bound what any of it can touch.

Bounded blast radius. When a capability-held agent is confused — and phase-honesty requires saying when, not if — the damage is limited to the authority in its hands. Prompt injection against an agent holding read-access to one folder and append-access to one file is an incident. The same injection against an agent holding your ambient authority is a career event.

None of this is new. Dennis and Van Horn described capabilities for multiprogrammed systems in 1966, and capability operating systems have been built, verified, and largely ignored by the mainstream ever since — because for fifty years the mainstream actor was a human, and humans found ambient authority convenient. It was the right design waiting for a problem painful enough to justify it. Autonomous, injectable, machine-speed actors are that problem.

This has to live at the OS layer

Here's the part that can't be papered over with a framework. Capability discipline is only as strong as the layer that enforces it. A capability system implemented inside an agent framework is a polite fiction: the framework can refuse to offer a dangerous tool, but the process underneath still holds your ambient authority, and anything that escapes the framework's abstractions — a shell command, a subprocess, a clever path — inherits all of it. That's not defense. That's a sign that says "please."

For grants to mean anything, denial has to be enforced below every route the agent can take, which is the same structural argument we've made about why agent trust belongs in the operating system: containment is a property of the environment the actor runs in, not of the actor's good manners. This is the arrangement MagenticOS is built around, and it's already on the public record: every consequential action passes a typed capability broker — no raw shell, no raw sudo. Default-deny isn't a mode you enable. It's the floor.

Capabilities also compose with the other properties an agent-native operating system owes you. A grant you can enumerate is a grant you can audit, which is half of what makes agent work inspectable rather than write-only: the record of what an agent did means more when it sits beside the list of what it could have done. Trust you can state, next to actions you can replay.

The phase-honest caveat, as always: MagenticOS is in alpha, targeting 2026-12-07, and an alpha is a beginning, not a verdict. The claim in this post is not "we have solved agent security." The claim is that the trust model is decided at the foundation, and we think this is the right foundation — visibly, in the open, where the argument can be checked against the code.

The takeaway

The app-permission model isn't wrong because anyone blundered. It's wrong because it encodes assumptions — trusted program units, human-speed actions, attention as the throttle — that agents void completely. Patching it with more prompts and more supervision just relocates the problem to your patience.

Capability-based security replaces the unanswerable question "do you trust the agent?" with one that has an actual answer: what did you hand it? Default-deny by default, typed grants, blast radius you chose in advance. That question belongs in the operating system, because that's the only layer positioned to enforce the answer. Sixty years after the idea was written down, it finally has its actor.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/capability-based-security-for-ai-agents. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: What a lead agent actually hands to a specialist
description:
Most "multi-agent" systems are one agent with a scratchpad. The lead writes a note to a helper, the helper answers once, the note is thrown away, and the next task starts from nothing. That is not delegation. It is a function call with a personality.

Real delegation has a boundary you can point at: a short brief that goes out, a report that comes back, and a rule about when the lead is allowed to say the job is finished. Get those three right and the rest is plumbing. Get them wrong and you have built a system that confidently reports work nobody did.

I write for AgentParley, a hosted crew of specialist agents, so read the product parts knowing that. The mechanism below is what I would build into anything that delegates, including a system with no vendor in it.

The problem in one sentence

A specialist that inherits the parent's whole conversation inherits the parent's confusion, the parent's token bill, and the parent's permissions — and then reports back into a context nobody can audit.

What actually crosses the boundary

A brief, not a transcript. Four fields, and the discipline is in what you leave out:

  • The job, in one or two sentences. What "done" looks like, not the story of why it matters.
  • The inputs it needs, by reference. A file path, a URL, a row ID, a query. Not a pasted copy of the parent's reasoning — a pointer the specialist can resolve itself.
  • The constraints that bind it. Budget, deadline, format, and the things it must not do.
  • Where the answer goes. A named destination, so the report has somewhere to land that is not "back into the chat".

Everything else stays with the lead. The parent's conversation is not context, it is history — and history is what makes a prompt expensive and a decision hard to trace.

The reason is not tidiness. A specialist with a narrow brief can run on a cheap model, because the job is narrow. A specialist handed the whole conversation needs the parent's model to understand the parent's mess. Per-agent models only pay off if the briefs are actually short.

Named specialists are not anonymous workers

The difference between a helper and a colleague is what persists. A named specialist has its own model, its own tools, and its own permissions — and those are set by you, not inferred by the lead at runtime.

That is where the security boundary lives. The agent that reads the web should not be the agent that holds SSH access to your servers. If every helper inherits the parent's reach, then the widest permission in the system is the permission of every task in the system. Narrowing a specialist's tools is not a nicety; it is the only thing that keeps a prompt injection in a fetched page from becoming a command on a host.

Parallel is a scheduling property, not a slogan

Delegation only buys you speed if the lead hands out several pieces before waiting for any of them. That means the lead's own loop has to be able to hold open work: dispatch, keep planning, collect.

Two things have to be true for that to be safe. First, the number of things running at once is a limit you set, and work over the limit waits its turn rather than failing. Second, a waiting specialist must not be spending anything — an agent blocked on a colleague, a timer or a build should make no model calls at all. Parallelism that bills while idle is just a faster way to spend.

Specialists talk to each other, and that is the hard part

The interesting case is not lead-to-specialist. It is specialist-to-specialist: the researcher finds that the budget question depends on a date the numbers agent already knows, and asks it directly instead of routing through the lead.

For that to work, the pair needs a conversation that outlives one task. If every exchange is a one-off message, the second question starts from zero and the answer is worse. A standing thread between two named colleagues is the difference between asking a coworker and filing a ticket.

It also needs a rule about who may talk to whom. A free-for-all between agents is a permission-escalation path with extra steps. Each agent needs a list — everyone, a short list, or nobody — and a specialist that holds sensitive access should be reachable only by its lead and its crewmates. Messages between agents are the place to hook a filter too: a plugin that sits on that traffic can redact secrets, add a guardrail or stop a message outright, which is the only enforcement point that sees what one colleague tells another.

The report, and the rule that makes it mean something

A report is not a summary of effort. It is the answer, plus enough evidence for the lead to check it: what was done, what was found, what is uncertain, and where the artefact is.

Then the rule that separates a crew from a pile of agents: the lead does not call the job done while a report is outstanding.

This has to be enforced by the runtime, not requested in a prompt. A model asked politely to wait will, under pressure, decide it has enough and answer. So the platform holds the lead's reply until every specialist it dispatched has reported, every open to-do item is closed, and no new message has just arrived. If a specialist fails, the lead is told rather than left waiting forever. If a specialist goes quiet, its last message is delivered anyway so the lead is never blocked on silence.

The same rule applies to the lead's own to-do list. An agent that writes itself a list and then declares victory with items still open has not finished; it has stopped.

A small illustrative handoff

Not a real incident — a sketch of the shape, so the fields are concrete:

lead → researcher
  job:         Find the three cheapest regions for this workload, one source per price.
  inputs:      shared/pricing.csv (rows 40-58); https://provider.example/regions
  constraints: this month's prices; no estimates; if a region has no public price, say so.
  report to:   shared/regions.md, then reply here with the three names and their sources.

researcher → numbers
  question:    Does the egress line in pricing.csv already include the per-GB rate?
  (the same standing thread as last week, so the earlier answer is already in it)

researcher → lead
  report:      Three regions found. Two have public prices; the third publishes only a floor.
               Written to shared/regions.md. The floor is the uncertainty - flagged, not guessed.

lead: waits. Does not answer the user until the report lands.

The point of the sketch is the third line of the report. A specialist that says "here is what I could not establish" is worth more than one that fills the gap, because the lead can act on a known gap and cannot act on a confident invention.

The honest limit

None of this makes a crew smarter than its briefs. A lead that splits a job badly will get three well-executed answers to the wrong three questions, in parallel, faster. The runtime can enforce that the lead waits, that permissions are narrow, and that reports are attributable. It cannot enforce that the plan was any good.

And the boundary costs something: a specialist that only sees its piece will sometimes miss a constraint the lead knew and did not write down. The fix is a better brief, not a bigger context window — but it is a real tax, and it is paid on every handoff.

The completion gate is the part people skip, and it is the one that decides whether your system's "done" means anything.

Disclosure

For AgentParley, these are platform properties rather than code you write: per-specialist models and permissions, colleague lists, the concurrency cap, and the completion gate. In your own system, you have to enforce them yourself.

The comparison that goes with this post, including the section on where self-hosting is the better pick:

https://agentparley.ai/openclaw-alternative

and the plans and limits:

https://agentparley.ai/

title: Projection maps of my website's RAG vectors, and what they could not tell me
description:
I wanted to see what the vectors behind my website's search actually looked like. This is a companion to a longer article on my site, which has the maps, the exact-neighbor comparison, the chunk diagnostics and a figure pack with the method notes. Here is the method and the two things I keep coming back to.

What I plotted

On 6 November 2026 I took a snapshot of the site's published index: 85 pages, split into 1,128 text chunks, each a 512-dimensional embedding from openai/text-embedding-3-small. I normalized each vector to unit length, kept the metadata aligned with its row and checked that all 85 sitemap pages were present. There were no empty chunks, no zero or non-finite vectors and no exact duplicate chunk bodies. The plots were calculated from the existing vectors; no new embeddings were generated.

I drew the index in two dimensions three ways. PCA gives a linear baseline, t-SNE emphasizes local neighborhoods, and UMAP builds its view from a neighborhood graph. The t-SNE example uses cosine distance, perplexity 30 and seed 42; UMAP uses cosine distance, 30 neighbors, minimum distance 0.1 and the same seed.

First, measure the map

Before reading anything into a cluster, I checked how much of the original neighborhood each map kept. For every point, I compared its ten closest neighbors on the map with its ten closest vectors in the original space.

Projection Ten nearest neighbors retained
PCA 13.1%
t-SNE 75.1%
UMAP 64.5%

These percentages measure the map's fidelity, not search accuracy. They describe these settings on this corpus, not a general ranking of the methods. What they told me is that the islands are places to investigate, and that their spacing and apparent size are not reliable semantic measurements. An isolated point might be a distinctive passage, an index page or an extraction problem, and only its text can tell those apart.

Then read the text behind the dots

I confirm a map's suggestion with exact cosine neighbors in all 512 dimensions, and then I read the chunks.

The strongest cross-page pair in the index had a cosine similarity of 0.944. Reading it showed repeated article listings on the Writing index and the MCP series page. The similarity was understandable; it was not evidence of two independently written passages reaching the same conclusion. That is why I read the text before treating a group as a topic or a pair as unwanted duplication.

The chunk diagnostics explain much of the map's shape. 81.4% of the ten nearest neighbors come from the same page: longer articles contribute more points, passages from one page often share a subject, and the embedding input includes the page title and heading path. The snapshot also has five chunks below 200 characters and 24 at the 1,500-character cap. Inspecting adjacent chunks on one page found a URL split after https://docs.strapi.io/cms/fea, with tures/admin-tokens) beginning the next chunk. That is a concrete boundary defect. Its effect on retrieval still needs testing.

What this is not

This is an inspection of a website retrieval index, not an evaluation of a complete RAG answering system. The site combines vector and keyword results, so the exact neighbors are vector similarities, not the site's search results. Before claiming retrieval quality, I would test representative questions against reviewed answer-bearing passages and compare the actual ranked results. The visual checks tell me where to look and what to test next.

The full article, with the figures and the method notes: https://pournasserian.com/writing/visually-validating-rag-vectors

title: The Engineers Called "Delta": How a Palantir Experiment Became AI's Hottest Job
description:
Picture a software company in the early 2010s with a strange problem: its software was powerful, its customers badly needed it, and almost none of them could actually use it.

The company was Palantir. Its customers were government agencies and large enterprises sitting on huge, messy, disconnected data, often in secure environments that no outside tool could simply plug into. Shipping a product and waiting for customers to figure it out wasn't going to work.

So Palantir did something unusual. Instead of keeping its engineers at headquarters, it sent them out to live with the customer.

The engineers called "Delta"

Internally, these engineers were known as Deltas, officially Forward Deployed Software Engineers. Their job was simple to describe and hard to do: sit with the customer, understand the real problem, and write whatever code it took to make the software work in that customer's world.

Palantir described the difference neatly: a normal product engineer serves many customers with one capability. A forward deployed engineer serves one customer with many capabilities.

It wasn't a side team. According to The Pragmatic Engineer, until around 2016 Palantir had more forward deployed engineers than "normal" software engineers. Some worked in air-gapped environments with no internet. One former FDE described working on the final assembly line at Airbus.

For years, the model looked like a Palantir quirk. Then generative AI arrived.

History repeats itself

Fast-forward to the AI boom, and AI labs hit exactly the same wall Palantir did.

The models were astonishing in demos. But a model on its own doesn't reduce support tickets, process insurance claims or speed up a factory. It only creates value once someone connects it to a company's documents, systems, permissions and rules, and proves it works well enough to trust.

So the AI labs borrowed the playbook:

  • OpenAI built a forward deployed engineering team that started with a handful of engineers and expanded to cities including San Francisco, New York, London, Paris, Munich, Dublin, Tokyo and Singapore.
  • Anthropic said it planned to grow its applied AI team, which includes forward deployed engineers, fivefold.
  • Cohere and a long list of AI startups followed with FDE roles of their own.

The Financial Times reported that job listings for forward deployed engineers rose by more than 800% between January and September 2025. A job title that once belonged to one company had become one of the fastest-growing roles in tech.

What the job looks like today

The modern AI FDE does what the Deltas did, with a new toolkit. A typical engagement moves through four stages:

  1. Embed: spend time with the people doing the work and learn how things really happen.
  2. Scope: turn "we want AI" into one concrete, measurable problem.
  3. Prototype: build something rough in days and put it in front of real users.
  4. Production: make it secure, tested and reliable enough to keep running after you leave.

Along the way, an AI FDE builds retrieval (RAG) so the assistant answers from the client's own documents, agents that take actions only after human approval, secure connections into business systems, and evaluations that prove the system is good enough to launch.

And then comes the part most engineers underestimate: explaining all of it to a business leader in plain language, including where the AI is still uncertain.

Why this role is worth paying attention to

Most engineering roles ask you to be good at one thing. The FDE role asks for an unusual mix: solid coding, comfort with messy real-world data, product judgement, and the ability to earn a client's trust. That combination is rare, which is exactly why demand has outpaced supply.

The good news is that it's learnable. Most of the toolkit is open source, and the customer-facing skills come from practice, not credentials.

Where to start

If you're an FDE aspirant, check out Introduction to Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE). Instead of teaching tools in isolation, it follows a new FDE named Sam through one complete client engagement, building an AI assistant step by step with LangChain, LangGraph, MCP, LangSmith and FastAPI. Along the way you make the calls yourself in branching scenarios: whether to automate refunds, whether to launch after evaluation scores drop, and how to present results to a business leader. No paid API keys are needed to follow along.

The role Palantir invented to solve its own problem has become one of the best entry points into applied AI. The next Delta might be you.

Sources: The Pragmatic Engineer: What are Forward Deployed Engineers? · eWeek: OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere step up FDE hiring · PYMNTS: FDEs emerge as one of AI's fastest-growing jobs

— Team SkillMint

title: PLaMo 3 Translate 0.8B Gets Down to About 423MB of Weights
description:
An MLX version of PLaMo 3 Translate 0.8B, the smallest model in PFN's translation-focused LLM family, now has weights of only about 423MB. It is a mixed-quantization model called "mixed_3_4", published on Hugging Face by an individual converter.

Unless noted otherwise, every size, speed, and memory figure in this post is the converter's own measurement (Mac mini M2 Pro, 32GB, mlx-lm 0.32.2). The main measurements for the mixed_3_4 version are:

  • Weights: about 423MB
  • Decode speed: about 352 tok/s
  • Peak memory (MLX-managed): about 565MB

This follows my previous article, "Using PLaMo 3 Translate on a Mac". This time I cover how the mixed-quantization version is built, the measurement results, what to watch for when choosing it, and the license terms.

PLaMo 3 Translate and the available model versions

PLaMo 3 Translate is PFN's translation-focused LLM. It comes in four sizes (0.8B / 2B / 8B / 31B) and supports 53 languages. The weights were published on Hugging Face on 2026-11-05.

PFN's official announcement on X is below. It serves as a primary source for the release.

https://x.com/preferred_jp/status/2118134261912092801

Here are three sizes to use as reference points:

  • Official MLX-4bit version (0.8B): about 0.98GB of weights (from the comparison in the 4bit-compact model card)
  • The earlier uniform 4-bit version (4bit-compact): 501,002,761 bytes of weights, about 501MB
  • This mixed_3_4 version: about 423MB of weights

The size reported for the uniform 4-bit version varies by source. The model card says about 501MB (about 505MB for the whole repository), but the converter's X post says "480MB". I use the model card's figure in this article.

The converter's post that says "480MB" is here:

https://x.com/sizumita/status/2119360329264271441

As a check on conversion fidelity, the model card for the uniform 4-bit version reports a per-tensor cosine similarity of about 0.996 between the dequantized weights and the BF16 original. The card says this is within the range expected for 4-bit affine quantization.

The model card for the uniform 4-bit version is at the page below. It describes the uniform 4-bit configuration and provides reference quality scores.

https://huggingface.co/sizumita/plamo-3-translate-0.8b-mlx-4bit-compact

The mixed_3_4 version was converted from the BF16 original, and its weights are smaller than those of the earlier uniform 4-bit version.

Using different bit widths for different parts of the model

The mixed_3_4 version is based on PFN's pfnet/plamo-3-translate-0.8b (BF16, unmodified). The conversion used mlx-lm 0.32.2's mixed_3_4 recipe (mlx_lm convert --quant-predicate mixed_3_4).

According to the model card, the bits are allocated as follows:

  • 4-bit: lm_head, plus the first, the last, and every third down_proj across the layers
  • 3-bit: everything else
  • Quantization method: affine, group size 64
  • Average: 3.804 bits/weight

The uniform all-4-bit version comes to 4.501 bits/weight. The mixed_3_4 version keeps part of the model at 4-bit and drops the rest to 3-bit, which brings the average down to 3.804 bits/weight. The model card also says this allocation follows the same strategy as llama.cpp's Q4_K_M.

The vocabulary is not trimmed; all 107,520 tokens remain.

You can read the full model card at the page below, including the allocation details and the original wording of the measurement conditions.

https://huggingface.co/sizumita/plamo-3-translate-0.8b-mlx-mixed34

The quality metric is slightly lower on average

With a smaller model, you naturally wonder what happened to translation quality. The baseline is the uniform 4-bit version. The converter compared the two versions using chrF++ under the same conditions (greedy decoding). These are the converter's own measurements.

  • FLORES-200 devtest (en→ja / zh→ja / ko→ja, first 100 sentences in each direction): average 31.37 (4-bit version: 31.56)
  • NTREX-128 (four directions including ja→en, first 200 sentences in each direction): average 29.57 (4-bit version: 29.90)

The model card states that the NTREX-128 news sentences were used neither for the conversion nor for choosing the method.

The mixed_3_4 version therefore scores slightly lower on average on both datasets. The converter's post describes the performance as "almost unchanged", but the measured chrF++ averages are slightly lower on both datasets.

The converter's post announcing the mixed_3_4 version (2026-11-09) is here:

https://x.com/sizumita/status/2119694681982541828

For reference, the model card says the uniform 4-bit version scores an average chrF++ of 31.56 on FLORES-200, roughly on par with the BF16 original's reference value of 31.20. The card itself notes, however, that the comparison includes implementation differences, so it should be read as "no degradation".

Even when the metrics are close, the translations themselves change

One point is easy to miss. Because the precision allocation is different, the mixed_3_4 version produces translations that differ from the 4-bit version's.

Even when the average scores are close, the two models do not translate the same sentence into the same text. On NTREX-128, the converter counted the sentences whose translation matches the 4-bit version byte for byte, and the match is far from complete (the per-direction counts are in the paid document below).

  • If you need identical translations: the model card points you to the 4-bit version
  • If you prioritize speed and memory: the mixed_3_4 version is an option

Minimal steps to try it on a Mac

Following the model card, install mlx-lm with pip install mlx-lm, load the model with mlx_lm.load, and translate with generate.

The tokenizer uses custom code bundled in the repository, so loading requires specifying trust_remote_code. The supported translation directions are the same as the original model's, including translation from multiple languages into Japanese and from Japanese into multiple languages.

License terms to check before you use it

The mixed_3_4 version is a derivative model under the PLaMo Community License. The model card states explicitly that it is an unofficial conversion and does not imply PFN's endorsement or affiliation.

The terms by type of use are:

  • Non-commercial use: free
  • Commercial use: prior registration with PFN is required. Limited to users with annual revenue (sales or income in the most recent fiscal year) of 1 billion yen or less; above that, a separate license is required
  • Redistribution: you must include the license text, display "Built with PLaMo", and keep "PLaMo" in the model name (Article 4)

The original license text is at the page below. Consult it for the full terms governing commercial use and redistribution.

https://plamo.preferredai.jp/info/plamo-community-license-en

If you are considering commercial use or redistribution, read this original text before you start.

Compare them on the same sentences first

The measurements in this post come from a Mac mini M2 Pro (32GB) with mlx-lm 0.32.2.

If you try it yourself, load both the mixed_3_4 version and the 4-bit version, translate the same handful of input sentences with each, and compare. Seeing the speed and the translation differences side by side makes it easier to judge which one best suits your needs.

Get the complete measurement data and runnable code ($5)

This post covered the headline figures, the bit allocation, the average quality scores, and the license terms. The paid document adds the full side-by-side measurements, every per-direction chrF++ score, the byte-identical match counts, and the complete runnable Python example.

Get it on Gumroad

What's inside:

  • Full size, speed, memory, and load-time comparison against the uniform 4-bit version, plus the whole-process RSS note
  • All per-direction chrF++ scores for FLORES-200 and NTREX-128, with the 4-bit version's scores alongside
  • The per-direction counts of translations that match the 4-bit version byte for byte
  • The complete runnable Python code from the model card, with the trust_remote_code note

Originally published in Japanese on note. This English edition was translated and edited with AI assistance; all commands and measurements are unchanged from the original.

title: Your Agent Is Logged In as You
description:
Open the audit log of any system your agent touched last week. Your name is on every line.

Not the agent's. Yours. The GitHub commit is authored by you. The calendar invite came from you. The API call carried your token, the file was written by your user, the email went out from your address. If something in that list was wrong — sent to the wrong person, deleted from the wrong folder, retried three times against a non-idempotent endpoint — the record says a human did it, and the human is you.

This is not a misconfiguration. It is how nearly every agent stack in production works today, and almost nobody has decided it should be that way. It is simply the path of least resistance: the agent needed access, you had access, so it borrowed yours.

How the borrowing happens

Look at where an agent's authority actually comes from and the pattern is the same at every layer.

At the shell, the agent runs as your Unix user. It inherits your home directory, your SSH keys, your sudo rights, your cloud CLI sessions. Anything you can do from a terminal, it can do, and the process table shows your UID.

At the API layer, it holds your OAuth token. You clicked "Allow" once, in a consent screen that offered two options — everything or nothing — and the agent has been presenting that token ever since. The service on the other end cannot tell the difference between you and the thing acting as you. By design, it is not supposed to.

In the browser, it drives your logged-in session. Cookies, saved passwords, the tabs you left open. To every site it visits, it is you.

Each of these is defensible in isolation. The agent has to run as something; it has to authenticate as something. But stack them and you have built a system in which a non-human actor performs consequential actions across a dozen systems while every one of those systems records a person.

What breaks

The first thing that breaks is the question "who did this?" — which sounds academic until you are asking it at two in the morning.

A production incident happens. Something was changed. The change log names an engineer. The engineer says, truthfully, that they did not make that change; they were asleep; they had an agent running a maintenance task. Now you have a record that is wrong in the most load-bearing field a record has, and no way to know how many other entries in the log share the defect. Every incident review that follows starts with an investigation into whether the people named in the logs were actually there.

The second thing that breaks is revocation. When the agent does something it shouldn't — and we have written about why instructions are a weak control against that — the correct response is to pull its access. But it doesn't have any. It has yours. Revoking the token revokes you. Rotating the key locks you out. The only way to take authority away from the agent without taking it away from yourself is to have given it separate authority in the first place, and you didn't, because nothing offered to.

The third thing is scope. Because the agent borrows your identity, it borrows all of it. You did not give it permission to read your email so it could schedule a meeting; you gave it your Google session. The task needed one calendar write. The token grants everything you have ever been allowed to do. We've argued that authority should be granted per capability, narrow and typed; identity borrowing is the exact opposite — it is the maximally broad grant, made by default, to an actor that cannot be distinguished from you afterward.

The fourth thing is blame, and it is the one people feel first. When the record says you did it, you did it. Organizations run on their records. A compliance regime that asks "which individual authorized this transfer?" gets your name. A security review that asks "who accessed this data?" gets your name. Agents have been added to the system and accountability has not moved an inch — it still lands entirely on the human whose credentials happened to be lying around.

The delegation problem has a name, and a partial answer

None of this is new to identity people. Acting on someone's behalf is an old problem with real solutions. The OAuth token-exchange specification, RFC 8693, defines a way to mint a token that says "this actor is acting for this subject," so a downstream service can see both parties. NIST's digital identity guidelines are built around the idea that a subject is a distinct thing that can be identified, authenticated, and held to account.

The machinery for "the agent is a principal, acting on behalf of a person, with authority the person delegated" exists. So why does almost no agent stack use it?

Because every piece of it is optional, and it lives in the wrong place. It lives in each service, each API, each integration — which means it exists only where some team happened to build it, in whatever shape they happened to choose. One SaaS product has service accounts with scoped permissions; the next has a single personal token. The shell has no concept of "a process acting for a user" beyond sudo's one-line log entry. The browser has no concept of it at all. An agent that wants to be properly attributed has to negotiate a different arrangement with every system it touches, and the default when no arrangement exists is: borrow the human.

Attribution, like receipts, is a property you get from the structure of a system or you don't get at all. You cannot ask the agent to log who it is — that is an instruction, and instructions are not controls. You cannot rely on each downstream service to have built delegation — most haven't, and the agent's task doesn't wait for them to. The property has to be produced by whatever layer sits between the agent and every consequential action it takes, so that it is true everywhere, by construction, without anyone remembering to arrange it.

What the correct arrangement looks like

Strip the problem to its shape and the arrangement is not mysterious.

The agent is its own principal. It has an identity distinct from any human's. Logs that record it, record it. When it runs as a process, the process belongs to the agent; when it holds a credential, the credential names the agent.

Every action carries two names. The agent that acted, and the human on whose behalf it acted. Not one or the other — both. "Alice's deploy agent, acting for Alice" is a record you can reason about. "Alice" is a record that is wrong. "deploy-bot-7" with no link back to Alice is a record that cannot be held to anyone.

Authority is delegated, scoped, and separately revocable. The human grants the agent specific capabilities, not a copy of themselves. Pulling the agent's authority leaves the human's intact. Narrowing it to one calendar does not require trusting the agent with the inbox.

The arrangement is enforced at the point of action. Not in a policy document, not in a system prompt, not in the goodwill of each downstream service. Wherever the agent's intent becomes an effect on the world — a file written, a request sent, a command executed — that seam is where identity is attached and scope is checked. If every consequential action has to pass through one mediating layer anyway, that layer is where attribution belongs, because it is the only place that sees every action.

That last point is why we think this is an operating-system problem, not an application one. Applications can each solve it for themselves, and a few have. But the agent doesn't live in one application. It lives on the machine and reaches into all of them. The only layer with the same reach is the one underneath.

Where we are, honestly

MagenticOS is in alpha, and the rule we hold ourselves to is that aspiration and shipped capability never share a sentence. So, plainly: the thesis above is the thesis we are building toward — every consequential action passes a typed broker, so the broker is where an action picks up its actor and its scope. What the alpha ships is the runtime, that broker, and a reference shell. What the full arrangement looks like across a whole distro is later work, and we will say so when it is real rather than when it is designed.

In the meantime the diagnostic is free and worth running on whatever you have. Pick one system your agent touched this week. Open its log. Find the action. Read the name on it.

If the name is yours, you don't have an agent identity problem someday. You have one now, and your records are already wrong.

Originally published at magenticos.com/blog/your-agent-is-logged-in-as-you. Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by the author before publication.

title: Did my AI actually pay? The proof problem that starts the day your AI can send money
description:
Your AI can send money now. That stopped being hypothetical today: an AI payments app launched publicly this morning, and its pitch is simple. Connect the AI you already use, set limits, and tell it to pay. Recipients do not even need an account; they get a link and cash out to their bank.

So here is the first question of the agent money era, and it is not "can my AI pay?" It is this: when your AI says it paid, what do you actually hold?

The dinner test

Run the launch demo forward one week. You tell your AI to pay Maya $24 for dinner. The AI replies: done. Maya says nothing arrived. Now what?

I read the new app's own public documentation this morning, the pages that explain how an assistant connects and what it may do. Here is what you hold in that dispute, based on those pages:

  • An activity list inside the same company's app. It shows your payments and where each stands, and it is the company's own record, on the company's servers, behind your account login. Maya cannot open it. Neither can anyone else you might ask to arbitrate.
  • A status check the assistant can run against the same system. Same source, same problem: the answer comes from the party whose record is in dispute.
  • A duplicate guard with a short memory. Per the docs, each payment carries a key the assistant makes up, so the same call repeated within 10 minutes returns the first result instead of paying again. Ten minutes. After that window, the guard the docs describe is gone.

None of this makes the app dishonest. It makes the proof one-sided. The sentence "I paid Maya $24" is a claim in an agent's report with nothing independently checkable under it. We have a word for that on this side of the fence: a bareclaim.

Three questions after any AI payment

Every AI-initiated payment raises three separate questions, and they need three separate records.

Did the money move? Amount, recipient, settlement. A bank record, a wallet record, or a public ledger entry answers this, and only this. A widely cited TRM Labs analysis of x402 payment traffic made the point in its own title: the chain proves the payment, not the payer. Settlement tells you value arrived somewhere. It does not tell you which agent sent it, or why.

What was it executing? The instruction in the words it was given, the authorization behind it (a person approved this payment, or a standing rule approved this class of payment), and the limits in force at the moment it ran. This is the record that answers "who said this could happen," and it is the one that evaporates first, because it usually lives in a chat window.

Can anyone else check? Not the company restating its own database. A third party, the recipient, an accountant, a dispute process, recomputing the record for themselves, without an account and without asking permission. If the answer is no, you do not have proof. You have a screenshot with a login wall behind it.

What this looks like when the receipt exists

This morning I ran the payment path on Zambo, the system I operate, standing exactly where an agent stands before money moves. The call asked to activate a Day Pass the way a funded agent would: no human checkout, the agent payment route. The server answered with the live x402 v2 challenge, and the entire exchange was saved as an AER-1 receipt, including the outcome: no payment settled, because I ran it without a wallet.

The receipt is public. Open it and check it yourself: https://zambo.dev/run/810b1434-83f6-48d3-b7cd-5a29705086f4

What is committed in it, byte for byte, is the full payment instruction an agent would have to satisfy:

{
  "x402Version": 2,
  "accepts": [{
    "scheme": "exact",
    "network": "eip155:8453",
    "asset": "0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913",
    "amount": "990000",
    "payTo": "0xb753be5Eac5B29c711051DfF91279834e9C9b9AC",
    "maxTimeoutSeconds": 900
  }]
}

Read it as a person: pay $0.99 in USDC (990000 atomic units), on Base (eip155:8453), to one named address, inside a 900 second window.
