Braintrust Evals and experiments Span, trace, group, with sampling No Enterprise Pro $249/mo GB plus scores
Opik Tracing and evals Span, trace, thread, with sampling Apache-2.0 Free, full platform Pro $19/mo Spans
Laminar Tracing, evals, Signals Finished traces Apache-2.0 Yes (on-prem listed under Enterprise) Starter $30/mo GB plus Signal tokens
Helicone Gateway, request logging, cost Requests and sessions Apache-2.0 Yes (on-prem listed under Enterprise) Pro $79/mo Requests and storage
Datadog LLM Observability APM-native agent tracing and evals Spans, plus session-level Goal Completeness No No Pro from $160/mo (annual) LLM spans only
Splunk Agent Observability (Galileo) Evals and runtime guardrails Session, trace, span No Yes From $100/mo, billed annually Spans plus Luna tokens
Agnost AI Conversation analytics, failure detection, fixes Whole conversation, pass/fail per assistant message, no sampling No Enterprise (VPC) Starter $49/mo Events

Tracing and debugging

These tools record what the agent did on each request: model calls, tool calls, retrieval, latency, tokens, and errors. Start here if engineers need to debug a single bad run.

Langfuse

What it is. An open-source LLM engineering platform for tracing, evaluation, prompt management, and datasets with experiments. It is built on OpenTelemetry, so any OTel-instrumented app or collector can send traces to it.

Best for. Teams that want open source and self-hosting first, with prompts and evals in the same tool.

Limits. Online evaluation rules score incoming observations, with filters and a sampling rate, and the docs suggest lowering the sampling rate to control LLM-judge cost. Score alerts check aggregated values over a time window, so there is no alert for each individual failing score. Some self-hosted add-ons, such as the Instance Management API and UI customization, need an enterprise license key.

Pricing. Self-hosting is free. Cloud Hobby is free for 50,000 units a month and 2 users. Core is $29 a month and Pro is $199 a month, each with 100,000 units and then $8 per 100,000. Enterprise is $2,499 a month. A unit is a trace, observation, or score.

LangSmith

What it is. LangChain's platform for tracing, evaluation, and agent deployment. It works with many frameworks and providers, not only LangChain, and accepts OpenTelemetry traces at an /otel endpoint.

Best for. Teams building on LangChain or LangGraph who want tracing, online and offline evals, and deployment in one place.

Limits. Multi-turn thread evaluators wait for a thread to go idle (10 minutes by default, 2 minutes minimum) and are capped at 10 per workspace. Base traces are kept for 14 days; keeping a trace for 180 days costs extra. Self-hosting is an add-on to the Enterprise plan.

Pricing. Developer is free for one seat and 5,000 base traces a month. Plus is $39 per seat per month with 10,000 base traces, then pay as you go. Enterprise is custom.

If you are moving off LangSmith, LangSmith alternatives compares the options in detail.

Arize Phoenix

What it is. Arize's self-hostable project for tracing, evaluation, prompt management, and datasets with experiments, built on OpenTelemetry and OpenInference.

Best for. Teams that want a free, self-hosted debugging and experiment workbench from a vendor with a managed upgrade path.

Limits. Phoenix uses the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI open source. Arize documents managed online eval tasks and Signal issue discovery under Arize AX, not Phoenix.

Pricing. Free to self-host, with no feature limits.

Laminar

What it is. Apache-2.0 agent observability with OpenTelemetry-native tracing, an evals SDK and CLI that run locally or in CI, and Signals that read each finished trace for behaviors you describe in plain English.

Best for. Engineering teams that want open-source tracing plus CI evals, with an LLM watching every trace for specific failure patterns.

Limits. Signals are not on the free plan. They are billed by the tokens used to analyze traces, and Signal alerts go to Slack or email.

Pricing. Free with 1 GB of data and 7-day retention. Starter is $30 a month (3 GB, then $2 per GB). Pro is $150 a month (10 GB, then $1.50 per GB). Signals cost $0.05 per million input tokens and $0.30 per million output tokens.

Helicone

What it is. An Apache-2.0 AI gateway with built-in request logging. You point an OpenAI-compatible client at Helicone's gateway URL to get routing across 100+ models, fallbacks, cost and latency analytics, sessions, and prompt management.

Best for. Teams whose first monitoring question is cost, latency, and provider reliability, and who want a gateway anyway.

Limits. It is request-centric. The repo describes no dedicated evaluation feature, so agent-quality checks need another tool. Helicone's site says it "is now part of Experiential Labs" with "details to come soon," so watch for product changes.

Pricing. Hobby is free for 10,000 requests and 7-day retention. Pro is $79 a month and Team is $799 a month, each with usage-based pricing above the free allowance.

Evals

Eval tools score outputs, either offline against datasets before a release or online against production traffic. Start here if your main question is "did this change make the agent better or worse?" For a deeper look at production scoring, see best online evaluation tools for AI agents.

Braintrust

What it is. An evaluation and observability platform built around experiments, datasets, and scorers. Online scoring rules run at span, trace, or group scope. Trace and group scopes wait for a 30-second idle timeout by default, and you can set a sampling percentage.

Best for. Teams whose releases run on experiments and who want production scores to feed datasets directly.

Limits. Every score is metered, so scoring all traffic gets expensive at volume. Self-hosting (on-prem or hosted) is Enterprise only.

Pricing. Starter is free with 1 GB and 10,000 scores, then $4 per GB and $2.50 per 1,000 scores. Pro is $249 a month with 5 GB and 50,000 scores, then $3 per GB and $1.50 per 1,000 scores.

Arize AX

What it is. Arize's managed platform for tracing, online evals, experiments, and issue discovery. Online eval tasks run at span, trace, or session granularity with a sampling rate. Arize suggests starting at 10 to 20%. Signal groups recurring failures into ranked issues with trace evidence and a proposed fix.

Best for. Larger teams that want managed evals at every level plus issue discovery, with an enterprise path.

Limits. Signal is capped at 10 issues a month on Free and 25 on Pro. Repo access, custom monitors, and custom code evaluators are listed as Enterprise features.

Pricing. AX Free covers 25,000 spans and 1 GB a month with 15-day retention. AX Pro is $50 a month for 50,000 spans and 10 GB with 30-day retention. Evals are unlimited on every AX tier.

Opik

What it is. Comet's Apache-2.0 platform for tracing, online evaluation, and agent optimization. The full platform is free to self-host. Evaluators score traces, threads, or spans, with sampling up to 100%. Thread evaluators wait 15 minutes after the last activity by default, and scores can alert to Slack, PagerDuty, or a webhook.

Best for. Teams that want open-source, self-hosted evaluation with whole-conversation judges.

Limits. An evaluator's scope cannot be changed after you create it. Alerts fire when an average crosses a threshold.

Pricing. Open source is free. Cloud Free covers 25,000 spans a month with 60-day retention. Pro is $19 a month for 100,000 spans, then $5 per 100,000.

Product and conversation analytics

Traces show what the agent did. They don't show what users wanted, whether they got it, or how many gave up. That job needs per-conversation labels, such as intent, sentiment, and outcome, that you can count.

  • Agnost AI labels intents and sentiment on every user message, so failure rates can be read per user goal. Details are in the next section.
  • Braintrust Topics has an LLM summarize each trace through Task, Sentiment, and Issues facets, then clusters the summaries into named topics once at least 100 exist.
  • Datadog Patterns clusters production traffic into a topic hierarchy.

For product analytics tools (Amplitude, PostHog, Mixpanel) and contact-center tools, see best AI agent analytics tools and best conversation analytics tools for AI agents.

Failure detection and fixing

This is the newest job: finding failures you didn't write a check for, grouping them, and proposing a change. Pick by the unit that gets judged and by what happens after a failure is found.

Agnost AI

What it is. Conversation analytics and failure detection for production chat and voice agents, with an improvement loop that turns alerts into pull requests. It ingests OpenTelemetry and has its own SDKs.

Best for. Teams whose failures only show up across a whole conversation, such as an agent that forgets a constraint by turn six or confirms a refund it never processed, and who want failures to turn into a reviewed fix.

How it works. You write rules in plain English, for example "confirm identity before sharing account details." Once a conversation has been idle for 15 minutes, an LLM judge reads the whole conversation in a batch and marks each assistant message pass or fail against every active rule. There is no sampling setting: every conversation is judged, up to your plan's event limit. Each user message is labelled with an intent and a sentiment. When a rule's failure count crosses a threshold, Agnost sends a Slack or email alert. With Auto Improve connected, the alert starts a run that reads your repository and opens a pull request for a person to review.

Limits. Judging is not real time; it happens in batches after a conversation goes idle. Verdicts are pass or fail, not numeric scores. Alerts go only to Slack or email. There is no CI integration and no offline experiment workflow. Auto Improve tests a fix against past runs, but your review and your own CI are still the gate before merge. Teams that need dataset experiments usually pair Agnost with Braintrust, LangSmith, Langfuse, or Opik.

Pricing. Free covers 1,000 events a month with 7-day retention. Starter is $49 a month (10,000 events, 30-day retention). Pro is $499 a month (1,000,000 events, 90-day retention). Enterprise is custom and includes self-hosted VPC deployment.

Other tools in this job

  • LangSmith Engine scans tracing projects on a schedule, clusters and prioritizes recurring issues, diagnoses root causes against traces and connected code, and can open pull requests in GitHub or GitLab. It never merges them. Fix validation is in beta and only on LangSmith Cloud. Usage is billed in LangChain Standard Units at $1 each.
  • Arize AX Signal groups recurring production failures into ranked issues with evidence and a proposed fix. It has monthly issue caps on Free and Pro.
  • Laminar Signals check each finished trace against your instruction and JSON schema, cluster similar findings, and write a report with a suggested fix for each new cluster.

How these approaches compare when it matters is covered in self-healing agents: hype vs reality, and the agent monitoring detection benchmark measures how often failures are caught at all.

APM-native

If your on-call team already lives in an APM, putting agent telemetry there keeps one pager and one set of dashboards.

Datadog LLM Observability

What it is. Datadog's agent tracing and evaluation product, now also sold as Agent Observability. Template LLM-as-a-judge evaluators include Failure to Answer, Hallucination, Tool Selection, Tool Argument Correctness, and a session-level Goal Completeness check that runs on completed sessions. Insights flags recurring cost and reliability problems with a root cause and a recommended fix. It correlates with Datadog APM through the SDK.

Best for. Teams already standardized on Datadog.

Limits. LLM-judge templates run on an LLM provider account you connect, so judge tokens are billed by your provider on top of Datadog's fee.

Pricing. Free up to 40,000 LLM spans a month with 15-day retention. Pro starts at $160 a month on an annual commitment ($200 month to month) for 100,000 LLM spans, then $3.50 per 10,000 annually. Only LLM spans are billed; tool, retrieval, and workflow spans are free.

If you're weighing a move off Datadog, see Datadog LLM Observability alternatives.

Splunk Agent Observability (formerly Galileo)

What it is. Galileo, now part of Splunk after Cisco acquired it. It combines evaluation, tracing, token-cost tracking, and runtime guardrails. Evaluations run on small purpose-built evaluator models (Eval-G1, plus Luna models in Galileo's docs), and trusted evaluations can be enforced as real-time guardrails for PII leakage, tool misuse, and prompt injection.

Best for. Splunk and Cisco shops, and teams that want to score all traffic cheaply with small evaluator models and block bad outputs at runtime.

Limits. Pricing beyond the base unit is quote-based. LLM-as-a-judge metrics need an LLM integration set up first.

Pricing. From $100 a month, billed annually, for 1.2 million spans a year, plus 500 million Luna tokens. A free edition is linked but its limits are not listed.

Which should you pick?

If your team… Pick
Needs open-source tracing you can self-host for free Langfuse or Opik
Builds on LangChain or LangGraph LangSmith
Wants a free self-hosted debugging and experiment workbench Arize Phoenix
Wants open-source tracing plus CI evals and LLM trace Signals Laminar
Mostly needs cost, latency, and routing across model providers Helicone
Ships changes through experiments and datasets Braintrust
Wants managed span, trace, and session evals with issue discovery Arize AX
Already runs Datadog Datadog LLM Observability
Runs Splunk or wants runtime guardrails on small evaluator models Splunk Agent Observability (Galileo)
Needs failures judged across whole conversations, intents per user message, and alerts that open a PR for review Agnost AI

If security review, SSO, audit logs, or self-hosting decide your shortlist, see the best enterprise AI agent monitoring platforms. A common setup pairs one tracing or eval tool with one conversation-level layer. Conversation-level vs trace-level online evals explains why both catch things the other misses.

How to run a fair pilot

Send the same week of production traffic to two or three candidates and check:

  1. The unit. Does it judge the failures you care about, including multi-turn ones?
  2. The denominator. Can you see how many conversations were checked, not only how many failed? Sampling changes this number.
  3. The evidence. Does each failure point to the message or step that went wrong?
  4. The cost at your volume. Each vendor meters something different. The AI agent monitoring pricing guide has a worksheet.
  5. The path to a fix. When a failure is confirmed, how many steps until a change ships? The agent monitoring pilot checklist lists what to score.

Related reading

  • LangSmith vs Langfuse vs Braintrust vs Phoenix vs Agnost
  • Agnost AI vs Langfuse vs Arize for catching agent quality failures
  • Langfuse alternatives for user and conversation analytics
  • Braintrust alternatives for AI agent evaluation
  • Tools that turn AI agent failures into pull requests
  • Arize alternatives: options to Arize AX and Phoenix (2026)
  • Braintrust vs LangSmith: which to choose for agent evals
  • Best tools to monitor voice AI agents (2026)

Frequently asked questions

What are the best tools to monitor AI agents in production?

Pick by the job. For tracing and debugging: Langfuse (open source), LangSmith (LangChain and LangGraph teams), Arize Phoenix, Laminar, or Helicone. For evals: Braintrust, Arize AX, or Opik. For teams already on an APM: Datadog LLM Observability or Splunk Agent Observability (formerly Galileo). For finding failures across whole conversations and turning them into pull requests: Agnost AI. Most production teams run one tracing or eval tool plus one layer that tells them what users experienced.

Which AI agent monitoring platforms detect agent failures automatically?

Several now find failures you did not write a check for. LangSmith Engine clusters recurring issues from production traces and can open pull requests. Arize AX Signal groups recurring failures into ranked issues with a proposed fix. Laminar Signals read each finished trace against a plain-English instruction and cluster the results. Datadog Insights flags recurring cost and reliability problems. Agnost AI judges each whole conversation against plain-English rules after it has been idle for 15 minutes and alerts Slack or email when a rule's failure count crosses a threshold.

What is the best open-source AI agent monitoring tool?

Langfuse (MIT, except its ee folders) and Opik (Apache-2.0, full platform free to self-host) are the most complete open-source options, both with tracing, datasets, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. Laminar and Helicone are also Apache-2.0. Arize Phoenix is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0 rather than OSI open source.

Can I monitor AI agents with Datadog?

Yes. Datadog LLM Observability, now sold as Agent Observability, traces agent steps, runs template and custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluations including a session-level Goal Completeness check, and correlates with Datadog APM through its SDK. It bills only LLM spans: free up to 40,000 a month, then Pro from $160 a month on an annual commitment for 100,000 LLM spans.

Which agent monitoring tools can fix failures, not just detect them?

LangSmith Engine can open pull requests in a connected GitHub or GitLab repository and never merges them. Arize lists repo access as an AX Enterprise feature. Agnost AI's Auto Improve starts when an alert fires, tests the fix against past runs, and opens a pull request with the replay results for human review. In every case a person reviews and merges the change.

How much does AI agent monitoring cost?

Entry paid plans in November 2026: Opik Pro $19 a month, Langfuse Core $29, Laminar Starter $30, LangSmith Plus $39 per seat, Agnost AI Starter $49, Arize AX Pro $50, Helicone Pro $79, Datadog Pro from $160 (annual), and Braintrust Pro $249. Each meters something different (seats, traces, spans, units, GB, scores, or events), so price your real volume, not the sticker.

Originally published on agnost.ai.

title: SkillSpector: a security scanner for AI agent skills
description:
SkillSpector

Installing an agent skill is handing it the keys. A skill is Markdown plus scripts that run with your shell privileges, and most teams install them without a second look. SkillSpector, from NVIDIA, scans a skill before it is installed and checks it against 71 vulnerability patterns across 17 categories, from prompt injection and data exfiltration to dependency CVEs. It returns a risk score and a verdict, and it can run as an MCP server so agents scan before installing. In the research behind it, 26.1 percent of 31,132 skills analysed had vulnerabilities. Scan first, install second.

What you get

  • A 0-100 risk score with severity labels and clear recommendations, reported in terminal, JSON, Markdown, or SARIF output
  • Live CVE lookups against OSV.dev for dependency checks, with an automatic offline fallback
  • A Docker image if you want to run it without installing Python, and baseline suppression so re-scans surface only new findings
  • Install with uv tool install --python 3.13 git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git, Python 3.12 or 3.13 required

A skill runs with your shell privileges. Treat installing one like installing software from a stranger: scan it first, and only then decide whether it earns the keys.

Repo: https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillSpector

Quick poll

What would you use SkillSpector for first?

  • Scanning skills before I install them
  • Gating skill installs in CI
  • Running it as an MCP server for my agents
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found SkillSpector interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: Persist the Authority Behind Every Tool Call: The ADK Decision-Ledger Thread That Became a Pull Request
description:
Persist the Authority Behind Every Tool Call: The ADK Decision-Ledger Thread That Became a Pull Request

An agent framework can log everything an agent did and still fail to answer the only question that matters after an incident: was this call authorized, by whom, and under what policy? That is the problem open right now in google/adk-python, issue #6099, "Decision ledger: persist the authority, refusal, and approval behind each tool call." The thread has 79 comments. This morning its evidence base stopped being thread prose and became a pull request, #8224, that the maintainers can review as a diff.

This is a record of what that thread actually settled, what it deliberately left open, and why the same three design questions keep appearing wherever agents do real work.

The split the thread is built on

The load-bearing distinction, drawn early and never really challenged: traces and session events describe execution, while a decision ledger describes authority. A trace can tell you a tool ran. It cannot tell you whether it was allowed to.

Inside that split, the thread separates three kinds of fields:

  • Framework-attested fields: tool name, invocation or step id, principal, auth mode, policy source and version, confirmation id, decision state, timestamp. Things the framework itself knows at dispatch time.
  • Derived commitments: a canonical digest of the call arguments, and a digest of the result when one exists. Things computed from the call, not narrated about it.
  • Untrusted context: the model's stated rationale. Useful for a human reviewer, never treated as the authority record.

That third bucket is the one most logging designs get wrong. An agent explaining why it acted is testimony. A ledger that stores testimony as authority will eventually let the agent grade its own homework.

Three design questions, and what hangs on each

1. Is "cannot-tell" a stored value, or an absent row?

If a call has no ledger entry, a verifier cannot distinguish "no decision was needed" from "the decision was never recorded." Those two states need opposite responses. The proposal on the thread: the ledger stores the cannot-tell outcome explicitly, as a value, so absence of evidence stops impersonating evidence of absence.

2. Are the payload and result digests mandatory?

A decision record that names a tool but does not bind the exact arguments is a permission slip with the amount left blank. The thread's acceptance shape binds each decision to the call it authorized: canonical args digest at decision time, result digest when the call completes, and a pointer from the result back to the decision. That is what makes "executed equals authorized" checkable by someone who does not trust the agent's narration, or the operator's.

3. Can a reader aggregate per-call records into a run-level verdict?

No, and the thread is precise about why: a refusal on one call says nothing about its sibling calls in the same model response. A ledger that lets a reader roll forty calls into one green checkmark has destroyed the only granularity at which authority actually operates. The proposed rule: records stay per-call, and aggregation into a run verdict is a presentation choice that must never be mistaken for the record itself.

The part that made it a pull request: provenance discipline

Design threads usually die as vibes. This one developed a working rule worth stealing: a claim carries exactly the weight of its source, and no more.

The field mapping behind the discussion, which fields ADK exposes today and which it cannot tell, rests on independent source reads of the framework code. When a participant pointed out that proposals imported from an outside standard had been stated with more confidence than their review status earned, the correction was accepted on the record, in the thread, by the person who made the claims. The source reads were then pinned to specific commits so anyone can re-run them: re-running a read against current main either reproduces the finding or retires it.

This morning that discipline produced artifacts. The source-read inventory is now a document in PR #8224 (docs/source-reads-6099.md): five rows in the form: area, finding, severity, reproducible-from-pinned-commit, covering per-call integrity binding, ledger aggregation, evaluator origin-binding, irreversible-effect authorization, and identity-bound audit fields, with the cannot-tell tier preserved verbatim. A companion file (docs/guides/decision-table-crosswalk.md) maps the decision table for tool-call authorization fixtures. The PR's own summary of the offer: review a diff, not a thread.

Whether any of it lands is the maintainers' decision, and the thread says so itself. None of it needs to be accepted to be useful. It is already the clearest worked statement of the decision-ledger problem in a production agent framework.

Where this meets the execution side

The ADK thread is about the authority record: what was permitted, before the call. There is a mirror problem on the execution side: what actually happened, recorded so a third party can check it later without trusting the executor.

That mirror problem is what AER-1 standardizes. Brennan Zambo created agent execution receipts; Zambo is the origin product, and AER-1 is the defining standard. An AER-1 receipt (current draft: draft-zambo-aer1-26) commits to the recorded inputs, the saved result, and a SHA-256 digest over the canonical receipt bytes, and it closes with an outcome from a fixed vocabulary: verified, verification failed, rejected: unresolvable record, not checked, absent. Note the family resemblance to the thread's cannot-tell tier: "not checked" and "absent" are stored outcomes, not missing rows, for exactly the reason the ADK discussion arrived at independently.

The standard is testable, not aspirational: a public corpus of 143 test vectors and 146 checks, against which exactly one implementation is documented passing the full published corpus. Authority records and execution records are different artifacts, and a serious stack needs both: the ledger that says the call was allowed, and the receipt that proves the saved result was not changed after the fact. A receipt proves the saved result was not changed. It does not prove the answer was right, and it does not try to.

This is running in production, and you can check it

Zambo, the origin product, serves 153 tools behind one MCP endpoint (37 on the default surface). As of this morning the public counters read 146,756 receipts issued, 796 of them today, across 125,550 tool calls, with 329,812 package downloads across the fleet. Twenty-one verified payers hold passes. Yesterday morning a buyer paid $0.99 through the website checkout for a Day Pass, which is the front door working exactly as designed: every tool free once a day, plus 3 continue calls, one free wrap-up handover per day, and pickup always free, with the Day Pass removing the limits for 24 hours when the work gets serious.

Do not take any of that on faith; the point of the system is that you do not have to. This receipt was issued this morning for a live BTC price call: zambo.dev/run/f756dcfd-d28c-4ad6-97c4-059fa03e3e31. Open it, then run it through the public verification page and watch the digest recompute. That is the whole argument in one click: done is checkable, not trusted.

The ADK maintainers will rule on the decision ledger in their own time. The questions their thread surfaced, stored cannot-tell outcomes, mandatory digests, no aggregation across calls, are the questions every framework will have to answer as agents start spending money, touching production, and handing work to clients who ask what changed. The frameworks that answer them with records, rather than logs, are the ones whose agents will be allowed to do serious work.

title: I asked what exists for running routines. It has 128,257 stars
description:
"First I need to look at what exists." It exists, at 128,257 stars - and it appears nowhere in his corpus

Anton says he has too many routines. Far too many. Most run in Claude Code, a few in Codex, and he needs to work out how to manage a large number of them. He wants to find a separate harness, an open-source tool or some other solution that would manage all the routines centrally: launch them, distribute them across subscriptions, automate as much as possible so he does not have to handle them by hand. First, look at what exists. Then: one system to manage every routine and set which subscription, model and environment each one runs on. And if a routine cannot run on one subscription, let it switch to the second, the third and so on by itself - or let the system choose where to run it.

That is three requirements - scheduling, subscription routing, automatic failover on limit. Measured today: no single tool does all three. But each exists separately, and the biggest one he does not know about.

stablyai/orca: 128,257 stars, 8,125 forks, MIT, pushed today. Its own description is almost his sentence: "run a fleet of coding agents (e.g. Claude Code, Codex) with your own subscription", on desktop, mobile and a remote runtime. Two features land directly:

Automations: schedule prompts to run on any repo: nightly dependency bumps, weekly triage, flaky-test sweeps.

Accounts: see how much of your agent limits you've used and when they reset, and switch accounts without logging out.

So central scheduling and limit visibility are shipped, at a scale that makes Orca the default answer to "what exists". And the word "fallback" appears zero times in its README. So do "cron", "subscription" and "quota". Account switching is manual: you can see the limits and change accounts, but a routine will not change them for you.

⚠️ And the honest part: Orca is mentioned nowhere in his corpus. 128,257 stars, 8,125 forks, pushed the same day - and not one decision memo, insight note or DR registry line. That is the finding behind the finding: not that the tool exists, but that the sweep which finds it takes twenty minutes and had never been run.

willynikes2/agent-orchestrator: 67 stars, 9 forks, MIT, 35 days since last push. This one does the third requirement exactly:

wraps Claude, Codex, Gemini, Grok, and Antigravity CLIs (plus an optional Argon API reviewer) with automatic failover. When one agent hits its limit, the next one picks up seamlessly. All agents share context through a knowledge base server.

"One hits its limit, the next picks up" is his own sentence about the second and third subscription. In its README: failover 4, subscription 5, quota 3, rate limit 2. And schedul 0, cron 0 - no scheduler at all. It is the failover half with no clock, and it has not moved in five weeks.

christianreiss/codex-orchestrator: 19 stars, GPL-3.0, pushed today. The smallest of the three and the closest to the full list. In its README: cron 11, schedul 10, subscription 12, quota 13, switch 11. A Dockerised self-hosted control plane - project board, shared memory, merge arbitration, peer messaging, secrets, file drop - that starts agents remotely, schedules work and answers from a console or Android companion, with four engines treated as equals. Its failover count is 0: what it calls fallback is an offline auth window (24h fresh, 7-day fallback), not task failover between providers.

Three tools, three thirds:

requirement Orca (128k★) agent-orchestrator (67★) codex-orchestrator (19★)
central launch + schedule yes no yes
subscription / model per routine partial, manual yes yes
automatic failover on limit no yes no
maturity huge, active small, 35d quiet small, active
licence MIT MIT GPL-3.0

The tool closest to his whole list has 19 stars and runs on PHP under Docker. The tool with the ecosystem has no failover. The tool with failover has no clock.

And the scale such a system would manage is already measured. The routine registry holds 264 entries. On this laptop alone, the Windows scheduler carries 59 non-Microsoft tasks - 56 enabled, 3 disabled - of which 21 are Claude- or routine-related. So "too many routines" is not a feeling: it is 264 registered purposes against an OS scheduler that knows nothing about subscriptions, models or limits.

One of the three requirements is already solved locally, and it is worth naming before buying anything. Subscription routing exists as llm_routing.json - work classes mapped to vendor rails, with rail profiles, an account ladder and a data policy. That is literally "set which subscription each routine runs on". What is missing is the layer above it: one place that launches all 264 and knows which ones failed.

⚠️ And there is a door for our own work in this field. andyrewlee/awesome-agent-orchestrators - 2,452 stars, 361 forks, a curated list of exactly these tools. Awesome-list submissions from this account merge 2 of 11, but this is the one list whose subject matter is what we build - and we do not have a list entry, we have a 264-routine fleet, which is a case study.

⚠️ What I did not do. I installed and ran none of the three. Every claim above is README text plus GitHub metadata, so "Orca has no failover" means "its README never mentions one" - the docs site may say otherwise, and that is one page load. I also did not verify whether Orca's automations can pin a model or an environment per run, which is the middle requirement of his post.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261117.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261117.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI

Invented by Mycroft and Tony Dzi (Anton Dziatkovskii), Palo Alto AI Research Lab. Proudly made in Silicon Valley.

title: What to Log and Measure in a Production Agent Memory Service
description:
Start with a simple question: did the information the agent needed make it from memory into the model’s request?

A retrieval dashboard can look healthy while the application drops a useful record before the model call. Even when the record reaches the model, the task can still fail. To find out where to make a change, track the write, retrieval, context assembly, and final action separately.

Anthropic’s November 6 agent memory study offers one example. On a CL-Bench database task, Sonnet 4.6 earned a mean reward of 0.364 with memory and 0.641 with memory and refined instructions. Those instructions asked the model to read its memory before answering and test its explanations.

The result is specific to that task, but it illustrates why retrieval alone is not enough to evaluate an application. Teams also need to check what reaches the model and whether the resulting action succeeds.

Put these measures on the dashboard

Use live request data for reliability and latency. Use labeled replays or reviewed samples for measures that depend on knowing which record or action was correct. Show the sample count beside each rate.

Measure Definition and denominator Where to collect it
Write readiness Of accepted writes expected to create or update a known record and whose deadline has passed, the share whose expected result was visible by that deadline. Keep failed and overdue writes in the total. Write acknowledgment, task status where available, and a scoped read-back probe. Report failed and overdue jobs separately.
Lookup failures and latency Failed or timed-out lookups divided by attempted lookups. Report p95 latency over successful lookups, including empty results, and show the timeout count next to it. The application's retrieval call, from start to response or timeout.
Hit rate at k Labeled lookups with the expected record in the top k divided by labeled lookups with a known target. Keep k fixed across comparisons. Retrieval response, before context assembly.
Context delivery rate Of labeled turns that retrieved the expected record, the share that sent the record or its relevant content to the model. Compare retrieval results with the application’s final context assembly. Track which record IDs contributed to each included block.
Stale or out-of-scope context For each category, divide inspected requests containing a violating record by inspected requests containing any memory. The outgoing model request after scope and freshness checks. Count blocks separately.
Task success Runs meeting the workflow's outcome criteria divided by scored runs. In a delivery workflow, check the destination actually submitted. Tool result or business event, joined to the originating turn.
Memory processing tokens For sampled turns with complete usage data, report the tokens or other billed units used by memory-related processing. Keep extraction, embedding, and ranking separate where their usage is available. Provider usage and billing records for memory-related calls, including linked background work when reported. Show coverage and missing usage.
Memory added to the prompt Estimated tokens in included memory blocks divided by sampled model requests that contain memory. Final prompt assembly, using the model's tokenizer where available.

For write readiness, use an authorized probe with a known target and a fixed query. Record the probe interval alongside the observed time.

If the expected record does not appear, check both the write status and the search conditions. A search can miss a record because of its query, filters, or result limit. Count empty responses separately from lookup errors, since some turns need no memory.

For stale context, check the record against the current version or validity window. For scope, alert on any confirmed violation and report how many inputs were inspected. Review task success by case type, including routine recall, a corrected preference, and a case where the agent should ask for clarification.

Trace a turn from search to action

Give each user turn a trace ID. Record the write job ID when one exists, the retrieval outcome and duration, the record IDs returned and included, and the final action result. Link background jobs back to their originating turn. Keep user and memory IDs in restricted traces, and leave memory text out of routine logs. Use dimensions such as workflow, model version, and result status for aggregate metrics. The estimated prompt footprint is part of the main request. Keep it separate from provider-reported usage for memory-only calls.

OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions can help structure model and retrieval telemetry. The application still needs to define how it labels freshness, authorization, and task success for its own workflow.

With MemOS Cloud, keep the task ID returned for an asynchronous write and use Task Status to follow processing. Once the task completes, its response can summarize memory changes and the affected IDs.

Then use a scoped Search Memory request to check what the application can retrieve. During context assembly, record which returned memories contributed to the model request. This helps distinguish a record that was not found from one that was found but never reached the model.

Read the rates together

In an illustrative replay of 120 turns, search found the expected record in 96 turns, and 82 of those turns included it in the model request. The hit rate is 80%. Delivery among hits is 85.4%, and delivery across all 120 turns is 68.3%.

The 14 turns where the record was retrieved but not delivered point the team toward context assembly. Inspect those before changing the search index.

If the expected record arrived and the action still failed, hold that record and the tool responses fixed while testing revised instructions. If the agent proposed the right action and the system executed the wrong one, follow the tool call and its receipt. Use matched replays with and without memory when you want to measure its contribution to task success.

title: Qwen3 + Claude Code: Request Routing Sent 96% to the Cloud, Step Routing Kept 48% Local
description:
Send Claude Code's whole requests to a local Qwen3 and almost nothing goes through. One recent measurement on an RTX 4070 counted 100 real requests and 96 had to go to the frontier model. Then the same workload was split into single Claude Code steps and counted again: 97 of 200 steps were fine on the local model. Same box. Same requests. The thing that changed was the routing granularity.

Both numbers are from the companion material for a Kindle book by kenimo49 (Local LLM or Claude Code?), with MIT-licensed reference code on GitHub as local-step-router. I want to walk through what those two numbers imply for anyone who has a local LLM sitting idle and a Claude Code bill that is not.

Request-level routing doesn't carry the material

Here is the first number again. 100 real daily requests were labeled for whether a local LLM on a single RTX 4070 with 12 GB of VRAM could handle them. Qwen3-8B at Q4 fits that VRAM band with room for context (llmhardware.io on Qwen3 VRAM). Of the 100, 4 could stay local (and only because they contained confidential data that shouldn't leave the machine); the other 96 had to go to the frontier model. Zero were a clean fit for a local model on merit.

The reason is not the model quality. A one-line request like "fix the test that just failed" is a pointer, not material. The actual work lives in the repo, the stack trace, the last three commits. Hand that one line to a local model and there is nothing it can bind to. Hand it the same line after Claude Code has gathered the trace and opened the file, and a 4B judge can tell you whether the diff compiles.

If you have tried "swap Claude Code for a local model" and been disappointed, this is probably why. The failure is routing, not the model. Swapping the model when the actual problem is granularity is the AI-era version of buying a bigger car to beat traffic.

Step-level routing changes the math

Claude Code does not act as a single request. One "fix the failing test" turns into dozens of steps internally: WebFetch, Read, Grep, Edit, Bash, Write, Task. Each of those steps has a return shape the orchestrator knows how to consume.

Counted at that granularity, the companion book's measurement said 97 of 200 Claude Code steps were fine on the local model. 48% of the work. The split was not uniform. Some step types routed cleanly, others didn't. The local-step-router repo's router.py encodes the pattern as rules first and a probability judgment second.

The rule is the interesting part.

A one-line rule beat a 9B model's probability

The LP for the book quotes a result worth sitting with: a one-line rule, "WebFetch goes local", beat a 9B model's probability judgment on the same task. Not by a little. The rule was simpler to implement, deterministic, and routed more work correctly than asking a local model "is this step safe locally?" and reading the number back.

That is the pattern the companion code implements. router.py decides by step type first. judge.py only runs on the edge cases the rules can't settle. If you read Ollama's native /api/chat endpoint for the top-token logprob, you can get a confidence number out of a 4B model for a yes/no question in a single token. The threshold you draw on that number is where the second number in the title comes from.

# conceptual shape of the router (see local-step-router/router.py for real code)
def route(step):
    if step.type == "WebFetch":
        return "local"
    if step.type in ("Read", "Grep") and step.size < THRESHOLD:
        return "local"
    # only the undecided cases call the model
    confidence = judge_with_logprobs(step)
    return "local" if confidence >= calibrated_threshold else "frontier"

Rules do the bulk. Probability judgments cover the rest.

The threshold isn't 0.5

The second place a lot of "local LLM as judge" setups go wrong is treating 0.5 as the obvious threshold. It is not. The LP reports a measured case where a local gatekeeper let a production DB password through with 0.69 confidence. The model's ordering was perfect (secrets scored higher than non-secrets on average), but the raw scale was off.

The right line is drawn from your own labeled data, not from 0.5. On the book's evaluation set, calibrating the threshold cut missed secrets from 20 to 2. Same model. Same inputs. Only the decision rule changed. If you have ever drawn the 0.5 line and had a judge wave something through anyway, that is what you were looking at.

The companion repo ships a threshold.py CLI for this. You give it labeled examples, it reports the highest threshold with zero misses on your set, and you can decide how much margin to leave. The math is unsurprising (it is the "pick the lowest FPR at TPR=1" move), but having it as a tool next to the router means the calibration gets redone as the data drifts, instead of baked in once and forgotten.

Three traps where logprobs just disappear

If you are going to read a probability out of a local model, there are three places the number quietly becomes meaningless, all documented in the book's Chapter 6 outline:

  1. The OpenAI-compatible endpoint silently drops logprobs. If you point your code at Ollama's v1/chat/completions and the native API at /api/chat, the native one returns top-token probabilities. The OpenAI-compatible one has dropped them in some Ollama versions without raising an error. A 2026-Q4 Ollama release note is worth checking before trusting a logprobs field over OpenAI-compat.
  2. Thinking models don't put the answer in the first token. Qwen3 series models with thinking mode on will emit a reasoning trace first and the yes/no later. Reading the first token's probability gives you the probability of a reasoning-trace token, not the decision.
  3. A top-20 candidate list hides low-probability answers. If the character you were watching for isn't in the top-20, the probability reads as zero without an error. For binary judgments ("Y" vs "N") this is not a problem; for routing across many labels, it is.

The book spends a chapter on these because each one fails silently. The code runs, the number comes back, it is just wrong.

Rules decide the fixed parts. Probability covers the rest.

If I had to collapse the two numbers in the title into one takeaway: route at the step level, decide by rules where you can, and only use a local probability for the rest. The 96 vs 48% gap is the cost of routing at the wrong granularity. The "rule beat probability" result is the cost of using a model to decide things a one-line rule already settles.

The book's blueprint, the local-step-router code, and the threshold worksheet are companion material to the data above. For the other side of the same question (how many hours of use per day flip the economics from frontier API to local), the author's Claude Code Max vs API vs Qwen hour-of-day breakeven breakdown is the closest public companion. For the raw tok/s side, RTX 4070 + --cpu-moe flag notes measure the 2.8x speedup from one llama.cpp flag.

The pattern transfers. Count your own steps. Decide the fixed parts by type. Keep the local judge for the edge cases, and calibrate its threshold from your own data instead of 0.5.

The book: Local LLM or Claude Code? 96% of Requests Failed Locally, Half of the Steps Didn't. Measured routing between a local LLM on one RTX 4070 and a frontier model, with the blueprint and the companion code (MIT) above.

title: AI Side Hustles 2026: What Upwork and Fiverr's Own Data Says About AI Freelancing
description:
AI side hustles in 2026.
Which ones actually make money?

On Upwork, one kind of AI work saw earnings go up 45%.
Another kind saw earnings per contract fall 13%.
Same tools.
Opposite results.

I made a video about it.
This article has what the video has no room for: a table of seven AI side hustles with what Upwork's and Fiverr's reports say about each, the skills each one needs, how to start this week using the menus Upwork and Fiverr actually show, and a checklist before you start.

The short version

  • On Upwork, freelancers doing AI work earn 34% more per hour than those not using AI (Upwork Future Workforce Index 2026).
  • But generative AI and creative production work saw contract starts grow 90% while earnings per contract fell 13% (Upwork).
  • Freelancers doing more complex work with AI saw earnings rise 45% (Upwork).
  • On Fiverr, demand for Claude Code specialists rose 938% in six months, and searches for n8n AI automation rose 125% (Fiverr Business Trends Index 2026).
  • AI-related demand grew most in Video & Animation, at 278% (Fiverr).
  • Searches for human video editing grew too: 36%, and 27% for short-form video editing (Fiverr).
  • The split is not AI or no AI. It is whether the buyer could do it with one prompt.

I have worked in IT for over 20 years.
I have run my own company in Japan for 22.
Today, AI makes twelve videos and twelve carousel sets a day for my company.
So I did not want to guess about this.
I read both reports myself.

The two reports

Both came out this year.

Upwork Fiverr
Name Future Workforce Index 2026 Business Trends Index 2026
Published July 14, 2026 June 9, 2026 (GlobeNewswire)
What it measures A survey of 2,400 U.S.-based skilled workers (March to April 2026), plus Upwork Marketplace platform data Global search data on Fiverr
Period compared Platform data: Q1 2026 versus the same period last year November 2025 to April 2026, compared with May to October 2025
What the numbers are Contract starts, hourly earnings, earnings trends, survey answers Percentage growth in searches

Keep the last row in mind.
Upwork counts contracts and earnings.
Fiverr counts searches.
A search is not a hire.

Upwork: AI work pays more per hour, on average

Upwork's first number is the good news.
"Freelancers performing AI work on the Upwork Marketplace earn 34% more per hour than those not incorporating AI."

The full report adds that this holds "across every work category".
It also says freelancers are ahead of full-time employees with AI agents: 41% use AI agents for autonomous task execution, against 34% of full-time employees.

But 34% is an average.
Inside it, AI work is moving in two directions.

The side that pays less

Upwork calls it generative AI and creative production.
Making images, text and other content with AI tools.

Contract starts grew 90% year over year.
Earnings per contract fell 13%.

The full report has one more number the video does not.
"Overall, AI-based execution tasks saw earnings fall 28% year over year."
Upwork defines these as AI work that "generally focuses on producing discrete outputs, such as text, images, or video".

Upwork's own reading: "lower-complexity AI execution may become less lucrative as it scales."

Think about why.
If anyone can type a prompt and get the result, the buyer can do it too.
Or hire the next person for less.

The side that pays more

Freelancers doing more complex work with AI saw earnings increase 45% year over year (Upwork; the full report dates this to Q1 2026).

AI-augmented professional services, where people who already know a field bring AI into it, grew 72% in volume, with earnings rising 22% (Upwork).

Upwork has a name for this person: the AI Orchestrator.

The full report spells out what that person does.
Someone who "understands business goals, selects and coordinates the right tools, manages AI agents and workflows, evaluates output quality, and applies human judgment where context matters."

So the split is not AI or no AI.
It is judgment or no judgment.

Fiverr: what businesses are searching for

Fiverr's data points the same way.

"Demand for Claude Code specialists has surged 938% on Fiverr over the last six months."
Fiverr says businesses want freelancers who can use it "to automate their workflows, build AI agents, and ship products faster".

The same release lists related searches:

  • n8n AI automation: +125%
  • Vibe coding: +61%
  • AI voice agents: +49%

These are not press-one-button jobs.
You have to understand someone's business before you can automate it.

By category, AI-related demand grew fastest in content, not in back-end work.

Fiverr category Growth in demand for AI-related services
Video & Animation +278%
Programming & Tech +94%
Digital Marketing +62%
Data +3%

Video: AI makes more of it, people still edit it

Video is the biggest mover on Fiverr.

  • AI UGC video ads: +265%
  • AI video ads: +63%
  • YouTube automation faceless channels: +239% in Digital Marketing, +230% in Video & Animation
  • YouTube thumbnails: +52%
  • YouTube video promotion: +31%

Here is what most videos about AI side hustles skip.
Searches for human editing grew as well.

  • Video editing: +36%
  • Short-form video editing: +27%
  • Reels editing: +57%

Fiverr also compares platforms.
Instagram grew 147% in Digital Marketing and 149% in Graphics & Design.
TikTok grew 26% in Digital Marketing and 17% in Video & Animation.

AI makes more video.
Someone still has to make it good.

Seven AI side hustles, and what the reports say about each

These are the side hustles the video covers.
The numbers are the reports' own.
Neither report gives a dollar rate for any of them, so there are no dollar figures here.

AI side hustle What Upwork says What Fiverr says
AI content creation (images, text, content) Generative AI and creative production: contract starts +90%, earnings per contract -13%. AI-based execution tasks overall: earnings -28%. Not broken out
Your field plus AI AI-augmented professional services: volume +72%, earnings +22% Not broken out
AI orchestration (complex AI work) Earnings +45% for freelancers doing more complex work with AI Not broken out
AI automation with Claude Code or n8n Not broken out Claude Code specialists +938%. n8n AI automation +125%. Related: vibe coding +61%, AI voice agents +49%. Programming & Tech +94%.
AI video ads Not broken out AI UGC video ads +265%. AI video ads +63%. Video & Animation +278%.
Faceless YouTube channels Not broken out YouTube automation faceless channels +239% (Digital Marketing), +230% (Video & Animation). YouTube thumbnails +52%.
Human video editing Not broken out Video editing +36%. Short-form video editing +27%. Reels editing +57%.

One number covers all AI work on Upwork: 34% more per hour than work without AI.

The skills each one needs

The middle column uses the reports' own descriptions where they have one.

AI side hustle What the work is, in the reports' words What you need to bring
AI content creation "Producing discrete outputs, such as text, images, or video" (Upwork) A field you know, so the output turns into a result the buyer cannot get from one prompt
Your field plus AI "Domain experts integrate AI into established fields" (Upwork) Real experience in the field. The AI is the add-on.
AI orchestration "Understands business goals, selects and coordinates the right tools, manages AI agents and workflows, evaluates output quality" (Upwork) Judgment, communication, and accountability for the outcome
AI automation (Claude Code, n8n) Claude Code: "writing, testing, and deploying". n8n: "connects apps and AI models into automated workflows" (Fiverr) Understanding the client's workflow before you automate it
AI video ads AI UGC video ads and AI video ads (Fiverr) Knowing what makes an ad work for the client's product
Faceless YouTube channels Fiverr reads the growth as "optimizing distribution and packaging, not just production" Packaging: titles, thumbnails, promotion
Human video editing Video editing, short-form video editing, Reels editing (Fiverr) Editing judgment. The part AI does not do for you.

What I see in my own company

I see this every day.
AI makes twelve videos a day for my company.
Every one of them goes through review before it goes out.

The making got cheap.
The judging did not.
That is where the value moved.

How to pick

This is how I would think about it.

  • One. Start from a field you already know. Your job, your hobby, your industry.
  • Two. Sell the result, not the output. Not a hundred AI images. A product page that sells.
  • Three. If the buyer could do it with one prompt, do not build a side hustle on it.

Upwork's report says the same thing in its own words.
It tells freelancers to sell "business results rather than AI-generated outputs".

The menus, as Upwork and Fiverr name them

Before the steps, here is where things are.
I took these from each company's own help center.

Fiverr: creating a Gig

  • Go to My Business > Gigs > Create a New Gig, or click your profile picture and select Create a New Gig.
  • Gig creation is only available on desktop.
  • The steps are Overview, Scope & pricing, Description & FAQ, Requirements, Gallery and Publish.
  • The title starts with "I will...".
  • You can offer up to three packages: Basic, Standard and Premium. Each has a delivery time, a revision count and a price in USD.
  • The description can be up to 1,200 characters.
  • You must upload at least one image, and can add up to three. Use images you own.
  • New freelancers can have up to 4 Gigs active at once.
  • Before you publish, Fiverr asks for identity and tax information.

Upwork: creating a project in Project Catalog

  • Go to Find Work and choose Your services, then choose the green Create Project button.
  • Add a title, a category, and up to five search tags.
  • Offer up to three tiers: Starter, Standard and Advanced. Prices can range from $5 USD to $500,000 USD.
  • Add a gallery, client requirements, a project summary, project steps and FAQs.
  • Submit it. It goes to Under Review first.
  • You can have up to 20 projects in Project Catalog at a time.

Upwork: sending a proposal to a job post

  • On the job post page, select Apply now.
  • Set your terms, estimate how long it will take, and write your cover letter.
  • Submitting a proposal uses Connects.

How to start this week

None of these steps promise income.
They get you to a first offer in front of buyers.

AI content creation

  • Pick one field you already know. Not "AI images". Product pages for one kind of shop, for example.
  • Make three samples that show a result, not a raw output.
  • On Fiverr, create a Gig. Write the title as the result: "I will..." plus what the buyer gets.
  • In Requirements, ask for what you need to make it fit the buyer's business.
  • Before you publish, ask yourself the one-prompt question. If the buyer could get it alone, change the offer.

Your field plus AI

  • Write down the field you have worked in and one task in it that AI now speeds up for you.
  • Offer that task as a fixed result in Upwork's Project Catalog: Find Work, Your services, Create Project.
  • Use the Starter, Standard and Advanced tiers for three sizes of the same result.
  • In project steps, show where your own judgment comes in.

AI orchestration

  • Pick one business workflow you know from end to end.
  • Write it down as steps: which tool, who checks, what the output is for.
  • Upwork's report says to build evidence of impact: case studies, before-and-after workflow examples, measurable efficiency gains. Prepare one.
  • Send proposals to job posts where the client describes a business problem, not a tool.

AI automation with Claude Code or n8n

  • Automate one real workflow of your own first, so you have a working example.
  • Write it up as a before and after.
  • On Fiverr, create a Gig in the category that matches what you deliver.
  • On Upwork, create a project or apply to job posts.
  • Use Requirements to ask how the client's work runs today, before you build.

AI video ads

  • Make one sample ad for a product you could actually sell.
  • On Fiverr, create a Gig in the category that matches what you deliver.
  • Put the sample in the Gallery.
  • Use the three packages for length or number of versions.
  • In Requirements, ask for the product, the audience and the platform.

Faceless YouTube channels

  • Fiverr's numbers point at packaging and distribution, not just production.
  • So offer a part of the channel you can do well: thumbnails, titles, or edits.
  • Create a Gig in the category that matches what you deliver.
  • Show finished thumbnails or edits in the Gallery, not a description of the method.

Human video editing

  • Cut one short-form video from raw footage you own.
  • Create a Gig with that sample in the Gallery.
  • Say which platform the edit is for. Fiverr's numbers differ by platform.
  • On Upwork, apply to editing job posts with the same sample.

Checklist before you start

  • Pick one field you already know.
  • Write the result you sell in one sentence. It should not be "AI images" or "AI text".
  • Ask the one-prompt question: could the buyer get this alone?
  • Make samples from material you own. Fiverr's help center says to use images you own, with no copyrighted material or images sourced from the internet.
  • Prepare one case study or before-and-after example (Upwork's advice to freelancers).
  • Read Fiverr's Gig policies and Prohibited Services guidelines before you create a Gig.
  • Use a desktop browser for a Fiverr Gig. It cannot be created on mobile.
  • Have identity and tax details ready. Fiverr asks for them before you publish, and Upwork may ask you to confirm identifying information when you start a proposal.
  • Remember that Fiverr's numbers are search growth, not hires.
  • Check the dates. Both reports compare periods that ended in April 2026 (Fiverr) and Q1 2026 (Upwork's platform data).

What the numbers do not tell you

  • Fiverr's numbers are search growth, not hires.
  • Upwork's survey is about U.S. workers.
  • Upwork classifies AI jobs with an LLM-based pipeline, and says itself: "there is great uncertainty with measuring AI work."
  • Neither report gives dollar earnings for any side hustle.

But both reports point the same way.

And one more number from Upwork.
Skilled freelancers are now 38% of U.S. knowledge workers, up from 28% the year before.
58% of full-time employees say they are considering freelancing, up from 36%.

More people are coming.
The easy AI work will get more crowded, not less.

AI did not make side hustles easy.
It made judgment the thing people pay for.

Sources (official pages, read November 6, 2026):

  • Upwork, "Upwork's Future Workforce Index 2026" press release, July 14, 2026 (upwork.com/press)
  • Upwork Research Institute, "The Future Workforce Index 2026: AI, Freelancing, and the New Value of Work" (upwork.com/research/research-future-workforce-index-2026)
  • Fiverr, "Businesses Race to Hire Claude Code Specialists As Demand Surges 938%", GlobeNewswire, June 9, 2026
  • Fiverr Help Center, "Creating a Gig" (help.fiverr.com)
  • Upwork Help Center, "How to create a project in Project Catalog" and "How to submit a proposal on Upwork" (support.upwork.com)

title: AskDB: AI-written SQL and charts, without AI seeing your data
description:
People want to use AI to run reports on their databases. They also don't want to give AI access to their database. It's a Catch-22.

AskDB is an open-source TypeScript text-to-SQL toolkit: it turns a question into checked SQL for your app to run. The model sees your schema and the notes you write, never your data.

Today I'm announcing the release candidate for AskDB 1.0. The current build is 1.0.0-rc.3.

The whole flow in 41 seconds: watch the demo.

Where NL-to-SQL goes wrong

NL-to-SQL is an old problem. Systems that answer English questions from a database go back to BASEBALL (1961)1 and LUNAR (1971)2. Studies of large language models such as OpenAI's Codex writing SQL go back to early 20223. So the problem is not new.

The problem now isn't generating plausible SQL. It's conveying all the business context, terms and lingo consistently, so the AI generates SQL that's correct, not just plausible. It's in what the schema doesn't say, and in what the LLM assumes or hallucinates.

For example: a model that sees orders.total_amount integer doesn't know the amount is stored in cents. It doesn't know that when your finance team says "sales" they mean paid orders, not every order. Those facts live in people's heads, or have to be explained to the model every time someone asks a question.

What you want is to write those nuances down once, as notes on the schema, keep them in version control where you can keep improving them, and have them reach the model the same way on every question. That's what AskDB does.

What that looks like

Here's a snippet of a schema from the repo's test fixtures. The orders table has no sales column. "Sales" is a business word, defined in the schema's Markdown. Here's part of tables/orders.md:

---
id: table:public.orders
name: orders
...
columns:
  - id: table:public.orders#total_amount
    aliases: [revenue, sale_amount]
    description: Stored in cents. Use `total_amount / 100.0` for dollar values.
  ...
---

## Common query language

- "sales" usually means paid orders (`status = 'paid'`)
- "revenue" usually means `sum(total_amount)` where `status = 'paid'`

The question is "How much did we make in sales, in dollars?" This is the schema part of the prompt AskDB built for it:

The prompt as text 
Database schema:
TABLE public.users -- aliases: accounts, members
-- Registered user accounts. One row per signed-up user.
  - id uuid (PK NOT NULL) -- aliases: user_id
  - email text (NOT NULL) (sensitive)
  - created_at timestamptz (NOT NULL) -- aliases: signup_date, registered_at; When the user account was created.
-- common query language --
-- - "users" and "members" refer to this table
-- - "new users" usually means accounts created in the selected date range
-- - "active users" typically means users who placed at least one order
-- business context --
-- Each user has a unique email address used for login. The `email` column is sensitive — filter on it only when necessary and never display it in group-by reports.

TABLE public.orders -- aliases: purchases, sales, transactions
-- Customer purchase orders. One row per submitted order.
  - id uuid (PK NOT NULL) -- aliases: order_id
  - user_id uuid (NOT NULL)
  - status text (NOT NULL) -- aliases: order_status; values: pending|paid|shipped|cancelled; Order lifecycle state. Most reporting filters on `paid`.
  - total_amount integer (NOT NULL) -- aliases: revenue, sale_amount; Stored in cents. Use `total_amount / 100.0` for dollar values.
  FK (user_id) -> public.users (id)
-- common query language --
-- - "sales" usually means paid orders (`status = 'paid'`)
-- - "revenue" usually means `sum(total_amount)` where `status = 'paid'`
-- - "new orders" usually means orders created in the selected date range
-- business context --
-- Orders move through `pending → paid → shipped` and may end in `cancelled`. The `total_amount` column is stored in cents.

-- concepts --
-- Customer; synonyms: user, client, buyer, account holder; links: public.users; A person who has signed up and placed at least one order.
-- Revenue; synonyms: sales, gross sales, top line; links: public.orders.total_amount; Sum of `orders.total_amount` where `status = 'paid'`, expressed in cents.

Question: How much did we make in sales, in dollars?

It isn't DDL or SQL. It's a condensed format of the tables and the notes written about them.

Everything the model needs is in that text: "sales" means paid, and amounts are in cents. Concepts that span more than one table, like the Revenue concept at the bottom, come from a second file, concepts.md.

The call is one function in @askdb/core:

import { ask, loadSchema } from "@askdb/core";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";

const result = await ask({
  question: "How much did we make in sales, in dollars?",
  schema: loadSchema("./schema"), // the schema artifact directory
  dialect: "postgres",
  model: openai("gpt-4o-mini"), // any Vercel AI SDK model object
});

With @askdb/core 1.0.0-rc.3 and OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini, it returned this (trimmed):

{
  "sql": "SELECT SUM(total_amount) / 100.0 AS sales_in_dollars\nFROM public.orders\nWHERE status = 'paid';",
  "verdict": {
    "outcome": "allow",
    "findings": []
  },
  "sensitiveGuardrail": {
    "passed": true,
    "references": []
  },
  "unboundSql": "SELECT SUM(total_amount) / 100.0 AS sales_in_dollars\nFROM public.orders\nWHERE status = $1;",
  "params": ["paid"]
}

The model divided by 100 and filtered on paid because the notes told it to. unboundSql and params are the same query with its values pulled out, ready for your driver to bind.

The verdict comes from AskDB's checks, which run on every SQL string before your code sees it.

The schema artifact

AskDB keeps what it knows about your database in one directory, the schema artifact. It has two layers.

The physical layer (schema.json): the tables, columns, types, keys and relationships. askdb introspect writes it by reading the database catalogs (information_schema, pg_catalog, sys.*, sqlite_master). Introspection collects no sample values.

The enrichment layer (the Markdown files): one file per table or concept you choose to describe, written by people. You can write those files by hand or in Studio (more on that below). Because it's all files, your data team reviews a change to "what sales means" in a pull request, and you can see line by line what the model will receive.

The physical layer is enough for SQL that runs. The enrichment layer is what makes it right for the business. Without the two notes above, the model could just as well have summed every order and reported cents as dollars: valid SQL, wrong answer.

When you ask a question, AskDB folds the two layers into the compact text you saw above and sends it to the model with your question. It holds back the notes on any sensitive table or column, and the example questions, which are there for retrieval.

A large schema is too big to send whole on every question. Past about 22 tables, or when the rendered schema routinely passes 8K tokens, turn on retrieval with @askdb/rag. It indexes the same artifact in a vector store and puts only the relevant slice into each prompt. @askdb/rag stays on 0.x at 1.0, so its API may still move.

ask() takes no database connection, so it never sees your rows or query results and can't send them. Introspection connects only at build time to read the catalogs. It sends nothing to a model. A value reaches the prompt only as text you wrote into the artifact, such as an enum list, or text the user typed in the question. Two caveats. Anything you write in the Markdown goes to the model verbatim. A label you pass in tenantScope.context, such as a customer's name, goes into the prompt as written too. And as you'd expect, retrieval adds a second provider: your embedding model receives every schema chunk when you build the index, and the question on each call.

Studio: enrich and test before you ship

You don't have to write the Markdown by hand. npx askdb studio opens AskDB Studio, a local web app on your machine that reads and writes the schema artifact directly. It's where I'd start: describe a table, add its aliases and common query language, then ask a question in the Playground and read the SQL and its check results. If the SQL isn't what you expected, tighten the notes and ask again, without leaving the tab. That loop (enrich, ask, re-enrich) is how you get reliable SQL for the words your team uses, before any of it touches your application.

Studio can also draft descriptions and aliases with your model for you to confirm. For a draft, it sends the model the table's column definitions and the names of up to four linked tables. Running the Playground's SQL against your database is off by default; turning it on means giving Studio a read-only role. Studio is still on 0.x at 1.0, so its UI may change. The Studio tour walks through every view.

When retrieval leaves out a table

Retrieval puts a table in the prompt only when one of the chunks it returns points to that table. Writing this blog, I hit the failure that follows from that.

On a made-up 63-table SaaS schema, I asked "What's our monthly recurring revenue from active subscriptions?" Only subscriptions was described, with the rule for an active subscription. Retrieval returned chunks from subscriptions, usage_records and subscription_events. It didn't return plans, where the prices live. The model never saw a price, so it counted the active subscriptions and multiplied by 10. The answer was $20. The right answer was $38. The SQL was a valid read-only query, so every check passed.

The fix was two files:

  1. tables/plans.md gave the table a description, aliases such as "subscription plans" and a business-context line saying MRR is built from plans.monthly_price.
  2. concepts.md got a monthly recurring revenue concept that links subscriptions and plans; when retrieval returns a concept, AskDB puts every table it links into the prompt. After re-indexing, the concept and the plans notes ranked first, and three runs out of three joined plans and returned 38.

The lesson is the same one the checks teach: they test the query's shape, not its numbers. Test the questions your users ask. The tutorial Find the right tables in a large schema walks through this case with the real output.

Your app runs the SQL

The library, the CLI and the HTTP API return SQL and never execute it. Your application runs it under its own database role. The one exception is Studio's Playground Execute button, a local development tool that's off by default.

I made this choice because the database role you already trust to run queries should be what bounds generated SQL. AskDB doesn't host inference either: you bring the model and the key, and it doesn't proxy, log or cache the requests. Use one of @askdb/ai's built-in providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure, Vercel AI Gateway) or pass any Vercel AI SDK model object to ask(). @askdb/ai uses the Vercel AI SDK under the hood, so the choice is between passing in the model your app already uses and letting @askdb/ai build one from your AskDB config.

The three checks

AskDB runs three checks on the returned SQL before passing it back to you:

  1. The read-only check, on for every built-in dialect. It makes sure no data-changing statement (UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE and the like) comes back.
  2. The tenant check, on when the schema has a tenant-policy.md and the caller's scope isn't global.
  3. The sensitive check, on when something is marked sensitive.

To show refusals, I stubbed the model to return SQL I wrote. The errors below are AskDB's real output on rc.3.

DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';:

{
  "name": "SqlValidationError",
  "message": "SQL must start with SELECT or WITH (got 'delete').",
  "verdict": {
    "outcome": "deny",
    "findings": [
      {
        "check": "read-only",
        "form": "sql",
        "rule": "SQL_NOT_SELECT_OR_WITH",
        "message": "SQL must start with SELECT or WITH (got 'delete').",
        "hint": "Regenerate as a read-only SELECT (optionally with WITH). INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and procedural calls are blocked in dev guardrails."
      }
    ]
  }
}

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; DROP TABLE users; is refused with rule SQL_MULTI_STATEMENT.

With a tenant policy that scopes orders by agency_id, SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; throws TenantGuardrailError with rule MISSING_TENANT_PREDICATE: "Tenant-scoped table 'orders' is missing required tenant predicate. Expected one of: agency_id, …" Adding OR 1 = 1 next to a correct predicate gets the same refusal. When the predicate is there, AskDB binds the tenant ID as a driver parameter ($1) and returns it in tenantParams for your driver.

SELECT id, email FROM users; comes back with "outcome": "warn" and a SENSITIVE_COLUMN_REFERENCED finding. In strict mode it throws SensitiveReferenceError.

The database is the boundary

AskDB doesn't parse SQL. The checks are token- and pattern-based. They catch the common ways a model gets it wrong, and unusual or adversarial SQL can get past them. The database role your application uses is the boundary. The CLI's own --explain output says so:

"remediationNote": "Heuristic, lexer-based defense-in-depth checks only—not a SQL parser and not a security boundary. Execute generated SQL under a read-only database role, and review it before trusted execution."

Run generated SQL under a read-only, least-privilege role. Enforce tenant isolation in the database, for example with Postgres row-level security. Set statement timeouts and cap the rows you read. AskDB never adds a tenant filter, a row limit or a timeout to the SQL.

An experimental chart planner

@askdb/client/charts asks your model to plan a chart from the question, the query with its literal values masked, and the result's column names, column kinds (date, currency, category, measure…), row count and truncated flag. The model never sees the rows. If you keep sensitive columns out of prompts, pass that setting and the schema artifact to planChart(), and the model gets no SQL or column name that touches a sensitive column. It returns a chart spec, and your app draws the chart from its own data. A minor release of @askdb/client may change it; it's outside the 1.0 API freeze. The tutorial Chart your first answer adds a chart to the Quickstart's project.

Known limits

  • Little system-schema filtering. With a tenant policy, rc.3's tenant check refuses Postgres's planner-statistics relations (pg_stats and its relatives). Other queries against pg_catalog, information_schema or SQL Server's sys aren't rejected. - A call to one of your own functions that writes passes the checks, and so does an expensive join.
  • No protection from prompt injection. Anyone who can write the question or the schema Markdown can influence the SQL.
  • No protection from untrusted schema files. Whoever can write the schema directory changes what AskDB loads and what the model sees. Load schema files only from sources you trust.
  • MySQL's ANSI_QUOTES mode isn't supported. MySQL and MariaDB have no row-level security policies, and SQLite has no users or grants, so use a database per tenant there.

The 1.0 support claim covers five engine families: PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite and SQL Server. CockroachDB has a built-in dialect that reuses the Postgres spec, but it's outside the 1.0 claim: the end-to-end tests don't cover it.

AskDB is for engineers who embed it in a Node app, a CLI workflow or an HTTP service and own the schema, the keys and execution. Analysts use it through an app someone built on it. It doesn't guarantee business correctness: a person still reviews critical queries.

At 1.0, AskDB stops at the SQL behind a report. Reports and a first-party MCP server are planned for after 1.0. Until then, agents use the CLI and the HTTP API.

Try it

You need Node.js 22.23.4 or newer.

npm install --save-dev askdb
npx askdb init --yes --database sqlite --sqlite-file ./shop.db

The RC is on npm's latest tag, so a plain install gets it. If you're coming from a 0.x version, update the range in your package.json: a 0.x range won't match 1.0.0-rc.3.

The Quickstart goes from install to running the returned SQL on a small SQLite shop database. The code is at github.com/Ygilany/AskDB, Apache-2.0.

This is a release candidate, and I need people to try it before 1.0.0. Point it at your own schema, ask it the questions your team asks, and tell me what breaks. Issues, ideas and pull requests are all welcome; CONTRIBUTING.md has the setup.
