title: Dev News Digest: 18 Nov 2026, 18:00
description:
A quick roundup of developer news since the last digest.

Security

  • nginx2root: unauthenticated RCE in nginx's HTTP/2 code: Several research teams, including Xint and Wiz, independently found critical nginx flaws disclosed today in a coordinated F5 security release. The worst, CVE-2026-123007, affects every release from 1.9.5 (2015) through 1.31.8 with HTTP/2 enabled, and Xint chained it with a Linux kernel SCTP bug to get root on the host, even from inside a Docker container. Update to 1.31.9. Until you can, turning off HTTP/2 blocks two of the five nginx bugs but not the other three. Xint
  • Java4Shell follow-up: Cloudflare ships WAF rules: Cloudflare added six managed rules for paid plans that detect malformed Base64 linked to the OpenJDK decoder flaw. They only log by default, because some legitimate tokens look like exploit attempts. Cloudflare says a WAF cannot see every path to the bug, such as outbound TLS responses, so patching the Java runtime is still the only real fix. Cloudflare Blog
  • Windows 11 tracks which coding agents you run: A reverse-engineering write-up shows that a Windows diagnostics component checks for executables such as claude.exe, codex.exe, copilot.exe and cursor.exe, plus tools like python, node, gcc and dotnet, and reports their use through optional diagnostic data, which is on by default. If this concerns you, turn off optional diagnostic data in Windows settings. xusheng.dev

AI & tooling

  • Microsoft releases seven MAI models at Ignite: The lineup includes MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash for coding, a cybersecurity model, a realtime voice model and an image model. Microsoft pitches them on price rather than top benchmark scores, claiming near-frontier coding quality for a fraction of competitors' per-task cost, which matters for agents that run all day. Microsoft AI
  • Hugging Face hands inference routing to OpenRouter: Hugging Face's Inference Providers will now send requests through OpenRouter, which picks a provider by price, speed and reliability. If one provider fails, the request moves to another, so developers should see fewer failed calls to open-weight models. The New Stack
  • Google open-sources ABFS for huge Git repos: Android's Another Build File Service is a content-addressed filesystem and cache that loads source and build outputs only when they are needed. Google says Android checkouts dropped from about 36 minutes to under 8 seconds and full builds from about 80 minutes to around 2. The project is pitched at parallel workspaces for both developers and coding agents. Google Developers Blog

Engineering

  • LinkedIn tames Spark shuffle with Apache Celeborn: LinkedIn moved most Spark and Flink jobs onto Celeborn, a shared remote shuffle service. Daily shuffle fetch failures fell from about 750 to 20, compute costs dropped 10% and runtimes improved 14%. InfoQ
  • Booking.com's 20-year data and ML platform story: A talk on how Booking.com scaled MySQL, retired Hadoop for the cloud and built model serving and feature stores that now handle about 400 billion predictions a day, including the parts that went wrong. InfoQ

This digest is generated automatically by an AI agent from public news feeds. Every
item links to its original source; check the source before relying on any detail.

title: Beep: an open-source ADE that runs your coding agents across all your machines
description:
Most of us have more than one machine: a laptop, a build server, maybe a box with a GPU. Coding agents mostly ignore that. They run where you opened them, and moving work to another machine means pushing branches, copying files and starting the conversation again.

We built Beep to fix that for ourselves, and we just open-sourced it under MPL-2.0.

What it does

Syncs your projects between machines. Project files stay in step on every machine you link. The sync is compatible with Syncthing, so it works next to a setup you already have.

Connects machines peer to peer. Machines form an encrypted mesh over iroh. They talk to each other directly. A relay only helps when a direct connection is not possible, and traffic stays end to end encrypted.

Runs the agents you already pay for. Claude Code and Codex work with your existing subscriptions, next to OpenCode, Pi and our own harness, Flsh. You pick the machine for each task, and Beep shows your plan usage next to your work.

Gives you terminals everywhere. Persistent terminals on any machine in the mesh, from one window.

There is no account to create and none of our servers sits between your machines.

Why another ADE

The ones we tried had at least one of three problems: they were heavy (300 MB and up), they assumed a single machine, or they added a subscription on top of the ones we already had.

Beep has a Rust core and a Tauri UI. The download is 26 MB on macOS and 31 MB on Windows.

It started as a personal assistant. We dropped that part for now, because the multi-machine control panel was the thing we opened every day.

Try it

You can click through the real UI on sample data, in the browser, with nothing to install: beep.flashmind.com.

To run it for real:

  1. Download Beep and open it.
  2. Choose Set up all. It installs what is missing (Git, Claude Code, Codex) and signs you in.
  3. Use Add a machine to link your second machine.

Current limits

  • Desktop builds: Apple silicon Macs, Windows x64 and Linux x64. No Intel Mac build.
  • The Linux AppImage is 133 MB.
  • The phone app is still in testing. It pairs as an observer: it hosts no projects and runs no code.

Feedback

Issues and PRs are welcome on GitHub. We would most like to hear how the sync and the machine pairing work on your setup.

title: What AI Dev Planner Actually Builds: Web Development Services, and What Makes Them Different
description:
Most web development agencies sell you a website. AI Dev Planner sells you working software — a website, a web app, a SaaS platform, or an AI system — built to be used every day, owned by you, and able to grow without a rebuild.

Here is what that actually means, service by service.

1. Custom Web Development

Not a template with your logo on it. A custom website or web application built around how your customers actually use it — your workflow, your content, your calls to action.

Who it is for: a startup or growing business that has outgrown a template, or whose product cannot fit one.

What you get: a fast, mobile-first site or web app on a modern stack, including Next.js and React, designed to grow into a web app, a SaaS platform, or a customer portal later — not a site you have to rebuild when version two arrives.

2. SaaS Development

Multi-tenant SaaS platforms, from first release to scale: subscription billing, team management, role-based access, and the architecture that lets one codebase serve many customers safely.

Who it is for: founders building a subscription product, or a business turning an internal tool into a product others pay for.

What you get: multi-tenancy, billing, and access control from day one, not bolted on later. A typical SaaS MVP is $25,000–$65,000 over 8–12 weeks, scoped in writing before building starts.

3. MVP Development

A fixed-scope, production-grade first release — not a demo, not a six-month project that never ships.

Who it is for: a founder who needs to validate an idea with real users, or a team that needs to prove a product before committing a full budget.

What you get: a written scope that says what version one includes, what it deliberately leaves out, and what “done” looks like. Then a launchable product in weeks, not months, with a plan for what comes after launch.

4. AI Engineering

Custom AI applications, enterprise AI integration, and autonomous agents — built with guardrails first.

That means: connecting enterprise language models, vector search, and private retrieval (RAG) pipelines into your existing software and databases without rewrites; and deploying agents that can execute business workflows with tool-calling, execution guardrails, and human-in-the-loop approvals.

Who it is for: a business with real data and a real workflow to automate — not a company looking for an AI demo.

What you get: secure AI systems with clear limits, checked outputs, and a human where it counts. If an AI feature cannot be trusted with your customers’ data, AI Dev Planner will say so — or say “not yet.”

5. Mobile Applications

title: Import UX: Should Uncertain AI Rows Start Selected or Deselected?
description:
I used AI tools to help draft and edit this post. I checked the facts and the wording, and the original lives at geekindata.com. The diagrams are on that page.

Default-deny uncertain import rows

Key takeaways

  • Uncertain and incomplete AI import rows stay deselected until a human opts in.
  • Validity rules bind to the live section schema (visible columns), not a hard-coded spreadsheet layout.
  • Footer status separates selected count from valid-to-import count.
  • Unknown codes require explicit opt-in; never silent closest-master coercion.
  • Prompt field schema and UI selection policy version and ship together.
  • Import audit logs auto-eligibility, manual opt-in, and unknown acceptance.

Auto-selecting every AI-analyzed row feels helpful. It is how bad master data enters production with a smile. Users trust the model highlight. They click Import. Months later someone asks why an unknown code became a real record.

Treat AI import UX as governance. Default-deny uncertain rows. Bind validity to the live section. Separate selected from valid. Make unknown codes an explicit human act.

Named model: default-deny, section-aware

  • Section schema: eligibility reads the columns the active section actually shows, including conditional fields, using the same metadata that renders the form.
  • Default-deny: pre-check only rows that pass validity. Partials and unknowns start unchecked and need deliberate opt-in.
  • Dual footer: show selected and valid-to-import as two numbers so the policy is legible without a training deck.
  • Unknown opt-in: present unmatched codes as unknown; keep the row deselected until create or map is accepted under authority.
  • One surface: change extraction prompt fields and UI selection rules in the same change whenever possible.
  • Audit: log auto-eligible, manual opt-in, and unknown acceptance so stewards can reconstruct intent later.

Figure 1. Named model: default-deny, section-aware. Eligibility follows the live section. Uncertain rows stay unchecked. Selected and valid are two numbers. Opt-ins leave an audit trail.

Context and constraint

The pattern shows up in AI import flows where the model is decent and the selection policy is reckless. Complete rows mixed with partial guesses, all pre-checked. Operators imported at speed. Data stewards cleaned for quarters.

Section-aware import means the validity rules read the columns the user actually sees for that section, including conditional fields. Hard-coded layouts rot the first time the form changes. Deliberate opt-in for unknown codes beats silent coercion into "closest" master values.

Figure 2 is the Learn surface where the extraction contract is chosen. That field list must match what the UI can validate and display.

Figure 2. Import UX is governance. Selection policy and field validity belong with the live schema, not a default-select-all. Source: Microsoft Learn: create a document processing model.

Figure 3 is the document-type step. Who may import, and which rows count as valid, should be enforceable policy rather than a UI suggestion.

Figure 3. Who may import, and which rows count as valid, should be enforceable policy rather than a UI suggestion. Source: Microsoft Learn: create a document processing model.

Design

1. Default-deny uncertain and incomplete rows

Pre-select only rows that pass validity for the active section. Everything else starts unchecked. Make opt-in explicit for partials and unknown codes. Speed comes from confidence, not from selecting the whole page by default.

2. Validity follows the live section schema

If a section hides columns, do not require them. If it shows them, enforce them. Bind rules to the same metadata that renders the form. Spreadsheet-shaped assumptions belong in tests as fixtures, not as the only source of truth in code. Figure 4 is that binding drawn as two sections.

Figure 4. Section-aware eligibility. Require what is visible. Ignore what the section hides. Recompute when the user switches section. Cached rules from a prior layout are how you import rows that no longer meet the rules on screen.

3. Footer: selected versus valid to import

Show both numbers. "12 selected, 9 valid" teaches the policy without a training deck. Disable Import when selected includes invalids, or require a second confirmation that lists the exceptions. Pick one pattern and keep it stable. Figure 5 is the dual count made visible.

Figure 5. Selected versus valid to import. One number hides risk. Two numbers teach the policy. Unknown codes stay deselected until create or map is accepted under authority.

4. Unknown codes need deliberate opt-in

When AI proposes a code not in master data, do not coerce. Present it as unknown and keep the row deselected until the user accepts creating or mapping it under their authority. Silent coercion is how duplicate masters are born.

5. Prompt schema and UI policy ship together

The extraction prompt's fields must match what the UI can validate and display. If the prompt invents columns the section does not have, you get beautiful JSON and unusable rows. Change prompt and selection rules in one PR whenever possible.

6. Audit the import decision, not only the payload

Log which rows were auto-eligible, which were manually opted in, and which unknowns were accepted. Governance questions arrive later. Your log is the answer.

Section-aware rules in concrete terms

A section that shows attribute A and attribute B requires both before a row is auto-eligible. A section that hides attribute C must not block import for its absence. When the user switches section mid-session, recompute eligibility. Caching validity from a previous layout is how you import rows that no longer meet the rules on screen. Bind eligibility to what is visible now.

Pair AI confidence with human authority

Model confidence scores are inputs to eligibility, not replacements for policy. A high-confidence wrong code is still wrong. Combine confidence thresholds with schema validity and master-data membership. When those disagree, prefer deny and show why. Operators then spend attention on the ambiguous tail instead of rechecking rows the platform already trusts. That allocation is the governance win: human time on uncertainty, machine speed on the clear majority.

Why "helpful" defaults fail stewardship

Pre-checking every AI suggestion optimizes for the happy path in a demo script. Production imports are full of partial OCR, ambiguous codes, and sections with conditional required fields. Stewardship needs friction on uncertainty. The UI should make the safe path the fast path: confident rows import quickly; uncertain rows require a conscious click. That single inversion prevents months of master-data cleanup disguised as business as usual.

Train operators on why rows start unchecked. Without that one-minute explanation, people fight the defaults and reintroduce select-all habits through muscle memory. Governance UX only works when the policy is legible in the moment of import.

Common mistakes

Select all by default.
Fast import, slow regret.

Hard-coded column lists.
Form changes; validation lies.

One status number.
Users cannot see why Import is risky.

Closest-match coercion.
Wrong master, confident UI.

Prompt drift without UI update.
Extracted fields nobody validates.

No audit of opt-ins.
Stewards cannot reconstruct intent.

Use as-is or adapt

Use as-is

  • Uncertain and incomplete AI import rows default deselected.
  • Validity rules bind to live section schema and visible columns.
  • Footer separates selected count from valid-to-import count.
  • Unknown codes require explicit opt-in; no silent coercion.
  • Prompt field schema and UI selection policy version together.
  • Import audit includes eligibility, opt-in, and unknown acceptance.

Adapt before you use

Default-deny feels slower in demos. It is faster than master-data cleanup. Section-aware rules need metadata plumbing. The alternative is brittle layouts. Dual footer counts add a bit of UI complexity and remove ambiguity. Strict unknown handling requires a path to create or map codes; without that path users invent workarounds. Logging opt-ins has privacy and retention implications; define them.

Primary references: Microsoft Learn on AI Builder and document processing models, plus Power Apps forms and controls guidance. Pair with your master-data ownership rules so UX policy matches stewardship.

Default-deny uncertain rows. Bind validity to the live section. Separate selected from valid. Make unknown codes an explicit human act. That is how import UX protects the platform instead of flattering the demo.

title: Why I'm Building Backpacks
description:
Most of what we save, we never see again. I'm building an app to fix that.

It's not because we don't care. We save constantly. A recipe at midnight. A flight confirmation. A thread that finally explained the thing. A café someone recommended. A line from an article we wanted to remember forever. We screenshot it, share it, bookmark it, and tell ourselves we'll come back.

We don't.

Not because we forgot it mattered. Because we can't find it. It's screenshot number four thousand-something in Photos. It's in a "read later" list we haven't opened since we made it. It's in a folder we named on a good day and never named anything again.

When you can't find what you saved, you basically never saved it.

Every lost save is a small thing. A dinner you didn't cook. A trip you didn't plan. An idea you had once and had to have all over again. But small things add up. Most of us are walking around with a second brain we can't search.

So I asked myself a simple question. What if saving took one tap, and finding took one word?

No folders to keep up. No tags to invent. No account to make. You save from any app, the way you already do. And later you type whatever you remember, even one word that was inside a screenshot, and it's there.

That's Backpacks.

Share a link from any app and it's saved. Bring in your screenshots. Backpacks reads the text inside them on your iPhone, so "Lisbon" finds the flight booking, "wifi" finds the café password, and "pricing" finds the slide from that meeting.

Links, screenshots, images, files and notes all live in one library.

Sign in with Apple only if you want iCloud sync. Otherwise just open it and start.

I don't think the problem was ever that people save too much. I think the tools made us organise before they let us find.

Backpacks flips that. Save first. Think never. Find it when you need it.

I'm building it because I'm the person with thousands of screenshots and a bookmarks folder called "important" with nothing important in it. If that's you too, it's free on the App Store.

Here's to saving. Here's to finding. Here's to never losing the good stuff again.

— Aman

title: What 88 studies of LLM agents for production rarely report testing
description:
Originally published at cchinchilla.dev.

More and more papers on LLM agents talk about production. One agent triages incidents for a cloud provider, another automates a release decision. I wanted to know what those papers test before they make that claim.

So my coauthors and I ran a systematic review. Eighty-eight studies, read in full and coded twice.

The short version is that they report testing what a benchmark run can show. Take the things that matter once an agent has been running for a while (reliability over time, recovery from its own failures, monitoring, resistance to attacks). Each goes unreported in more than 88% of the studies, and all four together in 73%.

What we reviewed

The review is out in Information and Software Technology: Production-oriented evaluation and testing of LLM-based agents: A systematic literature review. It follows the Kitchenham–Charters guidelines for systematic reviews in software engineering and is reported against the PRISMA 2020 checklist.

We searched Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and the ACM Digital Library for work from 2023 to March 2026, then followed citations, and the 88 studies that made it through make up the review corpus. A later search, extended to September 2026, found 314 more. We kept those apart as an update sample with its own analysis.

"Production-oriented" needed a definition we could defend. Plenty of papers say real-world in the abstract and then run on a public benchmark, and if you take the abstract at its word you end up reviewing benchmark papers with a deployment story attached. So we built an instrument for it, the Real-World Relevance Signals (RWRS).

It has twelve signals of documented production evidence, among them real users, real data, deployment infrastructure, operational metrics and CI/CD integration. Twenty-three calibration rules say what doesn't count. A Docker container used to isolate an experiment isn't a production environment; an API bill mentioned as a limitation isn't a production challenge.

Every study needed at least two of the twelve signals to get in. Strong production evidence takes five or more, and at least one of them has to be real users, reliability or safety. Thirty-five of the 88 studies have it. How far each system got is a separate question. Forty-six are prototypes, 18 are pilots and 24 (27%) report production or large-scale deployment.

Four gaps, almost everywhere

Start with what the studies do test. We recorded which dimensions each study evaluates, meaning qualities such as task completion, latency or tool calling. The average study evaluates 2.85 of them. Accuracy benchmarking and end-to-end task completion dominate, the kind of thing you can measure offline with a script.

Then the gaps. For each study we also listed the dimensions that mattered for what it claimed but that it never reported evaluating, 4.98 on average. Every study in the review claims production relevance, so we held all 88 to the dimensions a running system needs, such as long-term reliability and failure recovery, prototypes included. Other dimensions depend on the system, and a small internal tool wouldn't be marked down for skipping cost at scale.

The four that lead the list are below, for the review corpus and the update sample.

Dimension Missing, review corpus (88) Missing, update sample (314)
Long-term reliability 98% 96%
Monitoring coverage 91% 86%
Failure recovery 90% 82%
Adversarial robustness 89% 87%
All four 73% 61%

The original post has an explorer for this table that doesn't survive being pasted into a feed: it splits the review corpus by deployment stage, production evidence and study quality, with a 95% confidence interval on each rate.

Each one is missing in most studies at every deployment stage, from prototype to production. All four are missing together in 73% of the studies (95% confidence interval 62–82%) and in 20 of the 24 production deployments. Long-term reliability goes unreported in every one of those 24.

Two objections are worth answering. The first is that the gaps only reflect weak papers. They don't: among the 56 studies we rated high or moderate quality, 70% still miss all four.

The second is that the field may have moved on since March. The 314 studies in the update sample are a broader mix, with more safety alignment work and more hierarchical agents. Each of the four dimensions is still missing in at least 82% of them, and all four together in 61%. That's lower than the 73% in the review corpus. The paper traces part of the difference to the extra safety alignment work, and the update's coding read adversarial robustness differently. Under that reading the review corpus misses all four in 67% of its studies, and the difference from the update is no longer significant. Within the update sample, studies published before and after March 2026 show similar rates (60% and 62%).

Testing more of what a benchmark can measure doesn't close the gaps either. Of the 63 studies that test both accuracy and end-to-end task completion, 49 leave out all four.

A single run can't assess most of what the four need: reliability over months, recovery from an injected failure, whether your monitoring would notice it, resistance to inputs crafted to mislead the agent. Most of it needs a system that keeps running and changing while you watch it.

Be fair to these teams, though. "Missing" means not reported. A team may well test things it never writes up, since papers have page limits, incident reviews rarely get published and nobody gets a citation for the regression suite that quietly caught a bad prompt change. The review corpus also leans recent and narrow. Of the 88 studies, 68% are from 2025 and 49% come from cloud operations and software engineering.

Any search misses studies, so we estimated how many ours missed. Measured against a broader Scopus search, our query found about 86% of the eligible studies whose main contribution is evaluation and 63% of all eligible ones. The studies it missed show the same gaps.

Automated, but outside the pipeline

The tooling to run evaluations automatically exists, and teams use it. Fifty-four of the 88 studies describe fully automated evaluation, and six of those wire it into CI/CD. The rest don't get past the script. Across the whole corpus, 8 studies (9%) implement or contribute a CI/CD pipeline, those six among them. In the update sample the share holds at 9%.

Monitoring lives in its own stack as well. Of the 23 studies with observability or full monitoring infrastructure, only two also wire evaluation into a CI/CD pipeline and only one tests the agent's reliability under load.

So in the studies, the evaluation suite runs before release and the dashboards run after it, and the review finds the two largely decoupled. The paper notes that existing approaches specialise in one mode, offline or deployed. It's the open loop from the Article 72 post.

Safety, and the one association that held throughout

Formal safety mechanisms (red-teaming, adversarial testing, compliance checks, prompt-injection defence) appear in 17 of the 64 prototype and pilot studies and in 2 of the 24 production deployments. That's 27% against 8%, so the deployed systems report fewer of them. The difference isn't statistically significant. I read it as a pattern worth watching.

The 35 studies with strong production evidence report guardrails that require human approval far more often than the other 53, 31% against 6% (Fisher's exact p = 0.002). We re-ran the comparison under ten RWRS variants. Some move the bar to four, six or seven signals, and others drop the signals that overlap the outcomes being compared, safety among them. Human approval stays significantly more frequent under every one (p ≤ 0.03). The difference also shows in the update sample (p = 0.006) and survives adding the 12 eligible studies from a sample of the broader Scopus search (p = 0.001).

Where the documented production evidence is strongest, studies report a person signing off on risky actions more often. CI/CD shows up more in those studies too, significantly in the main comparison but in only three of the ten variants, and again in the update sample.

Multi-agent systems and untested protocol conformance

Multi-agent and hierarchical architectures make up 39% of the corpus. Only 12 of those 34 studies evaluate how the agents coordinate. I'd argue coordination is where a plausible answer from one agent turns into a wrong decision in the next.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent2Agent) now define contracts you could test against, such as message schemas, capability declarations and message ordering. Twelve of the 88 studies mention MCP or A2A, and none reports testing conformance to either protocol. One study in the update sample does evaluate MCP interoperability against a contract.

An LLM judge is one more model whose output something downstream trusts. Only 5 of the 88 studies combine objective measurement, an LLM judge and human evaluation, and the paper lists calibration across the three as an open problem. That's the problem behind who calibrates the judge.

What to test before you ship

The paper turns its findings into a five-step checklist for teams preparing an agent for deployment. Here it is, with a note on each step.

  1. Document your production evidence. Go through the twelve RWRS signals (Table 2 of the paper) and write down which ones your evaluation covers. Real users or simulated ones? Production data or a benchmark?

  2. Test the four gaps explicitly. Long-term reliability, failure recovery, monitoring coverage and adversarial robustness each need their own tests. Start with the cheapest one, a failed tool call injected on purpose, and check that the agent recovers and that your monitoring notices.

    The original post has a self-check at this step: tick the RWRS signals your evaluation documents and the gaps it tests. It scores the production evidence the way the review did, from below the bar to strong, and names the gaps still untested.

  3. Put a quality gate in CI/CD. At least one gate that blocks promotion when a metric regresses. Eight studies in the corpus already run evaluation inside a CI/CD pipeline, despite non-deterministic outputs and the cost of running it on every commit.

  4. Add a formal safety mechanism, and human approval for high-risk capabilities. Red-teaming, prompt-injection defence or compliance checks. Of the practices the paper compares, human approval is the one most consistently tied to strong production evidence.

  5. Observe in production and feed it back. Logs, traces and alerting, plus periodic re-evaluation. When something drifts, turn it into a case in the offline suite.

If I had to pick one change from the review, I'd keep the evaluation suite running after release, inside the delivery pipeline, and let production write its next test.

The paper is open access at its DOI. The replication package, with the data, the extraction and a notebook with 595 automated checks, is on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0.
