I wanted to game while my AI agent ran tests — so I built it a cursor of its own

The problem

I run coding agents on my home PC in the evening. They are genuinely useful: while I play a game, an agent can run a test suite, click through a desktop app, and report back.

Except for one thing: the agent uses my mouse.

Screenshot-and-click computer use works by moving the one real system cursor and taking the foreground. That is fine when nobody is sitting at the PC. It is miserable when somebody is — mid-game, the cursor teleports, a window jumps to the front, and my input goes somewhere I never intended.

I didn't want a second PC, and I didn't want a VM. I wanted one machine where a human and an agent work at the same time, in different windows, without fighting over a single pointer.

The obvious options, and why each one failed me

1. SendInput / coordinate clicking (what most computer-use agents do)
There is exactly one system cursor. Any design that injects "real" mouse input is, by construction, a design that steals it. No scheduling trick fixes that; it's the wrong layer.

2. A VM or a second session
Isolation works, but it's heavy, and it changes the problem: the agent is no longer testing my apps in my session, with my files and my logged-in state. For some people that's the right answer. For "run tests on this PC while I use this PC," it wasn't mine.

3. MouseMux
MouseMux is a real, well-made product: multiple independent cursors on one Windows desktop, and it now even ships an MCP "Input Mapper" so an AI agent can get its own virtual user. If several humans share one PC — point of sale, trading desks, remote collaboration — stop reading and go buy it.

It didn't fit my case, for three reasons:

  • My "second user" is not a human with a second mouse. It's software. I don't need an input device layer; I need an input policy layer.
  • I want to be able to audit everything the agent can do. A closed binary that emulates the Windows input layer is hard to reason about — and on a gaming PC, "emulates the input layer" is exactly the shape anti-cheat systems are suspicious of.
  • I wanted a hard rule a product can't promise me: the agent never moves the real cursor. Ever. If it can't act without doing so, it refuses.

4. Virtual HID drivers (FakerInput and friends)
Same anti-cheat problem, worse: now there's a kernel-adjacent input driver on a machine that runs games with strict anti-cheat. I wasn't willing to install that on my gaming PC.

The insight

Here's the thing I got wrong at first: I assumed an agent needs to click, the way a human clicks.

Most Windows applications don't actually require that. Native controls accept window messages (BM_CLICK, EM_* and friends). Modern frameworks expose UI Automation patterns — Invoke, Value, Selection and so on. Both work in the background, on a window that is not in the foreground, without moving the pointer at all.

And for the controls that accept neither? The honest answer is not "fall back to the real mouse." The honest answer is "this one, I can't do." A refusal is a feature: it keeps the guarantee intact, and it keeps the human's session untouched.

What I built (overview)

A small, driverless, user-mode tool — one executable, no network calls — that gives an agent its own way to act:

  • Order of attempts, always the same: window messages first, then UI Automation patterns, then an explicit refusal. There is no code path that switches to real-cursor input.
  • One approved window. The agent can only act on a window a human has approved. Password fields and elevated (admin) windows are refused outright.
  • An Arm switch. The agent can act only while armed — a time-boxed state a human turns on from the tray. Disarmed means inert, no matter what any connected agent asks for. (In the current version, approval is one click to arm, and actions inside the armed window are pre-approved — which makes the Arm decision itself the safety-critical one, and I treat it that way.)
  • Read-back verification. After acting, the tool reads the resulting state and reports what actually happened — done, already done, unknown, or failed — instead of assuming a click landed.
  • A full log. Every action is recorded, because "the agent did something while I wasn't looking" is only acceptable if I can replay exactly what.

An earlier experiment is worth naming because it failed in an instructive way: synthetic pointer injection. Technically it worked. Practically, it moved the real cursor and stole the foreground — the exact bug I was trying to fix — so I threw it out. The most dangerous component in a design like this is the one that "works" by breaking your core guarantee.

About games and anti-cheat, explicitly

To be clear about what this is not: it is not a game automation tool, it never interacts with a game process, and my rule is that agent operation stays out of protected matches entirely — the tool is excluded from my gaming setup's resident startup, and I exit it before playing anything with strict anti-cheat.

The anti-cheat relevance runs the other direction: the design is boring on purpose. No driver, no virtual HID, no input injection, no process interference. Those absences are the feature.

When you should NOT build this

  • Several humans, one PC? Buy MouseMux.
  • You need a real security sandbox? Use a VM. A background-input tool in your own session is isolation of attention, not of trust.
  • Your apps are games, custom-drawn canvases, or anything that ignores window messages and exposes no accessibility tree? Background input will mostly fail, and failing honestly is all you'll get.
  • A headless browser or an API can do the job? Use that. Desktop automation is the last resort, not the first.

Build your own only if your constraints look like mine: one PC, one human who refuses to give up the mouse, agents that must act in real desktop apps, and a hard requirement that "no" is an acceptable answer from the tool.

What's next

In a follow-up I'll go through the failure catalogue in detail — the approaches above, what each one actually did when measured, and the acceptance checks I use to prove the real pointer never moved.

If you're evaluating MouseMux (or Anode, NexusWindows, agent-desktop, Cua Driver — this space got busy fast) for an agent use case, I'd genuinely like to hear where my decision tree diverges from yours.

Draft v1 — 2026-11-19. Personal project, built and run on my own hardware. No employer systems, data, or know-how involved.

title: OpenAI's Models Rewrote AMD's GPU Circuits — and Got 14% More Out of Them
description:
AI models writing code is old news. AI models redesigning the chips that run them is the new frontier — and OpenAI just published receipts. In a technical report released November 18, "Advancing chip design with OpenAI models," the company says its frontier models rewrote the circuit code of AMD's flagship GPU and improved power, performance, and area by up to 14%.

That is against a baseline AMD's own engineers had already tuned hard. OpenAI describes it as roughly a year of design progress in less than five months. And the changes are not sitting in a slide deck: AMD has already put some of them into a chip design sent for manufacturing, with the rest written into production design files for future products.

The models worked directly on SystemVerilog RTL, the code that describes a chip's actual logic. Each rewrite was checked with Synopsys electronic design automation tools to confirm the block still behaved exactly as specified, then measured on the three-way trade-off engineers call PPA: power, performance, and area. AMD also verified single-digit percentage PPA gains across key blocks of its next-generation flagship CPU using model-written designs.

OpenAI's own chip project tells the same story. The company began using GPT-4o to help design Jalapeño, its first custom inference chip, in early 2025. Model-proposed changes cut standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit — measured in real silicon. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area while cutting latency from two clock cycles to one. The chip went from initial design to tape-out in nine months.

Keep the caveats in mind. Fourteen percent is an "up to" figure on specific GPU IP, not a whole-chip gain. OpenAI named no AMD product, gave no breakdown between power, speed, and area, and reported no measurements from finished AMD silicon. All of it is vendor-reported, not independently reproduced. Still, a double-digit gain on an already optimized design is the kind of result that normally takes months of expert work.

OpenAI is now going further. It has partnered with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsys, a model that can use Synopsys's tools the way expert chip designers do. If the AMD results hold up in finished silicon, chip design may be one of the first fields where AI does expert-level engineering at scale — and the chips it designs will run the next generation of AI models.

Read the full story, with all the numbers and caveats, on Rohan Tech Official: https://rohantechofficial.com/tech-news/openai-ai-redesigned-amd-flagship-gpu/

title: Gemini 4 Neon Is Google's New Mid-Tier Model — Faster Than Carbon, Cheaper Too
description:
Google keeps shipping. Less than two months after the Gemini 4 family debuted, there is a fourth member: Gemini 4 Neon, announced November 18 by DeepMind's Koray Kavukcuoglu. It lands right between Carbon and Hydrogen, and it is aimed squarely at developers who want strong reasoning without the wait.

Carbon handles the hardest long-horizon work. Hydrogen is the fast, cheap everyday option. Neon takes the middle ground: high-frequency complex coding, analytical reasoning, and enterprise workflows. Google calls it "frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion," and the early numbers back up the positioning.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Neon scores 61 at its highest "xhigh" thinking level — third overall, behind GPT-6.2 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2, and a point ahead of Carbon. In coding, it scores 59 on the Coding Agent Index through Antigravity CLI, three points ahead of Carbon.

Speed is where it pulls away. Artificial Analysis measured roughly 110 output tokens per second, close to double Carbon's 57. A typical task runs about $6.44 versus $7.76 on Carbon, and finishes in around 21 minutes instead of 36. One wrinkle: Neon uses about 15% more output tokens per task, so the saving comes from cheaper tokens rather than fewer of them.

Pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15 — a 95% discount. That is 25% below Carbon's standard $4/$20 rate, and it matters from December 1, when Carbon's introductory $2/$10 pricing ends. From that date, Neon is cheaper per token than Carbon as well as faster. It carries a 1 million-token context window and four thinking levels (low, medium, high, xhigh) so teams can trade intelligence against cost.

There is no free tier. Neon is rolling out to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, where it replaces Argon in the model picker, and to developers through the Gemini API, AI Studio, and Antigravity. Google is also preparing a cybersecurity version aimed at finding vulnerabilities and fixing code.

For most developers, Neon looks like the practical pick of the family. Carbon stays the choice for the hardest single problems; Hydrogen stays the cheapest quick answer. Neon is the daily driver for repo-scale coding and long-running agent work.

Read the full breakdown — including the benchmark details and what changes on December 1 — on Rohan Tech Official: https://rohantechofficial.com/tech-news/google-gemini-4-neon/

title: Why Semantic HTML is Non-Negotiable in the AI Search Era
description:
When building a new website or shipping a feature page, it is tempting to wrap everything in <div> and <span> tags, style them with Tailwind or CSS Grid, and call it a day. Visually, the browser renders it identically.

To search engine crawlers and AI answer engines (like Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, and Perplexity), however, a page built entirely out of <div> soup is just an unstructured wall of text.

Semantic HTML uses HTML elements that explicitly describe the meaning and role of the content inside them-not just how it looks. In 2026, writing semantic markup is no longer just an accessibility best practice; it is the foundation of Technical SEO and AI search visibility.

Why AI Engines & Search Crawlers Depend on Semantic HTML

Search engines and Large Language Models (LLMs) don't "look" at your CSS layout, they parse the Document Object Model (DOM) to extract entities, relationships, and citable passages:

  1. Cleaner Content Chunking for RAG & LLMs: AI search engines rely on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to extract exact passages that answer user queries. Semantic boundaries (<article>, <section>, <aside>) tell parsers where core content begins and ends, preventing navigation menus or footer boilerplate from polluting your page's embeddings.
  2. Crawl Efficiency & Main Content Identification: Googlebot uses structural signals to distinguish primary content (<main>) from repetitive site-wide elements (<header>, <nav>, <footer>).
  3. Stronger Entity & Schema Alignment: Pairing native HTML5 landmarks with JSON-LD structured data reinforces entity context and reduces ambiguity for knowledge graphs.
  4. Built-in Accessibility (a11y): Screen readers rely on landmarks and heading hierarchies to navigate pages meaning every semantic improvement simultaneously boosts UX and SEO.

The Essential Semantic HTML Blueprint for Every Page

Whenever you scaffold a new page or component template, implement these core elements:

1. Document Landmarks (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <footer>)

Replace generic layout wrappers with structural landmarks:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
    <title>Page Title | Brand</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <header>
      <nav aria-label="Primary Navigation">
        <ul>
          <li><a href="/docs">Docs</a></li>
          <li><a href="/pricing">Pricing</a></li>
        </ul>
      </nav>
    </header>

    <main>
      <article>
        <header>
          <h1>Technical SEO for Developers</h1>
          <time datetime="2026-11-19">November 19, 2026</time>
        </header>

        <section>
          <h2>Why Semantic HTML Matters</h2>
          <p>Core explanatory content goes here...</p>
        </section>
      </article>

      <aside aria-label="Related Resources">
        <h2>Related Guides</h2>
      </aside>
    </main>

    <footer>
      <p>© 2026 Your Brand</p>
    </footer>
  </body>
</html>
  • Rule of thumb: Use only one <main> tag per page so crawlers and assistive technologies immediately know where the primary content lives.

2. Logical Heading Hierarchy (<h1> through <h6>)

Headings act as the table of contents for both Googlebot and AI summarization models.

  • Use one descriptive <h1> that aligns with your page's <title>.
  • Follow a strict sequential order (<h1> → <h2> → <h3>) without skipping levels just to get a smaller font size.
  • Never use <p class="text-3xl font-bold"> for section titles, and never use <h3> just for visual styling control appearance with CSS.

3. Self-Contained Content vs. Thematic Groups (<article> vs. <section>)

  • <article>: Use for standalone, syndicatable content that makes sense on its own such as a blog post, product card, documentation entry, or user comment.
  • <section>: Use to group thematically related content inside a page or article, ideally paired with its own heading (<h2> or <h3>).

4. Rich Media & Data Context (<figure>, <figcaption>, <table>)

  • Wrap diagrams, charts, and code output screenshots in <figure> with a descriptive <figcaption> and meaningful alt attribute so image search and multimodal AI models understand the visual context.
  • Use genuine <table>, <thead>, <tbody>, and <th> elements for comparative data, AI engines frequently extract structured HTML tables directly into featured snippets and comparison answers.

5. Crawlable Links & Interactive Controls (<a> vs. <button>)

  • Always use <a href="/valid-url"> for navigation. Search crawlers do not reliably follow <div onclick="..."> or <button> elements to discover internal pages.
  • Reserve <button> strictly for in-page actions (opening modals, submitting forms, toggling menus).

Pre-Ship Developer Checklist

Before merging your next PR, run through this quick audit:

  • [ ] Does the <html> tag declare a valid lang attribute (e.g., lang="en")?
  • [ ] Is primary page content wrapped in a single <main> landmark?
  • [ ] Is there a single <h1> followed by unbroken <h2> → <h3> nesting?
  • [ ] Are all internal links real <a href="..."> tags with descriptive anchor text?
  • [ ] Does the markup pass the W3C Markup Validation Service without structural errors?

Official Documentation & Authority Resources

For deeper implementation specs, bookmark these official references:

  • Google Search Central: Google Search Essentials (Technical Requirements & Best Practices)
  • Google Developer Documentation Style Guide: HTML and Semantic Tagging Guidelines
  • MDN Web Docs: Semantic HTML Curriculum & Reference
  • W3C Standards: W3C Markup Validation Service

How does your team enforce semantic markup in code reviews—do you use ESLint plugins like eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, Lighthouse CI, or manual PR checks? Drop your workflow in the comments!

title: Open-weight coding models had a big October. How a solo builder should decide whether to switch.
description:
October was a busy month for open coding models:

  • Reflection Beam 1.0: open weights, built for coding and agent work, 501B total / 23B active parameters, 1M context.
  • Recursive Flint: Apache 2.0, about 40B total / 2.5B active.
  • DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017): MIT weights, 1M context, with shorter outputs per DeepSeek.
  • MiniMax M3.1 Flash: agent and coding model, weights published.
  • Kimi K3.1 Pro: API now, full weights promised by early November.

Each launch post has a benchmark table where the new model wins. None of those tables used your codebase.

So here's how I'd decide, as one person paying the bill myself.

First: what are you actually optimising?

"Should I switch to open weights?" is really three different questions:

  1. Cost. Is my monthly bill a problem?
  2. Control. Do I need the code or data never to leave my machine, or a model that won't change under me?
  3. Quality. Is it actually better at my tasks?

Most solo builders are asking about cost and hoping for quality. Be honest about which one it is, because each has a different test.

The cost question is about tokens per finished task

The price per million tokens is the wrong number. What matters is cost per task that ends up merged.

A cheaper model that needs three tries, or writes twice as much, or needs you to fix its output, can easily cost more. Agent work makes this worse, because a weaker model takes more tool calls to get to the same place.

So measure: pick 10 real tasks from your backlog, run each model on them, and count tokens, turns, and whether you'd merge the result.

The control question has hidden costs

Running a 500B-parameter mixture-of-experts model yourself isn't a laptop job. Even with only 23B active, all the weights have to sit in memory somewhere. For most solo builders, "open weights" in practice means someone else's hosted API for an open model, which is good for price and choice, but it isn't privacy.

The models that actually run locally are the small ones. Flint's ~2.5B active parameters are the interesting part of that release.

The quality question needs your own tasks

Benchmarks tell you a model can code. They don't tell you whether it follows your rules: your stack, your "NOT TypeORM", your ban on floats for money.

That's where project rule files matter more than the model. The same CLAUDE.md-style instructions given to two models show you quickly which one actually listens.

What I'd do this week

  1. Keep your main model for the hard, design-heavy work.
  2. Try an open model on the high-volume, low-risk jobs: renames, test scaffolding, doc updates, lint fixes.
  3. Measure cost per merged task for a week.
  4. Move work across only where the numbers say so.

What I'd tell you before you start

Open models are now good enough that "should I switch?" is a real question. Answer it with your own backlog, not a launch post. The best setup is usually a mix: an expensive model where judgement matters, and a cheap one where it doesn't.

Release details: "AI Model Releases: October 2026 Tracker", Digital Applied. Check each model card before relying on a number here, as several were updated after launch.

title: How Music LLMs Actually Work: From Tokens to Waves (MusicGen, DiT, and Building Your Own Engine)
description:
Everyone thinks Suno is magic.

It’s not. It’s tokenizers + transformers + diffusion + a lot of audio engineering.

If you’ve ever asked:

• “How does an AI turn a text prompt into a 3-minute song?”

• “Why does MusicGen sound decent but Suno sounds produced?”

• “Can I build a music-gen backend that doesn’t melt my GPU?”

This post is the technical map. No hype. Just the pipeline.

  1. The Big Lie: “It Generates Audio”

Music generation models don’t generate raw waveforms directly.

Raw audio at 32kHz = ~32,000 samples per second.

One minute = ~1.9M timesteps. Attention over that? Good luck.

So the industry uses a 3-stage stack:

Text / Lyrics / Melody
↓
Condition Encoder (T5 / CLAP / LLM)
↓
Music “Brain” (Transformer LM or DiT)
↓
Neural Codec Tokens (EnCodec / RVQ / VQ)
↓
Decoder / Vocoder / VAE
↓
Waveform (wav / mp3)

Two dominant paradigms in 2026:

Paradigm Core idea Examples

Autoregressive LM Predict audio tokens like GPT predicts words MusicGen, ACE-Step, Suno (rumored)

Latent Diffusion / DiT Denoise in compressed latent space Stable Audio, AudioLDM, DiffRhythm

Most production systems are hybrid: LM plans structure, diffusion renders texture.

  1. Audio Tokenization: The Part Nobody Talks About

Before any “music model” exists, you need a codec.

Models like EnCodec compress 32kHz audio into:

  • 50 frames per second • 4 RVQ codebooks per frame

• Discrete token IDs
waveform ──EnCodec Encoder──▶ [frame][codebook_0, codebook_1, codebook_2, codebook_3]
50 tokens/sec × 4 layers

Why this matters:

• Reduces 32k samples/sec → 200 tokens/sec

• Lets you use Transformer attention

  • Keeps acoustic detail better than MIDI

But there’s a tradeoff:

• More codebooks = better audio, harder to predict

  • Fewer codebooks = easier LM, worse fidelity

That’s why newer models (StepAudio, ACE-Step) experiment with single-codebook VQ + diffusion decoder instead of naive RVQ.

  1. MusicGen: The Cleanest Reference Architecture

Meta’s MusicGen is still the best open teaching model.

Pipeline

  1. T5 encodes prompt → text embedding
  2. Transformer LM autoregressively predicts EnCodec tokens
  3. Delay pattern aligns 4 codebooks
  4. EnCodec decoder → 32kHz waveform

Minimal runnable example:

pip install audiocraft

from audiocraft.models import MusicGen
import torchaudio

model = MusicGen.get_pretrained('facebook/musicgen-small')
model.set_generation_params(duration=8, temperature=1.0, cfg_coef=3.0)

prompts = [
"lo-fi hip hop beat, warm keys, vinyl crackle, 85 BPM",
"epic orchestral buildup with taiko drums"
]

wav = model.generate(prompts) # list of [1, channels, samples]

for i, audio in enumerate(wav):
torchaudio.save(f"track_{i}.wav", audio.cpu(), 32000)

Key params:

• duration: 8–30s (longer = quality drop)

• cfg_coef: how tightly it follows text

  • temperature: creativity vs stability

Architecture intuition:

[T5 text emb] ──► Transformer LM ──► EnCodec token stream
│
delay pattern
│
EnCodec decoder
│
waveform

MusicGen proves one thing:

You don’t need end-to-end waveform modeling to get good music.

  1. The Diffusion Path: Stable Audio & DiT

Autoregressive models struggle with:

• long-form structure

  • global coherence • high-fidelity timbre

Diffusion fixes that.

Stable Audio / DiffRhythm style pipeline:

noise z_T
↓
DiT (Transformer denoiser)
conditioned on:

  • T5 text embedding
  • lyric phoneme embeddings
  • timestamp / section markers
  • BPM / chord grid ↓ z_0 (clean latent) ↓ VAE Decoder → waveform

Toy denoising loop:
import torch

def denoise_step(model, x, t, cond):
# model predicts noise; simplified update
pred_noise = model(x, t, cond)
return x - 0.5 * pred_noise

x = torch.randn(1, 64, 1024) # latent noise
for t in reversed(range(50)):
x = denoise_step(net, x, t, text_emb)
wave = vae_decoder(x)

Why DiT wins for music:

• parallel generation (not strict AR)

• better frequency stability

• easier to condition on time-stamped events (“chorus at 0:45”)

  1. How Suno/Udio Probably Work (Engineering Guess)

They don’t publish weights, but the leaks/behaviors tell us:

  1. LLM planner • receives prompt + lyrics

• outputs song structure: intro / verse / chorus / bridge

  • maybe ABC notation or chord CoT
  1. Token LM • generates coarse audio tokens

• controls melody + rhythm

  1. Diffusion renderer
    • refines timbre, reverb, vocal texture

  2. Vocal specialist
    • separate head for singing

  • pitch-constrained decoding (not normal TTS)
  1. Post-processing • loudness matching

• stem separation

  • watermarking (AudioSeal style)

So “Suno” is not one model.

It’s a music operating system.

  1. Controllability: The Real Hard Problem

Text-to-music is easy now.

“Make the snare hit harder in bar 16” is hard.

Useful control signals:

• Chord progression (Roman numeral or ABC)

• Melody chroma

• Reference audio clip

• Section timeline

• BPM / key / instrumentation mask

• Lyric timestamps

Example: MusicGen melody conditioning
model.set_generation_params(duration=10)
wav = model.generate_with_chroma(
descriptions=["ambient piano"],
melody_wav=reference_waveform,
melody_sample_rate=32000
)

JASCO-style systems go further: timed chords + drum grid + melody.

The future isn’t “better prompts”.

It’s structured music DSLs for LLMs.

  1. Building a Music-Gen Backend (Practical Stack)

If you want to ship this in an app:

Inference stack

FastAPI / Node gateway
↓
Task queue (Celery / Temporal)
↓
GPU worker:

  • MusicGen (fast drafts)
  • Stable Audio / ACE-Step (full songs)
  • Demucs (stem split)
  • FFmpeg (mastering) ↓ Object storage (S3/R2) ↓ Client player + waveform UI

VRAM budget

Model VRAM

MusicGen-small 4–6 GB

MusicGen-3.3B 16 GB+

Stable Audio 3 Medium 8–12 GB

ACE-Step XL 12–24 GB

Use:
• torch.compile

• chunked decoding

• KV-cache for AR

• FP16/BF16

• prewarm workers

  1. The 3 Bugs That Will Burn You

  2. Wrong sample rate

MusicGen = 32kHz.

Save as 16kHz → chipmunk audio.
torchaudio.save("out.wav", wav, sample_rate=32000) # NOT 16000

  1. Ignoring CFG scale

Too low → ignores prompt

Too high → robotic, overcompressed

Start: cfg_coef=2.5–3.5

  1. No watermarking

If you deploy publicly:

• add AudioSeal / WavMark

• log prompt + seed + model version

  • store raw output before mastering

Otherwise you’ll have legal + traceability issues fast.

  1. Evaluation: Don’t Trust “Sounds Cool”

Technical metrics:

• FAD (Fréchet Audio Distance)

• KL-PAANNs (semantic similarity)

• Chromagram accuracy (melody follow)

• Section consistency (intro vs chorus contrast)

• CLAP score (text-audio alignment)

Human metrics:

  • Does it loop naturally? • Would you put it in a game / reel / scene?

• Can you edit one instrument without regenerating the whole track?

  1. Where This Is Going (2026–2027)

• Symbolic + acoustic joint modeling

LLM writes chords → DiT renders audio
• Agentic music production

“Extend bridge, add strings, sidechain the kick”
• On-device music models

phone-local, <4GB VRAM
• Interactive DAW copilots

not “generate a song”, but “fix this mix”

  • Copyright-aware training licensed corpora + watermarking by default

Final Take

Music LLMs aren’t “AI composers”.

They’re:

Tokenizers + language models + diffusion decoders + audio DSP pipelines

Once you see the plumbing, the magic turns into engineering — and engineering is where you actually build something.

If you can make this pipeline run reliably, stream results, and let users edit stems — you’re not following the music AI trend. You’re building the studio.

clone + try locally

pip install audiocraft diffusers torchaudio demucs

Then stop prompting like a user.

Start architecting like a builder.

Suggested dev.to meta:

  • Title: How Music LLMs Actually Work: From Tokens to Waves
    • Tags: #ai #machinelearning #llm #tutorial #showdev #audio

  • Cover: dark background, waveform + transformer nodes + “Music = Tokens”

title: LibreChat com Ollama, LiteLLM e SearXNG: busca web no Docker Compose
description:
Um assistente com modelo local e busca na web

Uma pilha Docker Compose integra LibreChat, Ollama, LiteLLM, SearXNG e Firecrawl para criar um assistente de IA autohospedado. O LibreChat oferece a interface de conversa, o Ollama executa modelos no hardware do operador e o LiteLLM conecta os serviços por uma API compatível com a OpenAI.

O Firecrawl extrai o conteúdo das páginas encontradas, permitindo que o assistente combine informações recentes da web com respostas do modelo local. A infraestrutura de chat e extração fica sob administração do operador, mas o SearXNG encaminha as consultas aos mecanismos externos configurados, como Brave, Google e Bing.

O caminho de uma consulta

Apenas o Nginx fica exposto à rede. Ele recebe o tráfego HTTPS e o encaminha ao LibreChat, publicado na interface de loopback do servidor. Os demais contêineres se comunicam pela rede privada do Compose e são encontrados pelos nomes dos serviços.

Com a busca na web ativada, o LibreChat solicita resultados ao SearXNG, que distribui a consulta entre mecanismos como Brave, Google e Bing. Depois, o LibreChat envia ao Firecrawl os endereços encontrados; o serviço renderiza as páginas em um navegador Chromium sem interface e retorna o texto em Markdown.

O LibreChat passa o texto extraído e a pergunta ao LiteLLM, que encaminha a solicitação ao Ollama. MongoDB armazena contas e conversas, enquanto Meilisearch indexa o histórico para a busca na barra lateral. Esses dois serviços apoiam o chat, mas não participam do caminho da pesquisa na web.

Configurações para habilitar a busca

O SearXNG desativa a resposta em JSON por padrão, embora o LibreChat solicite resultados nesse formato. Sem habilitar JSON, a instância responde com o erro 403 Forbidden. O ajuste indicado no guia mantém HTML e acrescenta JSON à lista de formatos aceitos:

search:
safe_search: 1
formats:

  • html
  • json

O LibreChat também precisa de um raspador de páginas configurado. Sem ele, a interface pede que cada usuário informe uma chave de API e um endereço de serviço antes de iniciar a busca. O exemplo usa Firecrawl autohospedado e define rerankerType: "none", sem exigir chaves de serviços de reclassificação como Jina ou Cohere.

Para permitir conexões aos serviços da rede Docker sem desativar a proteção contra requisições forjadas a endereços internos, o guia lista os endereços permitidos sem esquema. O exemplo abaixo reúne os principais campos de busca e extração do librechat.yaml; as referências de ambiente são lidas pelo LibreChat a partir do arquivo .env.

webSearch:
searchProvider: "searxng"
searxngInstanceUrl: "${SEARXNG_INSTANCE_URL}"
scraperProvider: "firecrawl"
firecrawlApiKey: "${FIRECRAWL_API_KEY}"
firecrawlApiUrl: "${FIRECRAWL_API_URL}"
rerankerType: "none"
allowedAddresses:

  • "searxng:8080"
  • "firecrawl:3002"

O LibreChat bloqueia conexões de busca para endereços IP privados, de loopback e de link-local; por isso, os nomes dos serviços Docker precisam constar em allowedAddresses. A configuração também usa a versão de esquema 1.3.17 indicada pelo guia, pois versões antigas podem gerar avisos de configuração desatualizada.

Recursos e dimensionamento

Para reproduzir a instalação, são necessários um host Linux com Docker Engine e o plugin Compose, um domínio com registro A apontado para o servidor e as portas 80 e 443 acessíveis para o desafio HTTP-01 do Let’s Encrypt. O teste descrito foi feito no Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, com Docker 29.9.3 e Docker Compose 5.7.1.

Um servidor virtual com 8 GB de RAM apresentou falhas na fila de tarefas do Firecrawl quando a memória disponível caiu para menos de cerca de 1,9 GB. A migração para 16 GB resolveu o problema. No host de teste, com quatro vCPUs e um modelo de 0,5 bilhão de parâmetros carregado, o consumo total em repouso foi de 5,8 GiB.

O Firecrawl foi o serviço que mais consumiu memória em repouso, com 2,874 GiB. Um modelo de 7 ou 8 bilhões de parâmetros com quantização de 4 bits pode exigir mais 5 a 6 GB de RAM ou VRAM. Para uso em equipe, o guia sugere um host com GPU para o Ollama e de 16 a 32 GB de memória para os demais serviços.

Gateway de modelos e credenciais

O exemplo usa o modelo Qwen 2.5 de 0,5 bilhão de parâmetros, escolhido por funcionar em CPU e demonstrar a integração rapidamente. No LiteLLM, o nome público do modelo é qwen2.5-0.5b, e o prefixo ollama_chat/ direciona as solicitações ao endpoint de chat do Ollama na rede do Compose.

model_list:

  • model_name: qwen2.5-0.5b litellm_params: model: ollama_chat/qwen2.5:0.5b api_base: http://ollama:11434 general_settings: master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY

O LiteLLM centraliza um endpoint e uma chave para modelos locais ou hospedados, além de oferecer acompanhamento de gastos e alternativas de execução. Quem usa somente um modelo local pode conectar o LibreChat diretamente ao Ollama; chaves virtuais e limites individuais no LiteLLM exigem configurar o backend PostgreSQL.

O arquivo .env reúne 19 chaves no exemplo. O guia recomenda gerar valores aleatórios para os segredos, manter o prefixo sk- na chave mestra do LiteLLM e não alterar CREDS_KEY nem CREDS_IV depois que usuários começarem a salvar credenciais. Também orienta não carregar o arquivo inteiro no shell, pois o Bash trata UID como variável somente de leitura.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/guia-assistente-ia-autohospedado-librechat/

title: AWS launches SageMaker model leaderboard; IBM brings time-series models to Confluent
description:
AWS releases a standardized leaderboard for 70+ LLMs inside SageMaker Studio, while IBM and Confluent deploy time-series foundation models directly into streaming pipelines for real-time forecasting and anomaly detection.

Read the full article on Pneumetron →

AWS has released a standardized model comparison view directly inside Amazon SageMaker Studio. The new JumpStart Model Leaderboard ranks 70+ large language models from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee on reasoning benchmarks, inference speed, and estimated instance cost. The tool is designed to replace the current practice of stitching together benchmark scores and pricing from disparate model cards and third-party sites.

The leaderboard displays quality scores on three reasoning benchmarks—BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro—using evaluation harnesses and settings that AWS runs identically across every model. It pairs these scores with performance and cost metrics measured by sending a standardized test workload to a SageMaker endpoint deployed with each model's default configuration. Users can filter the list by license, provider, and modality, then select a use case profile and an optimization goal to view the specific deployment configuration that matches their workload. The interface uses a blue heatmap to highlight top performers in each column, and users can pin the model name column while scrolling through additional metrics.

AWS defines four optimization goals that dictate which configuration metrics appear in the table. Balanced shows the setup with the lowest estimated cost per token. Cost optimized targets the lowest hourly instance price, accepting higher latency. Latency optimized minimizes time to first token, while Throughput optimized maximizes tokens per second, often using speculative decoding. The performance metrics reported are time to first token, throughput per request, and instance cost. The cost figures are strictly SageMaker on-demand instance rates. AWS explicitly notes that these estimates exclude data transfer, storage, inference component costs, and discounts like Savings Plans or Reserved Instances.

To illustrate the trade-offs, the announcement provides an example for an internal help-desk assistant filtering for a commercially licensed model optimized for latency. The comparison shows how a larger model with a 95.9 score on BIG-Bench Hard and 87.2 on MMLU-Pro incurs a $37.66 hourly instance cost with a 2.33-second time to first token. A medium-sized alternative scores 94.2 and 84.9 respectively, drops the cost to $5.75 per hour, and halves the latency to 0.98 seconds. A smaller model further reduces latency to 0.27 seconds and cost to $2.61 per hour, but the reasoning scores drop into the high 70s and low 60s.


Illustrative image: blickpixel / Pixabay

Model BBH MMLU-Pro TTFT (s) Throughput (tokens/s) Instance cost ($/hr)
Model A (large) 95.9 87.2 2.33 37 $37.66
Model B (medium) 94.2 84.9 0.98 44 $5.75
Model C (small) 77.4 66.1 0.27 61 $2.61

The methodology aims to solve the comparability problem inherent in published benchmark scores. Different teams often use different prompts, generation settings, and hardware, making direct comparisons unreliable. AWS runs each benchmark with the same evaluation harness and settings across all models. Performance and cost come from sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint deployed with each JumpStart configuration, the exact configurations users can launch. AWS advises treating small score differences as ties, since they often fall within normal run-to-run variation. Teams should use the leaderboard to build a shortlist, then validate top candidates on their own data and prompts before production deployment.

At launch, the leaderboard covers LLM text generation. AWS plans to extend it to private hubs, other task types like object detection and text embeddings, and additional benchmarks as new models are added to JumpStart.

In a separate release, IBM and Confluent have integrated time-series foundation models directly into the Confluent data streaming platform. The integration brings IBM's time-series foundation models—part of a family that has accumulated over 50 million downloads—into Confluent Cloud and Confluent Platform. The models run natively as built-in functions within Apache Flink, allowing teams to apply forecasting and anomaly detection to streaming data without deploying separate GPU infrastructure. The models are designed to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, both in the cloud and on-premises.


Illustrative image: jarmoluk / Pixabay

Confluent describes the architecture as a "Streamhouse," a system that continuously captures, processes, and serves current business context. The platform brings together connect, stream, process, govern, and query capabilities to make current context available to applications, analytics, and agents. By invoking the time-series models inside Flink, data can be transformed and enriched as it flows, making predictions available to applications and agents in real time. The models provide a pretrained starting point that learns general patterns from diverse historical data, reducing the need to train a separate model for every individual time series. Depending on the task, teams can fine-tune the models or combine their outputs with other data and business logic.

The integration supports several specific model functions. AI_FORECAST generates demand or volume predictions with a P10–P90 confidence range, which can be refreshed as new observations arrive. AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES establishes an expected range for each series based on recent history, flagging readings that fall outside a chosen confidence level. PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume to help execution algorithms pace large orders, while TSPulse produces embeddings for similarity search across historical sensor patterns.

Organizations are using the models to automate operational decisions. In manufacturing, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry to forecast product quality hours ahead, allowing optimization processes to score control variable adjustments before they hit the production line. In retail and supply chain, the models forecast store-level demand to trigger automated purchase orders. Financial teams use the signals to compare individual card transactions against personalized spending ranges for fraud detection, or to forecast market volume for trade execution.

The models do not replace existing rules or specialized systems. Instead, they act as an intelligence layer that routes signals to operational applications, where business logic and human judgment make the final call. The integration requires setting up the Confluent streaming pipeline and configuring the Flink functions, but it removes the operational overhead of managing separate inference endpoints for time-series workloads.

Sources

  • aws.amazon.com: Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard | Amazon Web Services
  • huggingface.co: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Originally published on Pneumetron.

title: Building AI with AI
description:
In my previous posts, I've shared more about my AI workflows, extensions and tooling to help manage my administrative tasks at work. I've also explored how you can use AI to learn anything by getting it to build interactive guides and learning experiences.

This time, I want to share some lessons I've learned from building software with AI (coding agents) and also building AI-powered systems at work. Most of these insights come from hands-on experience building a few projects, primarily using Pi.dev and Cursor IDE, powered by OpenAI Codex and Cursor subscriptions.

Building with AI

First, let's talk about using AI coding agents to design and develop software. I build mostly web applications, so some these lessons may not apply to other types of software. Still, I think many of the principles are general enough to be useful regardless of what you're building.

1. Models are getting really good

Every few months, we get bigger and better models from the frontier labs. But things have moved and improved so much that even the smaller, open-weight models are now good enough for coding, especially for well-scoped problems and tasks.

Frontier models often feels smarter and better because they seem more capable of filling in the gaps when we don't provide enough details. They have stronger reasoning, broader knowledge and a better ability to infer intent, so it can sometimes feel like they are reading your mind. But if we are being honest, most of the time we haven't actually thought through what we want and are just glad they're able to fill in the gaps.

The danger here is that if we never thought about what we really want, the assumptions made by the models aren't necessarily correct and can take us down the wrong trajectory. Like a really smart person, they can provide really convincing justification for why their proposed solutions make sense. If we don't understand the domain well enough, we can easily be taken along for the ride.

2. Plans and research are useful up to a point

Most coding agents have a plan mode, which you should definitely leverage whenever possible. It helps you shape the problem and review the proposed solution before implementation.

You can also ask them to research alternative solutions and run experiments or spikes to validate assumptions, especially for changes that impact a large portion of your codebase.

However, remember that models are probabilistic and may not have all the required context, so plans and research can still miss things. The larger the scope you ask an agent to cover, the more opportunities there are for things to go wrong and the harder it becomes for you to comprehend and review the proposed changes.

I like to ask for diagrams, request flow or other visualizations to help me understand the proposed solution. Your input in scoping the problem, providing constraints and making strategic choices goes a long way towards building the right thing.

3. Treat the agent like a fellow developer

This may not be obvious to some of you, but I like to think of and talk to a coding agent as if it were another developer. Brief it as you would someone taking over a project from you and review its work by probing areas you think are important.

Give it as much context and background information as you can about the problem. Explain what you think the approach should be and discuss the trade-offs. Collaborate with the agent rather than viewing it simply as a machine that spits out code.

Recently I tried using Nico Bailon's pi-better extension, which rewrites your prompt using Felix Rieseberg's "Depth" prompt. It grounds the prompt in your existing code and files, giving the agent additional context that you might not have explicitly provided without expanding the scope of the task.

However, much like working with people, agents can sometimes become overly focused on a particular requirement and over-engineer a solution just to make sure it is satisfied. Even though you're collaborating with the agent, you're still the decision maker. You need to consciously play that role rather than delegate those decisions to it.

4. Don't trust the guardrails blindly

One of the best practices is to define an AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md instruction file containing coding guidelines, guardrails and dos & don'ts for your codebase. These instructions provide the agent with guidance on how it should work and what it should or shouldn't do.

However, models are non-deterministic. Giving the same prompt twice doesn't guarantee the same result. We shouldn't rely solely on these instructions to ensure compliance. Prefer actual code-based checks such as linters, type checkers and tests, wherever possible. Also, limit the agent's permission and access through your coding harness to prevent it from doing things it shouldn't.

Beware of reward hacking, particularly when asking agents to fix failing tests or change existing behavior. They might modify the test to make them pass or change a feature to match what the test expects, rather than addressing the underlying issue. Just because the tests are green doesn't mean the solution is correct.

5. Your eyes are still important

In the past, we tended to skip tests or not write enough of them. With coding agents, they will almost always write tests by default, and sometimes it can feel like they write too many. You may need to challenge them on whether all those tests are necessary.

As agents get better at using computer and browsers, I find them very useful as manual QA testers. You can simply ask them to test the application and explore whether things are working as expected. Since they can also read the related code, the bug reports they produce can be valuable input for the coding agent to investigate and fix.

That said, nothing beats using the application yourself to discover problems and issues. You have a better understanding of how things should work and it's difficult for an agent to evaluate usability, visual consistency, interaction patterns and overall feel of an application.

Building AI-powered applications

Now, let's talk about some of the insights and lessons I've learned building AI-powered workflows and applications. These are based on actual projects I've worked on, but it's obviously not an exhaustive list. The lessons are also limited to the types of features and capabilities I've worked with.

1. Look at your RAG extraction and retrieval first

One of the most common types of AI-powered applications I've worked on is a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system where you can ask an AI agent to search through a corpus of documents or knowledge base and return relevant information.

Naturally, the accuracy of the results is critical. It's worth starting at the ingestion stage and checking whether information is being extracted from the source documents properly. You can't retrieve information that wasn't captured in the first place.

Extracting text is generally more reliable than extracting information from diagrams, graphs and other visual content. Some services can convert these into text descriptions, making the information easier to chunk and retrieve. Don't overlook metadata such as document structure, page numbers and annotations either. These can provide useful context during retrieval and help trace information back to its source.

Next, review your retrieval strategies and algorithms before tweaking your agent's prompt or switching to a better model. Don't assume your RAG accuracy problem is an LLM problem. First, verify that you have extracted the right information and that your retrieval process is actually finding it.

2. You don't always need an LLM

In many agentic workflows, people have a tendency to rely too much on LLMs for things that deterministic code could perform much better and more reliably. LLMs are smart and can handle irregular inputs, but they're also much slower and more expensive than a few simple if statements.

Here are some examples of things you should generally avoid using LLMs for: calculations, enforcing business rules or permissions, validating data against a fixed set of requirements and orchestrating a predefined sequence of workflows. These are tasks where the expected behavior is known and can be expressed clearly in code.

Reserve LLMs for situations where you actually need reasoning or where interpreting the input isn't straightforward. For example, understanding a user's intent, extracting information from unstructured content or deciding which workflow should handle a request.

Even then, you don't always need the most capable reasoning model. System 1 Models or decision models such as TypeSafe Jev, OpenAI Decisions API and Gemini Decision 1 allow us to make fast probabilistic decisions within our workflows.

In fact, you can just ask your coding agent to review your workflow and identify which parts should be handled by deterministic code instead. It can even help you implement them. The key to building a robust agentic workflow is knowing where to use LLMs and just as importantly, where not to.

3. Enforce constraints outside the model

Just as you shouldn't blindly trust the guardrails set up around your coding agent, you should enforce and limit a model's capabilities through the harness or runtime it's operating in, rather than relying on prompts.

If you need to ensure a tool respects the user's access and permission levels, don't rely on the model to pass the correct user information to the tool. The tool itself should enforce those checks and constraints, using trusted identity and permission information that the model cannot manipulate.

Similarly, you can prompt your agent to always require human approval and implement a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approval process but the approval requirements need to be enforced by your harness, tools and runtime. The best way to prevent your model from doing something is to remove its ability to do it in the first place.

4. Understand your agentic primitives

It's important to have the right mental model of agents and how they work. By understanding the fundamental building blocks of an agentic system, you'll be able to combine them to create different types of agentic applications and workflows.

Here are some primitives to get you started. This space is evolving quickly, so make sure you keep up with the latest development.

Primitive What it represents
Model The underlying intelligence that interprets information, reasons and generates responses.
Instructions What the agent is supposed to do, including its role, objectives and behavioural constraints.
Tools What the agent can do, including interacting with external systems, retrieving information and executing actions.
Context Information available to the model when making decisions, including instructions, conversation history and retrieved information.
Session / State Information maintained during an interaction or task, including progress, intermediate results and execution state.
Memory Information retained for future use, such as user preferences, past experiences and accumulated knowledge.
Harness / Runtime The system that executes and manages the agent, including its environment, tool access and execution lifecycle.
Orchestration How multiple steps, workflows or agents are coordinated to accomplish a task.
Guardrails Controls around inputs, outputs and actions, including permissions, validation and human approval.

Use these primitives to build prototypes that emulate agentic products and workflows you see in the market. Design a deep research agent that can plan, conduct web searches across the internet and put together a report. Figure out how to build a Personal Agent like GrokBot, Instinct or Muse.

The best way to learn to build AI systems is to build one yourself, with the help of AI, of course.

5. Observe, evaluate and optimize your agents

When working with agentic systems, make sure you have some way to observe what's happening behind the scenes. Set up observability tools like MLflow to capture traces of your LLMs and tool executions. This allows you to see what exactly is sent to and returned from LLMs, which tools are executed and what results they produced.

These traces are invaluable when you are trying to figure out what's wrong or how to improve the performance, efficiency and latency of your system. You can even paste the full traces into your coding agent and ask it to help debug the issue. Agents can be quite persistent in trying to complete their tasks and their tool execution trajectories aren't always the most efficient in terms of token usage or number of tool calls.

You can also setup evaluations (Evals) to regularly check whether your agentic workflows are still behaving as expected as you tweak and update your system. They can help detect model drift and regressions as you improve your prompts, switch models and optimize your workflow.

Building in the age of AI

As AI agents continue to improve, they have greatly accelerated our ability to build software and complex systems. Things that used to take weeks can now be done in hours or even minutes. This changes the calculus of what's possible and opens up all sorts of new possibilities for us to explore.

But I've come to realize that we can only reliably move as fast as our mental models allow us to. When the agent executes faster than our understanding, we lose sight of the bigger picture. We may build something that works, but don't really understand how or why it works. Sometimes, we don't even know if it's what we intended to build.

Maybe as the models continue to improve and the tooling matures, many of these problems will become a thing of the past. Some of these insights and lessons may no longer be applicable by then. But I suspect that, as builders, we will always need to be clear on what we intend to build.

title: What Is a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise? A Guide for Leaders
description:
AI agents and people in one team, under one set of rules.

For the last two years, most companies have treated AI as a better tool. They gave people an assistant, tracked how often it was used and counted the hours saved.

That phase is ending. AI agents can now hold a role in a team, work inside the systems the team already uses and pass work back and forth with the people around them.

For leaders, the question has moved on from how much AI the company uses. They now have to decide which roles go to agents, which stay with people, and who answers for each decision.

This guide covers what a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise is, why it matters now and what it takes to build one. Each section links to a detailed article in this series.

The definition

A Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise is a company where AI agents and people work as one team, each with a job description, under one set of rules.

In this model, AI is a colleague, not a tool. People and agents are both hired into roles, both are accountable for what they do, and both record why they did it. That record stays with the company.

Any role can be held by an AI agent or a person, whether it is doing the work, making the decision or checking it. The mix changes from one process to the next, while the rules stay the same for everyone.

Why now: from assistant to teammate

In most companies today, AI is still an assistant. It drafts when asked and answers when prompted, and a person does the rest. Deloitte's State of AI in the Enterprise 2026 study, based on 3,235 business and IT leaders in 24 countries, found that only 23% of organisations use agentic AI even moderately. Most are still using AI to improve existing processes rather than to rethink how the business runs.

That is changing quickly. Gartner expects at least 15% of day to day work decisions to be made by AI agents on their own by 2028, up from none in 2024. It also expects a third of enterprise software applications to include agentic AI by 2028, up from less than 1% in 2024. Agents are arriving inside the software companies already pay for, as well as in the tools their own teams build.

Leaders expect this shift. In Deloitte's August 2026 survey of 501 US leaders, all at least piloting AI agents, 74% expect nearly half of their business processes to be redesigned around agents within four years. Yet only 15% have scaled agents across functions, and only 5% say their business processes are highly prepared. Most are adding agents on top of the way work already runs.

The same survey shows where the value lies. 75% of leaders say people and AI agents working together create more value than automation alone. Fewer than half, though, have defined how that collaboration works: which decisions agents can make, when people step in, who is accountable and how work is handed over.

Skipping that work is expensive. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027 because of rising costs, unclear business value or weak risk controls. Getting it right pays. A Gartner survey of 1,973 managers found that business units which redesign how work gets done, rather than only rolling out AI, are twice as likely to beat their revenue goals. (Detailed article: From AI Assistant to AI Teammate.)

The building blocks

A Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise rests on eight building blocks. Well run companies already manage people this way. The difference is that the same rules now apply to AI agents, in the same way and in the same place.

1. Roles for people and AI agents. Every member of the team, person or agent, has a job description: what it does, what it may decide, when it hands off, when it escalates and where its limits sit. An agent is hired into a role the same way a person is. (Detailed article: Hiring AI Into a Role.)

2. Decision rights. Every decision has one named owner, AI or person, and never "the system". Nobody, AI or person, checks their own work, so the maker and the checker are always different. (Detailed article: Who Decides, Who Does the Work, Who Checks.)

3. Earned autonomy. At first, a person or a second agent checks every task an agent completes. As the record shows the agent getting things right, its authority widens one task at a time, and when the record shows mistakes, it narrows again. The agent's own track record decides how far its authority goes. (Detailed article: Earned Autonomy.)

4. Work that moves both ways. Work passes from agents to people and back again, as it would in any good team. An agent might draft a reply that a person improves, or prepare an order that a person approves. High-risk or complex calls escalate to a named person, then to a manager, then to leadership. (Detailed article: Work That Moves Both Ways.)

5. Governance inside every task. A policy document is where governance starts. In a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise, the rules run inside every task and every decision, every day, for people and agents alike. (Detailed article: Governance That Runs Inside Every Task.)

6. Access and identity. Every agent has its own login and only the access its role needs: the systems it can use, what it can do in each and the data it can see. It never borrows the access of the person who set it up. (Detailed article: Access and Identity for AI Agents.)

7. Cost control. The cost of each task is estimated and capped before the work runs, and charged to a business budget, so leaders see AI spend before the invoice arrives. (Detailed article: Knowing the Cost Before the Work Runs.)

8. Enterprise memory. Every task, decision and handoff is recorded with its reason, from AI and people alike, and kept on the company's side. Over time, this becomes the company's memory of how it decides. It grows with every decision and stays when people leave or vendors change. (Detailed article: Enterprise Memory.)

One principle holds the eight together. Built agents, agents bought from SaaS or AI agent vendors, and people all follow one set of rules that the company owns. (Detailed articles: Bought, Built and People: One Set of Rules, and Measuring a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise.)

What it looks like on LeafCraft

LeafCraft already runs this way of working for companies in consumer electronics, AdTech and B2B SaaS. Their names are kept private here, but the work, the people involved and the results are real. Each story names the industry, the process and the use case, then explains what was going wrong, how agents and people now share the work, and what changed.

1. Consumer electronics: one AI across a phone and a pair of earbuds

Industry: consumer electronics. Process: product experience. Use case: one set of finance, health, career and lifestyle agents serving voice requests on AI earbuds and touch requests on a smartphone.

An Indian consumer electronics brand sells both smartphones and AI earbuds, and wanted AI built into both, so the devices could help people every day with their finances, health, career and lifestyle. That raised a hard design problem. People talk to their earbuds and tap on their phones, so the same help had to work through two very different inputs. Done the usual way, each device would have needed its own AI stack. A request started by voice on the earbuds would lose its context the moment the user picked up the phone. Voice commands could trigger actions with no check at all. And the brand's customers speak many Indian languages as well as English.

What LeafCraft did. LeafCraft gave the brand one platform for both devices. Here is how it helped under each of its five pillars.

  • AI and people as one team: LeafCraft's team built 10 agents for the brand, covering finance, health, career and lifestyle, and gave each one a clear role. When a user asks for something, by voice on the earbuds or in the app, LeafCraft sends the request to the agent whose job it is. Where an action needs a check, the agent waits for confirmation before it acts, so the user stays in charge of anything that changes their device.
  • Governance: Every agent has a job description and its own level of autonomy, set by the brand. Safe actions that are easy to undo can run on their own, and anything that changes the device or the user's data must pass a check first. This closed the risk of a voice command acting with no check at all.
  • Cost control: The cost of every request is known and capped before it runs, on both devices. The brand can grow usage without its AI bill growing out of sight.

What a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise is not

It is sometimes treated as a maturity score. One score can't describe a company that makes thousands of different decisions a day, so it is better judged one decision at a time: who leads, who does the work and who checks.

The number of AI tools a company runs doesn't measure it either. Agents with no named owner add up to sprawl.

It doesn't mean AI replacing people. AI and people sit on the same org chart in the same kinds of roles, and Gartner expects less than 1% of US jobs to be lost to AI through 2028.

No vendor can hand it to you. A vendor governs the agents inside its own product, while your rules, your cost limits and the record of your decisions need to stay with you.

What it means for each leader

CEO and managing director. AI pays back when the work itself is redesigned. Your part is choosing which processes go first and making the business own the result alongside IT.

CIO, CDAO and Chief AI Officer. Agents now arrive from SaaS vendors and from your own teams. One view of all of them, with the rules held on your side, is what lets you move from pilots to scale without losing control.

CFO and finance leaders. AI work should have a known cost before it runs, and a cap. Finance also needs maker and checker kept apart, and a record of every decision and its reason that auditors can open.

COO, supply chain and procurement. An agent that changes an order or a supplier commitment needs clear limits, a clean handoff and a fast route to a named person when something falls outside the rules.

Commercial, sales and revenue growth leaders. Pricing, schemes, claims and customer terms carry real money. Each of these decisions needs one named owner, and an agent's authority should grow only as its record earns it.

Risk, audit and compliance. After any incident, the first question is who approved it and why. The answer should come from a record kept on the company's side that nobody can change later.

CISO. Every agent is an identity. It needs its own login, the narrowest access its role allows, and that access removed the day the agent is retired.

Product and technology leaders at B2B software companies. Your customers will ask how the agents in your product are governed. Agents that fit inside a customer's own rules and record are becoming part of what you sell.

Where to start

There is no need to redesign the whole company at once. Start with one process.

  1. Name one senior owner for the rules, with the CIO, the business head and risk at the table.
  2. Pick one process and mark every role in it as a person or an AI agent, built or bought.
  3. Give every role a job description, a checker and an escalation path, and give every decision one named owner.
  4. Set access for each role, starting narrow.
  5. Set cost limits per role and per task before any work runs.
  6. Start the record on day one, with every task, decision and handoff and the reasons of AI and people.
  7. Widen authority when the record earns it, and narrow it when the record shows mistakes.
  8. Review the rules against the record on a fixed schedule.

Frequently asked questions

What is a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise?

A Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise is a company where AI agents and people work as one team. Each agent and each person has a job description, a named owner and clear rules. Any role in a process, whether doing the work, deciding or checking, can be held by an agent or a person, and work moves between them in both directions under one set of rules.

How is a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise different from giving everyone an AI assistant?

An AI assistant waits to be asked and helps one person work faster. In a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise, an agent owns part of the work inside a team. It has a role, an owner and limits, it hands work to people when a decision needs them, and people hand work back to it.

What are Hybrid Intelligent Teams?

Hybrid Intelligent Teams are teams in which AI agents and people hold roles side by side in the same process. In a bank's lending team, for example, an agent drafts the credit memo, the relationship manager adds what she saw at the customer's factory, the credit officer decides, and a separate agent checks that decision against lending policy.

Why does this matter now?

Agents can now do real work inside the systems teams already use, but most companies are adding them to old ways of working. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, and Deloitte found that most leaders are layering agents onto existing processes instead of redesigning how work gets done. Redesigning the team is what turns agents into results.

What are the building blocks of a Hybrid Intelligent Enterprise?

There are eight: roles for agents and people, clear rights over who does, decides and checks, earned autonomy, work that moves both ways, governance inside every task, access and identity for agents, cost control before work runs, and enterprise memory.

Can an AI agent check a person's work?

Yes. The rule is that no one checks their own work. Sometimes a person checks an agent, such as a senior developer approving a coding agent's pull request. Sometimes an agent checks a person, such as a policy agent reviewing a credit officer's decision before the sanction letter goes out.

What is earned autonomy for AI agents?

Earned autonomy means an agent starts with narrow limits and a person approving its work. As its record shows it getting things right, it is trusted with more. How much an agent may do on its own grows from evidence, and it can be narrowed again if the record changes.

What is enterprise memory?

Enterprise memory is the record of every decision made by agents and people, along with the reason behind it, kept by the company. It means knowledge stays when people move on, and agents can learn from how people resolved similar cases before.

How do you control the cost of AI agents?

Know and cap the cost of every task before it runs, agent by agent and process by process. That lets finance forecast AI spend and stops a single long running task from using up a month's budget.

Can agents bought from SaaS vendors and agents built in house work under the same rules?

They should. Agents that come with SaaS tools, agents bought from AI agent vendors and agents a company builds itself should all sit on one roster, next to the people they work with, under one set of rules for roles, approvals, cost and memory.

Where should a company start?

Start with one process that matters. Map who does, decides and checks each step, choose which roles go to agents, set the rules and approvals, cap the cost, and record every decision. Widen the agents' roles as their record builds, then move to the next process.

LeafCraft is a horizontal platform. It works as the AI infrastructure for hybrid intelligence, so it can help in any industry and in any process where AI agents and people work together. Industries LeafCraft supports today include:

  • FMCG and consumer goods
  • Consumer durables
  • Electronics and IoT
  • Paints and coatings
  • Liquor and beverages
  • Auto components
  • Chemicals and materials
  • B2B software
  • Banking, NBFCs and insurance
  • Global capability centres
  • Logistics and supply chain
  • Advertising and media

Whatever the industry or process, LeafCraft brings the same five pillars:

  • AI and people as one team: Agents and people hold roles side by side in the same process, and work moves between them in both directions.
  • Governance: Every agent and every person has a job description, a named owner, clear rules and approvals, and no one checks their own work.
  • Cost control: The cost of every task is known and capped before it runs, so AI spend can be forecast and limited.
  • One view: Every agent, built or bought, sits on one roster alongside the people it works with.
  • Enterprise memory: Every decision and the reason behind it is recorded and stays with the enterprise.

Sources
